en: Oṃ,
the first chapter of the Viśvāmitra-saṃhitā.

Salutation to the Unmanifest, the immeasurable, the cause of pure knowledge, the illustrious one, the abode of all that is auspicious, the Supreme Self, the Puruṣa. [1.1] In the Siddhāśrama, which removes all fatigue and is frequented by perfected beings and sages...
It was constantly made resonant by the sages chanting the traditional scriptures,
and it was filled with Vaikhānasas, Vālakhilyas, Phenapas, Ūṣmapas,
as well as sages who pound their food with stones and those who use their teeth as mortars.
[He was always served by waters filled with blossoming kahlāra, kumuda, and utpala lotuses;
by waters moonlit by bees emerging from blooming lotuses;
and by extremely cool waters full of food. 1.4.
It was beautifully adorned with lakes that dispel even the slightest fatigue,
and with *cūta*, *campaka*, *puṃnāga*, *nāgakesara*, and *kesara* trees;
with *tamāla*, *tāla*, *hintāla*, *kunda*, *āmalaka*, and *tinduka* trees.
With *kadamba*, *jambū*, *jambīra*, *vīraṇa*, and *udumbara* trees;
with *priyāla*, coconut palms, *vakula*, and *panasa* trees as well;
and likewise with hundreds of *kunda*, sandalwood, *mandāra*, and *devadāru* trees.

[The trees] were embraced on all sides by various lovely creepers— always bearing fruit, always flowering, and always adorned with young shoots— which bent down under the weight of their breasts in the form of flower clusters,
as if they were youthful women.
It was filled with bees that hovered about, greedy for the essence of the fragrance from clusters of full-blown flowers, appearing as if they were faltering while crying out;
and its interior was occupied by cuckoos whose sweet, charming warbling was enchanting.
It seemed to invite guests with the cries of intoxicated peacocks;
it was frequented on all sides by various flocks of birds, such as gallinules, bhringarajas, cuckoos, and krikaras. (1.11–1.12)
In the shade of cow-dung-smoothed grounds, the best of the twice-born sat comfortably;
some were experts in exposition, some were foremost reciters of the scriptures,
some were eloquent debaters, and others were knowers of the Purāṇas.
It was surrounded by various other trees— some knowledgeable in diverse sciences,

others presided over by the deities of the senses, some laden with sweet, ripe fruits, and others filling the quarters of the sky with the fragrance of their blossoms— and by many other such diverse trees.
[On the ground near the Āśrīkā trees, which are] constantly frequented by flocks of *kokila* birds and throngs of *kiṃnara*s singing songs that bring pleasure to the sense of hearing;
[in its interior, fragrant with musta grass, it is elevated by the musk-deer (*sauri*) released from the pits dug by boars. 1.16.
Its interior was darkened by young deer half-chewing the grass;
it was filled with cows whose udders were being sucked by tiger cubs;
and the crying of the children of sages was silenced by the affectionate bears.
In that place where clusters of drying grain were being seized by monkeys,
and which stood all around the sages who desired to climb the tall trees; and where elephants, out of curiosity, were engaged in the act of bending down the branches.
In that place where the doubt regarding the recitation of the Vedas was dispelled by the flocks of parrots spreading their songs,
and where the quarters of the sky were purified by the rising smoke of sacrificial fires,
he sat with his lotus feet being worshipped by the best of the twice-born.
He perceived the subtle meaning of every word of the Vedas and Vedāntas;
he was devoted to Sāṃkhya and Yoga, firmly established in all the scriptures, and blazing with ascetic fervor like another seeker of liberation. (1.22)
He possessed a powerful Brahminhood acquired through his own asceticism;
he maintained that purity which purifies all sacred fords and was one who had swiftly reached the further shore of the great ocean of the Pañcarātra.
His mass of matted hair was purified by the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of all his rites;
he was a knower of the specific nuances of worldly conduct and was devoted to the five daily observances (*pañcakāla*).
He was adorned with auspicious marks fashioned from white clay extracted from sacred bathing places (*puṇyatīrtha*).
His body was covered with twelve gentle vertical sectarian marks (ūrdhvapuṇḍra);
he was adorned with all five weapons held in the sky;
and though he was gentle, he was unassailable, being encircled by a halo of splendor.

Once, the best of sages named Kāśyapa approached the high-souled Viśvāmitra, the son of Gādhi, who was patient, self-controlled, sinless, and always compassionate toward the distressed, and whose wealth was his asceticism. || 1.28 ||
Having prostrated, he stood nearby with his joined palms placed upon his head. Then, seeing that the Brahmin had arrived— bowed low in humility— the Blessed Viśvāmitra spoke these words to him.
"O Brahmin Viśvāmitra, I hope you are well? I hope your asceticism prospers?
I hope your sacrifices are increasing and that they are being performed without interruption in your hermitage?"
I hope that no interruption occurs in your daily recitation at all times;
and I hope that the guests who come to your home, O Sage, are honored by you as is fitting. Tell me all this as I ask you.
"O Bhagavat, son of Kāyapa, all that you have asked is exactly so regarding me.
Since Your Honor thus bestows grace upon me, how could there be any inauspiciousness? (1.33)
Thus urged, Viśvāmitra sat down and said: "O child, descendant of Kaśyapa, you ought to tell me the true reason for your auspicious arrival."
Thus addressed by the sage, he sat with palms joined in reverence;
his mind overwhelmed by the force of Śuka’s speed, he spoke these words:
"O great sage, all the Vedas have been studied by me, along with their secret doctrines."

I have thoroughly studied, from beginning to middle to end, the treatises such as Mīmāṃsā and the Vedāntas according to their true meaning; yet, my mind is utterly bewildered by the examination of so many scriptures. (1.37)
There is no certainty in the mind that "this brings about the supreme good.
O ascetics, everyone nowadays says, "The Blessed One knows everything," for he is a great ocean of the nectar of Vedic knowledge. 1.38–1.39.
Therefore, having come here today with a desire to know the truth, [I ask]:
"O Blessed One! By what means do people like me—devoid of knowledge, with weary minds—cross over the ocean of existence? (1.40)
Be gracious; do not abandon me as I sit dejected in the presence of the king.
[Have compassion and grant me refuge at your lotus feet. Grant protection to people like me who are sinking in the shoreless ocean of saṃsāra.
Since you have enabled me to cross over by means of the raft of the knowledge of reality,
I therefore seek refuge in you today,
O Great Sage; tell me that means by which I may attain immortality.
When the son of Kāśyapa had ceased speaking after saying this much, the son of Godhī, being pleased, reflected for a moment and then said:
"Excellent, excellent, O highly wise one! My child Kāśyapa, you are very steadfast."
"That such a thought as this has arisen in you at so young an age—this was our greatest joy, O lady of most tranquil mind.
May your compassionate heart desire to grant us a reward. (1.46)
To you who are endowed with devotion and who fear the ocean of worldly existence,
I shall therefore speak, O child, that which brings about the supreme good.
This means was previously declared by Brahmā, desiring what is pleasing to me.
"O Sage, because of that former non-existence, I was greatly afraid.
Therefore, in order to quickly obtain the means for bringing about such cessation,
I thoroughly gratified the gods and the Brahmins with fierce asceticism."
Then the blessed Lord Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, being pleased,
out of compassion granted a vision of himself to him who desired to see him. Thereupon, his heart filled with joy, he joined his palms in reverence.
Prostrating like a staff upon the ground, I uttered this hymn of praise:
"Salutations to you, the creator of all worlds and that which dwells within them; salutations to you who protect by resorting to *sattva*, and who withdraw [the world] by resorting to *tamas*. (1.52)
Salutations to you, the Supreme Self, who is inconceivable and immeasurable. Salutations to you, the imperishable and changeless one, the destroyer of the suffering of devotees.
O Lord of the three worlds, composed of the three Vedas, pervading the universe—salutations to you!
Salutations to the Bountiful One who destroys the flood of sins;
salutations to the Bountiful One who makes the subtle even subtler and the unmanifest manifest. O Lord, you are more gross than the grossest unmanifest and subtler than the subtlest.
O Blessed One, whose body consists of ether, air, fire, water, and earth; O God, compassionate toward devotees, protect me by your grace!
You who are the inner self of all living beings, dwelling within their hearts. (1.56–1.57)
"O Lord, it is said that the elephant is always called 'Satya' (Truth).
Just as the earth produces all medicinal herbs at their proper time, so too do the sun and the moon divide [the world] by night and day. (1.58)
[Having fallen from their respective positions, the Yoga and Ātman-tantras have become exhausted.
|| 1.59 || And that wind which always breathes life into living beings, moving incessantly—O Lotus-seated One, this is done out of fear arising from you. || 1.60 ||
O Blessed One with golden hair and joined with a golden beard, those who are diseased indeed behold you as having the form of gold from your very nails;
O Lord of the life-breath of Sarasvatī, O one who pervades the universe, O remover of the suffering of people! || 161 ||
Victory to you, the inconceivable one composed of knowledge; victory to you, O Great Lord, who are the object of knowledge!

Victory to the cause of all, the cause of the very cause of sacrifice! Victory to the sovereign lord of the immortals of the universe; victory to you, who are to be known through the Vedas! 1.62–1.63.
To me, who was thus praising, bowing, and wretched,
the blessed Lord Brahmā, being pleased, spoke with a profound voice. (1.64) — Brahmā.
"Arise, O you of noble vows; I am pleased with you. Choose a boon.
Whatever you desire, I shall grant it; tell it to me.
Thus was I addressed by the Blessed Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest.
Having attained supreme joy, with my throat choked with tears, I made this request:
"If the Blessed One is well-pleased with me, who am so exceedingly devoted,
please tell me today the supreme means that brings about the highest good."
Having wandered over this entire earth for a long time, I have served many teachers; from them I obtained the fruits pertaining to the three aims of life.
Therefore, [I shall now cross] the ocean of saṃsāra, which is teeming with the crocodiles of sense-objects.
"Therefore, O Lord, I wish to be delivered from it; tell me the means for that.
O son of Gādhi, you of great wisdom, Brahmā, this virtuous thought has occurred to you."
In ancient times, the eternal Supreme Soul, Nārāyaṇa,
having assumed the form of a swan, slew all the Daityas in an instant; then the Lord,
having recovered the four Vedas from them, bestowed them upon Brahmā.
Then, having attained supreme joy and bowing to the God, the Teacher of the World, I addressed these words with my palms joined over my head:
"O Lord, the four Vedas were taken away from me by the Daityas; they have been restored to me by you."
I do not understand the meaning of these [Vedas] because of their complexity and their vast extent.
[Nor did it occur to me that they] bestow the fruit of Nirvana. Therefore, having condensed the meaning of the Vedas, which has Nirvana as its cause— || 1.74 ||
"Speak, O Lord, ocean of compassion, you who are affectionate toward your devotees!
Thus addressed by me, the divine Hari, the Lord of all worlds,
spoke with a voice deep as thunder and with a serene inner soul.
The illustrious Bhava said:
"O Brahmin, this is the supreme object of knowledge among all things to be known, which brings about the highest good;
it is the entire essence of the meaning of the Vedas and is most pleasing to me."
"I shall tell you the nectar known as the Pañcarātra; listen to me.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One then taught the entire Pañcarātra to Brahmā;
that I shall now declare to you.
Having spoken these words, the Self-Existent One, the purifier of the world,
respectfully imparted to me the knowledge known as the Pañcarātra.
Having given it, the Lotus-Seated One spoke this further statement:

"From this point forward, because you have spoken thus, O dear one, this Tantra on earth shall be known by your name as the *Viśvāmitrīya*. Having said this, the god Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, vanished.
From that time forward, that which is to be known has resided within my heart;
it remained hidden due to the non-appearance of a worthy recipient, but today you have arrived.
Now, O Kāśyapa, for one who is devoted and humble—
"I give that tantra to you; let it be taken to heart and attended to.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Introduction of the Tantra," in the *Viśvāmitra-saṃhitā*, a Great Upaniṣad within the *Pañcarātra*.
The Second Chapter. Kāśyapa said:
"O Blessed One, regarding that which was mentioned by you—that there exists a treatise called the Pañca—"
O Sage, what is the meaning of that word, and to what does it refer?
Of how many kinds is its form, and what is the extent of the treatise? Please tell me all this in brief and according to the truth. (2.1–2.2)
Viśvāmitra said: "O sage, listen; I shall declare that which I have been asked by you:
the five senses, the five objects of the senses, the five elements, and their qualities. (2.3)

Even the learned have declared that these [five] are denoted by the word "pañca. Furthermore, this verbal root *rā* is said to signify "taking" (*ādāna*). Thus, the five *rās* are those which take (*ādātṛ*) objects, sense-faculties, and the elements.
Because he protects human beings, it is remembered as the *Pañcarātra*.
The five systems, such as Sāṃkhya and Yoga, come into his presence;
for that reason, the meaning of the *Pañcarātra* is proclaimed by the most excellent of wise men.

Or else, O twice-born one, the meaning of the *Pañcarātra* is explained by the learned as follows: "Just as nights pass away in the presence of death, so too do all weapons perish in his presence. (2.7)
This scripture is proclaimed as being devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu, who is the object of knowledge of all the Vedāntas and the Lord of all gods;
it is the supreme means for achieving perfection for men submerged in the ocean of worldly existence.

The scripture of the Lord Viṣṇu, which has issued from the lotus-like mouth of the divine Vāsudeva— the Supreme Self, higher than the highest, the light beyond the beyond, whose nature is the supreme reality— [is this]. 2.10.
The meritorious nectar known as Pañcarātra destroys all sins. Just as Nārāyaṇa is remembered as the supreme among all gods,
so too is the Pañcarātra considered the highest among all scriptures.
Whoever worships Puruṣottama according to the ritual prescribed in the Pañcarātra, for him there shall be no worldly suffering; of this there is no doubt.
Having heard this from the mouth of Nārāyaṇa, [each] according to the full extent of his own intellectual capacity...
[Having understood that there is never any difference among the infinite teachers,] O son of Kaśyapa, although various differences exist therein in this world,
nevertheless, these tantras alone are indeed remembered as preeminent now. (2.14–2.15)
O Brahmin, O Sage, listen attentively as I describe some of them:
the Viṣṇusiddhānta, the Mātraya, the Paramā, the Viśvasaṃhitā,
the Sanatkumāra, the Satya, and also that which belongs to Viśvāmitra.
I have [studied] the Sāṃhya, the Jayā, the Sāttvata, the Pauṣkara, and the Puruṣottama;
likewise the Śrīpraśna, the Mahīpraśna, and the Māyāvaibhavika;
as well as the Māhendra-saṃhitā, the one called Pañcapraśna, and the Śrīkara.
The *Pahmodabhava*, the *Nāradīya*, the *Nalūbara*, the *Trailokyamohana-tantra*, the *Vāsiṣṭha*, and likewise the *Sanaka*;
the *Ahirbudhnya*, the *Cāndramasa*, and that known as the *Tattvasāgara*.
The Viṣvaksena, the Vihaṅgendra-saṃhitā, and likewise the Bhārgava;
the Pārameśvara, the Aupendra, the Mārīca, the Dakṣa-saṃhitā, the Śaunakīya, the Puṣṭitantra, and after that the Kapiñjala. || 2.20-21 ||
The Jaiminam, Vāmanam, Tantra, and the Brahmasiddhānta;
the Vaiyāsam, Hairaṇyam, Pārāśaryam, and Śāmbaram; the Vīramaṅgalikam, Prahlādam, and the Mūlasaṃhitā. || 2.22 ||
The Mārkaṇḍeya, the Mahālakṣmī-saṃhitā, and likewise the Kāpila;
the Brāhma, the one called Nārāyaṇa, and the Yājñavalkya, O Nṛkesarin; the Sāṃvarta, the Śrīkara, the Saura, the Saumya, and likewise the Bhāgavata. (2.23–2.24)
The Bārhaspatya, the Jāmadagnya, that which is designated as Yāmya, that which is known as Viṣṇusadbhāva, and also the Tejodraviṇa;
likewise, the Dhanadīya, the Kaumāra, and the Viṣṇuvaibhavika. || 2.25 ||
The Viṣṇupūrvahāsya and likewise the one known as Ānanda; the Hārīta, the Yogahṛdaya, and similarly the one called after Uśanas;
the Parapauruṣa, the Paulastya, and likewise the Gautama.
Also Śāklaya and Jābāla, and after that the opinion of Kātyāyana;
likewise the one known as Aupagāyana and the Vālmīki-saṃhitā;
then Bodhāyana, Agastya, Kāṣṇarya, and likewise Śātātapa.
The Bhāradvāja, the Paiṅgala, and likewise the Trailokyavijaya;
the Āgneya, the Vāruṇa, and the Aindra; the Brahmanāradasaṃhitā, the Umāmaheśvara, the Śukra, the one called Rudra, and the Pārṣasaṃhitā. (2.29–2.30)
The Śarvasaṃhitā [mentions] Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and the one named Nanda; likewise,
the Skandasaṃhitā [mentions] the son of Pracetas, Rāghava, and the one known as Kalki,
as well as the one named Mahāsanatkumāra and the one named Rudra.
The Vārāha, the one called Mihira, and likewise the Amṛtasaṃhitā—
O Sage, thus has the one hundred and eight Tantras been described.
He who understands these names of the Tantras is a partaker of liberation.

O Brahmin, the number of these texts, measuring one hundred crore verses, undergoes increase and decrease according to the succession of the ages (yugas). [Previously, it was declared by Brahmā to consist of ten thousand verses.]
Furthermore, O dear one, that [work] was composed by me out of dullness of intellect in five thousand [verses];
however, O son of Kaśyapa, observer of noble vows, I shall now explain it to you in brief for the sake of easy comprehension, measuring it at three thousand [verses].
Having heard this from the mouth of the Guru and having diligently obtained initiation,
one should perform all the rites beginning with the plowing of the ground and ending with the consecration (pratiṣṭhā).
In this world, together with sons, grandsons, and others, one shall enjoy all pleasures.
Having eaten at the end, one shall indeed attain the supreme, divine state of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Definition of Pañcarātra," in the *Viśvāmitra-saṃhitā*, a Great Upaniṣad within the *Pañcarātra*.
The Third Chapter:
Kāśyapa said: "O Sage, you have thus described the Guru; what are his characteristics as they are traditionally remembered?"
"What is his birth and what is his conduct? And what kind of person is a true disciple? Viśvāmitra. (3.1)
Listen, for I shall describe the supreme characteristics of a guru:

one born of a Brāhmaṇa father and a Brāhmaṇī mother, who has correctly mastered the Vedas along with their auxiliary branches (aṅgas), who has exerted himself in the science of grammar (śabdaśāstra), and who is many times purified in soul. (3.2)

He was proficient in the Nyāya-śāstra and expert in the Vaiśeṣika; he had reached the further shore of Mīmāṃsā and was firmly established in Sāṃkhya and Yoga. He was also highly skilled in astronomy, ritual manuals (kalpa), and phonetics (śīkṣā).
He was proficient in etymology, the science of meter, and likewise in the science of architecture;
he knew the essential truth of the meaning of all scriptures and was endowed with brilliant intuition. His mind rested in Vedānta, and he was an expert in the practical application of ritual acts.

He was proficient in the meaning of the Pañcarātra, devoted to the five-fold ritual cycle (pañcakāla), and a knower of the reality of creation and dissolution. He was a mine of compassion for the worlds, steady-minded, sweet-spoken, humble, and true to his word.
Free from envy, serene in soul, virtuous, eloquent,
with senses subdued, wise, and possessing the discernment between merit and demerit,
he is a knower of the specific qualities and defects of temples, images, and the like. (3.8)
Ever a protector, dwelling in purity, pure in appearance, and a refuge of auspiciousness;
free from attachment to faults, wise, always having conquered the senses, devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu, offering oblations, and the best among those who know the mantras. || 3.9–3.10 ||
The destroyer of all doubts, whose mind was most tranquil, seeing the Vaiṣṇavas who had arrived, rose from his seat and greeted them with salutations;
out of curiosity, he received them with worship, including the offering of water for the feet and other honors. (3.11)
With a mind focused on no other, constantly intent upon the worship of Viṣṇu,
devoted to the conduct of his religious observances, possessed of wisdom, eloquent, and dear to his guru—
he who eats only after the group of servants has eaten is esteemed by the virtuous. (3.12–3.13)
Averse to forbidden things and endowed with supreme faith,
he constantly bore the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* mark made of auspicious white clay;
and his body was marked in its proper places with the emblems of the conch, the discus, and other such signs.
One who possesses all limbs neither deficient nor redundant, who is adorned with ornaments,
endowed with the quality of beauty, and intent on pleasing the subjects—
he who is thus endowed with these characteristics is called an Ācārya. || 3.15–3.16 ||
I shall state the characteristics of disciples; listen to them with attention:

one born of the three [higher] castes, originating from a praiseworthy family, having mastered the Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs, constantly performing ablutions, and having conquered the senses. (17)
Endowed with learning and good conduct, truthful in speech, and devoted to recitation;
possessed of devotion toward the teacher, virtuous, and free from deceit;
ungreedy, sharing with others, grateful, and never deceiving the righteous. (3.18–3.19)
Content with his wife alone, devoted to listening to the scriptures,
examined for three, two, or even one year, O twice-born one,
he became serene in soul and endowed with devotion to Viṣṇu.
He should eat food that has not been kept overnight and avoid fickleness of tongue;
he should remain silent in the presence of his teacher and sit only upon the ground;
he should be intent on serving his mother and father and devoted to the performance of rites prescribed by the Śrutis and Smṛtis.
Behaving toward the wife and son of one's guru as toward the guru himself, being free from malice toward friends and avoiding association with those who are hateful,
turning away from prohibited conduct, and saluting the elders— 3.23.
Devoted to the service of the fire and tireless in the house of his guru,

he is a worshiper of the Vaiṣṇavas, possesses auspicious marks known through sacred knowledge, and always bears the vertical sectarian mark (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*) while constantly reciting the twelve names [of Viṣṇu]. (3.24–3.25)
One who wears excellent and radiant attire, is marked with the conch, discus, and other signs,

and is endowed with such qualities as these, is called a disciple of steady intellect. Women and Śūdras who follow the natural order of castes are likewise eligible if they are possessed of auspicious qualities.
If the Guru should, out of compassion, accept even them as disciples;
or if the Preceptor should be possessed of certain defects such as deafness and so forth—he must not be abandoned once he has been initiated into the maṇḍala. (3.27–3.28)
"One should bring that abundance of knowledge before him and transform defects into virtues.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Guru and the Disciple," in the *Viśvāmitra-saṃhitā*, the Great Upaniṣad of the *Pañcarātra*.
The Fourth Chapter. Kāśyapa said:
"O Guru, this tantra has been described by you as being for the sake of the Blessed One."
For what purpose is the word "Bhagavat," and of what nature is that Blessed One?
Viśvāmitra said: O best of sages, listen to my explanation of the word "Bhagavat."
Knowledge that is boundless, sovereignty that rests upon no other person;
power that surpasses all, as well as strength that is supreme among all; valor that cannot be taken away by others, and splendor that is ever-increasingly superior. (4.2–4.3)
These six, O Kāśyapa, are proclaimed by the word "Bhaga.
He in whom these qualities exist is called the Bhagavat.
[He is] single-tusked, two-armed, and resembles pure crystal.
Possessing a radiance equal to ten thousand moons, ten million suns, and ten billion fires,
he was difficult to behold due to his exceeding brilliance; he himself bore the conch and the discus,
wore the Kaustubha gem upon his chest, and was the abode of the beauty of the Śrīvatsa mark.
Always wearing yellow garments and adorned with a forest garland,
his body radiant with a crown, necklaces, armlets, and earrings—
such is the form of the Blessed One who is designated as Vāsudeva.
Those seeking liberation meditate upon that *yaṃ* situated in the center of the lotus of the heart.
From him, due to the inequality of the *guṇas*, there arose Saṃkarṣaṇa and the others;
[he was] Kāśyapa.
"O Brahman, it has been stated by you that Saṃkarṣaṇa and the others were born from the inequality of the qualities (guṇas); tell me that in detail. Thus spoke Viśvāmitra.
It was previously stated that the Blessed One [Vāsudeva] gives in three ways (4.10). There was another known as Vāsudeva, the cause of creation, maintenance, and destruction;
he had one face and four arms, and bore the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus (4.11).
Bearing the Śrīvatsa mark upon his chest and the brilliant Kaustubha gem, O Lord,
he likewise wore a divine, most enchanting garland of forest flowers;
gentle and clad in yellow garments, his complexion was like that of a peacock's neck.
By his own independent power, he divided himself into two forms.
Of those two Blessed Ones, one had the luster of pure crystal,
while the other, resembling a dark rain cloud, was called Nārāyaṇa.
From Vāsudeva was then born the one named Saṃkarṣaṇa;
from him arose Pradyumna, and from him Aniruddha came into being.
All of these possessed a single crown and were endowed with four arms.
Endowed with all the qualities of the sages and the castes, and equal to Vāsudeva,
he became known as Saṃkarṣaṇa due to his preeminence in knowledge;
Pradyumna, however, arose from his preeminence in strength and his preeminence in sovereignty.
All these, including Aniruddha, are endowed with their respective six qualities;
all of them have four arms and bear the weapons previously described.
From Vāsudeva, these three deities were first born.
And then, O best of the twice-born, there were four others of that same name;
these four arose in succession from the four [previous ones]:
Aśokṣaja, Nṛsiṃha, Vāmana, and Bhārgava. 4.19–4.20.
Janārdana, Upendra, Hari, and Kṛṣṇa by name— these eight forms arose from Vāsudeva, the God of gods. The first form is Brāhmī, then Prājāpatyā, and Vaiṣṇavī.
The divine, the ṛṣi-like, and the human are proclaimed as the first three;
the fourth is the āsuri, and the eighth is the paiśācī. O best of the twice-born, these eight forms have ten manifestations within the vyūha, beginning with Mīna, in their respective order.
From Vāsudeva were born Matya, Kūrma, and Varāha;
[from Acyuta, having become Acyuta, they were born from Vāsudeva].
There were also Babhru, Trailokyamoha, Dāśārha, and he known as Śauri.
O twice-born one, these five forms are named Annādhipati;
from Saṃkarṣaṇa come Hayagrīva, Śaṅkhodara, Nṛkesarī, the primordial Vaikuṇṭha-form, Mukunda, and Vṛṣākapi. (4.25–4.26)
And at that very moment, O twice-born one, Varāha, Ānanda, and the serpent-king were born; likewise, all the weapons,
beginning with the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, appeared simultaneously for all the forms.

Diadems, necklaces, armlets, and bracelets were produced; then Śrī and the other goddesses appeared, adorned with the divine mark of the Śrīvatsa. Furthermore, Garuḍa was born, manifested from the collection of [Viṣṇu’s] physical forms.
From Vāsudeva and the others, who are the embodiments of the Vedas, [the elephants] emerge in the form of their respective mounts:
Kumuda, Kumudākṣa, Puṇḍarīka, and Vāmana; Śaṅkukarṇa, Sarpanetra, Sumukha, and Supratiṣṭhita.
Praśrigarbha, Mānava, Śvaca, and these ten lords of beings (bhūtanātha),
together with all their attendants, became supported by Aniruddha.
He possessed hands and feet on all sides, and eyes, heads, and faces on every side.
From the Lord Aniruddha, whose self is connected with hearing from all sides,
the entire world— along with its gods, asuras, and humans— was born from his limbs;
likewise, Indra and Agni, the four Vedas, and the six auxiliary sciences (vedāṅgas) arose.
From his mouth the sky was born; from his head, the sun;
from his eye, the moon was born; from his ear, all the quarters of space came into being.
From his navel the atmosphere arose, and from his feet the earth was produced. (4.34–35)
From his prāṇa came Vāyu, from his apāna came Death, and from his hair came the clouds;
the divisions of time, beginning with the kṣaṇa, were born from his body;
and from the pores of his skin arose medicinal herbs accompanied by forest trees.
O twice-born one, there were many sacrifices accompanied by sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
The Brāhmaṇas emerged from his mouth, the Kṣatriyas from his arms, the Vaiśyas from his thighs, and the Śūdras were born separately from his feet. (4.37–38)
Having thus performed the creation of the world, the Lord, seated upon the ocean of milk,
reclined upon the couch of the serpent Ananta, accompanied by Śrī and Bhūmi,
while being meditated upon in the lotus-heart by Sanandana and other lords of yogis.
He was being saluted by Brahmā, Indra, Śarva, and the foremost of the Maruts; he was constantly attended by the gatekeepers beginning with Caṇḍa, by the lords of the Bhūtas beginning with Kumuda,
and by Viṣvaksena and Garuḍa.
"Viṣṇu, whose nature is inconceivable, lies [there] out of compassion for all beings.
Thus, from the diversity of qualities, the emergence of the different forms occurred;
O son of Kaśyapa, you have been told how the world arose in conjunction with these manifestations.
"Beyond this, O one of great wisdom, what else shall I tell you?
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Origin of the Forms of Vāsudeva and Others," in the *Viśvāmitra-saṃhitā*, a Great Upaniṣad within the *Pañcarātra*.
[Now begins] the fifth chapter.
Kāśyapa [says]:
"The creation of the world was taught by you as being directly from Aniruddha, not from the Blessed One; for we have heard it said that Brahmā creates the worlds. (5.1)
"Is that true or is it false? For my curiosity is indeed great.
I wish to know now; let everything be told, O Guru.
[Viśvāmitra]
The glorious Lord Narayana, whose abode is the Ocean of Milk,
desiring in the beginning to exercise his own sovereignty,
created the waters and deposited his own radiant, potent seed within them.
A golden egg came into being, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns.
From that, Brahmā himself arose, the grandfather of all the worlds.
The Blessed Viṣṇu, having seen him, commanded him for the purpose of creating the world.
Having said "So be it," Brahmā again created Sanaka and the others in that manner.
Then Brahmā spoke to them: "O sons, create progeny.
O twice-born one, although they were thus addressed, all those sons of Svāyambhuva remained as they were.
They did not set their minds upon the work of creating the world.
All of them became yogis who had conquered their senses;
they were free from the sense of "mine" and the ego, and were devoid of passion and hatred.
"Pure beings who are constantly devoted to the contemplation of reality"—
when he spoke thus to all of them [and to these others for the purpose of creating the world],
the Lord Brahmā became enraged toward his independent sons.
Then, from the forehead of the enraged god, whose eyebrows were knitted, there appeared a man possessing a dark-blue and red complexion. He cried out before his father, "Give me a name! || 5.11 ||
Then, seeing him weeping, Prajāpati spoke:
"Because you cried (*arodīḥ*), you shall be named Rudra.
The Lord said to him, "O son, divide your body into two."
Then Rudra, with a joyful mind, divided his body into two parts.
By one half he became a woman, and by the other half he became a man. From that couple were born millions of wondrous Rudras.

O Sage, among them there appeared eleven principal Rudras, four-armed, trident-handed, three-eyed, and of fierce form. Then the Lord Brahmā, seeing that creation of Rudras to be fruitless, [proceeded further].
Furthermore, for the sake of divine creation, he fashioned with his mind Marīci, Atri, Pulaha, Pulastya, Bhṛgu, and Dakṣa;
by them alone was the entire world, both moving and stationary, created.
Having thus brought about the creation of the world, the Lotus-Seated One,
having established himself in supreme meditation, remains beholding the Supreme Light.
Thus, O best of the twice-born, the creation of Brahmā has been narrated to you.
There is never any distinction whatsoever between Brahmā, Hara, and Viṣṇu.
Abiding in the three qualities (guṇas), the Blessed Lord Puruṣottama himself performs the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the world.
Having assumed the forms of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva,
the Blessed One [is such that] without him, not even the tip of a blade of grass is capable of moving. (5.21) — Kāśyapa.
What triad of qualities has been declared, and upon which quality does he preside?
Assuming what form does the Supreme One perform what action? (5.22) — Viśvāmitra.
Sattva, rajas, and tamas—these are declared to be the three qualities (guṇas).
Presiding over the quality of rajas, he who is named Brahmā creates this [universe].
Abiding in sattva, he who is called Viṣṇu protects the entire world.
By resorting to that [state], he, in the form of Rudra, withdraws all creatures;
for Kāśyapa is indeed the single cause of creation, maintenance, and destruction. (5.24)
"O observer of noble vows, I wish to know from whence this world arises;
O bull among the twice-born, tell me also wherein it dwells at its end. O best of the twice-born, if your mind is inclined toward grace, [please explain] this to me. (5.25–26)
Viśvāmitra said:
Nārāyaṇa has two forms, Puruṣa and Prakṛti; entering them by his own will, he agitates this pair. (5.27)
This primordial nature (prakṛti) is beginningless, composed of the three qualities (triguṇa), and imperishable;
it gives birth to this world of moving and non-moving beings by relying upon the Puruṣa.
From that [nature], when joined with the qualities and presided over by the Puruṣa, [the world arises].
O twice-born one, that Great Principle (Mahat) was indeed composed of those threefold qualities.
From that arose the ego (ahaṃkāra), which is proclaimed to be threefold by name: the Vaikārika, the Taijasa, and the Bhūtādi. || 5.29–5.30 ||

From the *vaikārika* ego, which is endowed with *sattva*, there arose the fivefold group of sense organs: hearing, touch, sight, taste, and smell. From the *taijasa* ego, which is joined with *rajas*, the five [sensory objects] were born.
The organs of action are speech, hands, anus, genitals, and feet.
From the *ahaṃkāra* associated with *tamas*, known as *bhūtādi*, the subtle element of sound (*śabdatanmātra*) was produced; from this, space (*ākāśa*) came into being. (5.32–5.33)
From space, O twice-born one, the subtle element of touch arose, and from that, air was produced.
From air, the subtle element of form arose, which in due order generated fire. From fire, the subtle element of taste arose, and from that, the waters were born.
From Adabhya, the subtle element of smell arose, and from that, the earth was produced.
Sound alone is proclaimed as the quality of space;
sound and touch are proclaimed as the two qualities of air.
The three qualities of fire are touch, sound, and form;
the four qualities of water are traditionally held to be sound, form, touch, and taste;
and the five qualities of earth are sound, touch, form, taste, and [smell].
And smell, O best of the twice-born—thus were the five elements born.
Possessing diverse potencies, they were individually unable to effect the creation of the world through their own power; therefore, they entered into combination. (5.38–39)
Impelled by the Pradhāna and the Puruṣa, all those principles beginning with Mahat and ending with the Viśeṣas produced the cosmic egg, the cause of the worlds.
In the navel of the god whose navel is the lotus, there was a vast sphere of gold.

Therefore, this world was created by that Self-Existent Lord. O best of Brahmins, just as the world, consisting of the moving and the unmoving, came into being from primordial nature (prakṛti), so too does it repeatedly undergo dissolution back into that very same source.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Creation and Dissolution of the Universe," in the Viśvāmitra-saṃhitā of the Mahopaniṣad within the Pañcarātra.
Chapter Six.
“O Blessed One, Kāśyapa, let it be told by this venerable teacher: what indeed should be taught to the disciples, and how is it grasped by them? (6.1)
"Viśvāmitra, the mantras should be taught by the teacher preceded by the Praṇava.
O twice-born one, first hear the extraction of the Praṇava. (6.2)
First having extracted Viṣṇu, and immediately after that Śrīdhara;
having united these two, one should practice them, and after that Mandara.
This is called the Praṇava, which proclaims the Supreme Brahman.
One should recite this single-syllable mantra with a protracted and acute accent.
Brahmā is its seer (ṛṣi), and its meter (chandas) is known as Gāyatrī. Its deity is the Supreme Self, Hari himself. (6.4–6.5)
The reality of the Buddha is known as the field; it is called the supreme state.
Its color is declared to be white; now hear from me the six limbs as well:
knowledge, sovereignty, power, strength, valor, and splendor.
Those [mantras] ending in *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, *huṃ phaṭ*, and *vauṣaṭ*— these too, ending in the dative case,
one should place in sequence upon the heart, the head, together with the crest-lock (*śikhā*), the armor (*kavaca*), and the weapon (*astra*), along with the eyes. || 5.7–5.8 ||
The first of these three should be the seed-syllable (bīja) adorned with the bindu and the vibhū;
they know that to be Śakti. One should recite this entire mantra, which consists of the essence (tattva), while its ṛṣi, meter, deity, seed-syllable, and power remain unperceived.

All mantras that lack their constituent parts are fruitless in the rite of recitation. Therefore, having understood everything, one should perform the rite of recitation after first bowing to one's own guru and following after his gurus.
After bowing to the mantra-form and the others, one should perform this recitation (*japa*).
First, the pervasive placement (*vyāpakanyāsa*), then the placement of the syllables (*varṇanyāsa*),
and thereafter the placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) on the hands and the body in sequence.
O bull among sages, having properly performed the rite of recitation (japa), one should practice it;
for the recitation of all mantras is traditionally taught as being preceded by the nyāsa of the Mātṛkās.
[One should place them] on the head, in the middle [of the forehead], then in the mouth, on the back, the two ears, and the pair of nostrils.
Having placed the vowels in order upon the two cheeks, the lips, the belly, and the pair [of breasts], as well as in the middle of the mouth;
and having likewise placed the four groups of consonants (vargas) sequentially upon the joints, the tips, and the palms of the hands and the feet.
The fifth [group] is on both sides, on the back, at the navel, and likewise on the belly.
Then there is a group of four on the chest, the armpits, the cheeks, and the throat.
After that, there is a group of four beginning with *ya*, followed by a group of four beginning with *śa*.

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the *mātṛkā* itself, or indeed [the mantra] accompanied by the form and power, upon the heart, the two hands, the pair of feet, the armpits, the heart, and within the mouth—
this recitation is prescribed for men as that which propitiates Vāgdevī.
O twice-born one, listen with a single-minded focus to the commentary on the Praṇava mantra:
the letter *A* signifies Viṣṇu, the letter *M* denotes the individual soul (*jīva*), and the letter *U* expresses the sense of "non-difference" (*avadhāraṇa*)—thus by these three letters. (6.19–20)

The meaning that the individual soul (jīva) belongs to Nārāyaṇa alone has thus been established. One should recite the mantra three hundred thousand times, perform libations (tarpaṇa) half of that number, and the fire-oblation (homa) should likewise be half of that; having performed it in this manner, the mantra [becomes effective].
One who has attained perfection should perform all rites by means of that very perfection alone.
Subsisting on vegetables, barley-gruel, or alms-food, one should perform ablutions at the three junctions of the day.
Constantly bearing the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra), one should frequent the temples of the deity and cow-pens.
On a mountain peak, on a riverbank, or situated by the shore of the ocean,
or else staying at the root of a *bilva* tree, one should perform the rite of recitation (*japa*).
Thus [for one who has mastered the *praṇava*] is the fruit pertaining to this world and the next.
It should be situated within the hollow of the palms; therefore, one should practice it in this manner.
There is no mantra superior to this, which bestows all accomplishments (*siddhi*).
All the Vedas have arisen from the *praṇava*, the leader of mantras.
He who, at the time of death, meditates on Hari while uttering the *praṇava* with his voice,
and abandons the body according to the path taught in the Yoga scriptures,
goes to the supreme abode known as Nārāyaṇa.
Now I shall declare the extraction of the eight-syllable mantra:
having first uttered the Praṇava, [one takes] Bhadrapāṇi together with Viṣṇu, joined with Ota-deva, Dakṣa, and Vighnaśa, along with Gopana. (6.28–29)
One should extract the Universal Soul (Viśvātman), the primordial deity, accompanied by the conch and other [emblems],
joined with the second vowel, and adorned with a forest garland; then,
joined with the Immeasurable (Aprameya), one should extract the four states of existence.
Thus is extracted the eight-syllabled mantra, which accomplishes all goals.
The seed-syllable is joined with the letter *o* and topped with a crescent moon;
the mantra ends with *śaktir āya*. Its internal seer (*antaryāmī*) is traditionally held to be the Sage (Vyāsa).
The meter is declared to be Gāyatrī, and the presiding deity is the Goddess preceded by the God.
The Supreme Self is designated as the deity, and the field is remembered as the supreme ether.
Its color is white; now hear the seers for each syllable.
Gautama, Bharadvāja, Viśvāmitra, and immediately after him Jamadagni, Vasiṣṭha, Kāśyapa, Atri, and the son of the pitcher (Agastya)—
these eight sages are proclaimed in succession as the progenitors of the social orders.
The eight meters, beginning with Gāyatrī and ending with Virāj,
have been declared; [the deities] Dharā, Dhruva, Soma, as well as Āpaḥ, Agni, Jaleśvara, Pratyūṣa, and Saṃprabhāsa— know these to be the deities for each syllable.

The fields are the supreme ether, the seven worlds beginning with Satya; [the earth is included within, in reverse order]. For the castes proceeding in their sequence, the principles (tattvas) are fire, wind, space, the sun, heaven, and the moon. (6.37–6.38)

The clusters of stars, in their sequence, belong to the eight [deities] of lightning-color. Alternatively, they are the "nārāḥ"—the assemblies of men or the sons of men—or else they are designated as "āpaḥ" (waters), because these are their place of movement (*ayana*). || 6.39 ||
"Because he is woven (*vāyate*) upon [the world], he is remembered as Nārāyaṇa.
O Brahmin, this is the meaning declared for him: "I am his; may I not become mine. Or rather, a man performs [this rite] for him. (6.40–41)
Having first received this mantra from his guru on an auspicious day—
specifically on the twelfth lunar day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa— with devotion,
he worshipped Nārāyaṇa within the excellent mandala of the lotus-disc.
Resembling a dark blue cloud, with eyes as long as lotus petals,
bearing a conch, discus, mace, and lotus in his four lotus-like arms, he possessed a gentle form and dark, curly hair.
Clad in yellow garments, with a face like the full moon,
possessing copper-red lips and a beautiful smile, adorned with shimmering makara-earrings,
and bearing the *śrīvatsa* mark and the *kaustubha* gem upon his broad chest. (6.45)
Adorned with all ornaments such as a crown, armlets, and necklaces;
wearing a forest garland and possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns;
seated upon a jeweled lion-throne together with the goddess Lakṣmī, the Earth.
Meditating thus and becoming pure, the wise one, subsisting on sacrificial food (haviṣya) and observing celibacy, should joyfully recite the supreme mantra eight hundred thousand times.
O Kāśyapa, being thoroughly purified, he should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) four hundred thousand times at dawn.
One should perform two hundred thousand oblations with milk-rice and likewise with sesame seeds,
as well as constantly with sacrificial ghee and fuel-sticks made from bilva wood.
For the person who has performed this, the Lord of Mantras becomes accomplished.
And he also beholds auspicious dreams that indicate the attainment of success (*siddhi*).
When a mantra has been mastered in this manner, it becomes the granter of all desires;
whatever one wishes for among dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, that very thing shall be attained.

Having first performed three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) with undistracted mind during the daily recitation and other rites, one should first perform the pervasive placement (vyāpaka-nyāsa) upon the hands and the body.
This placement is said to be of three kinds: that of emanation (sṛṣṭi), maintenance (sthiti), and withdrawal (saṃhṛti).
This placement, beginning from the right thumb and ending at the left thumb, is known as "creation" (sṛṣṭi); performed in reverse order, it is "dissolution" (saṃhṛti).
Furthermore, that which proceeds from the thumbs to the little fingers of both hands [is another method].

The *sthitinyāsa* (placement of stability) has been fully explained; the householder should perform that. The celibate student (*brahmacārī*) should perform the *sṛṣṭinyāsa* (placement of emanation), and the renunciant (*saṃnyāsī*) should perform the *saṃhṛtinyāsa* (placement of withdrawal).
That which is known as *sṛṣṭi* begins from the head and ends at the feet within the body. (6.55–6.56)
The withdrawal (saṃhāra) should be the reverse, ending at the heart and beginning from the navel.

The placement for maintenance (sthitinyāsa) is performed collectively; one should perform one of these three placements. Beginning with the index finger of the right hand, one should [place] the four syllables.
One should place [the mantras] joined with the *praṇava* at the beginning and end, extending as far as the little fingers (6.58).
Likewise, one should place the fourfold [mantras] with their seed-syllables (*sabījaka*) on the left hand as well;
one should place them upon the middle joints of the fingers using both thumbs (6.59).
Having likewise assigned the limbs to both hands as well—
from the thumb to the little finger— one should indeed assign the ten limbs;
one should then assign the remaining two limbs by placing them upon the tips of the fingers.

Having performed the pervasive placement (vyāpakanyāsa) upon the body as well, one should again place the eight syllables in sequence upon the navel, the heart, the secret place, the knees, the tips of the feet, and the heels; and likewise upon the head, the pair of eyes, the tip of the nose, and the heart.
Having joined the tips of the little fingers with the thumbs, one should first perform the placement;
with the four [other] fingers and the thumbs, one should perform the second placement.
This should not be in front of the knees, but on the feet together with the thighs.

One should place the eight syllables upon the head with the middle finger, and likewise upon the two eyes with the index finger; then again upon the heart with the tips of the ring finger, the little finger, and the thumb, and with the tips of the thumb and the index finger. (6.64–6.65)

Having performed the sequential placement (*nyāsa*) upon the six limbs— consisting of the six syllables, the five-crested form, preceded by the *praṇava*, belonging to the same class, and endowed with qualities such as knowledge—
one should likewise place the six secondary limbs (*upāṅga*) on the belly, back, arms, thighs, and knees.
One should place the two syllables ending in *namaḥ*, along with the dative case suffix (*caturthī*), upon the two feet.
One should then place the seventh and eighth syllables on the shoulders and the back.
Having performed the binding of the directions (*digbandha*) with the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*), one should thereafter [use] the index finger.
Having circumambulated three times with the *Agriprākāra* mantra, one should perform the rites such as recitation (*japa*) while moving upwards; thus should one act with unwavering resolve.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Extracting the Eight-Syllable Mantra," in the *Viśvāmitra-saṃhitā*, the Great Upaniṣad of the *Pañcarātra*.
Chapter Seven:
Viśvāmitra says, "Listen to the ritual procedure for the King of Mantras consisting of twelve syllables."
By the mere hearing of which one is liberated from all sins. (7.1) Having worshipped it, one should extract the twelve-syllable mantra from the wheel of the Mātṛkās.
One should first extract the *udgītha*, preceded by Viṣṇu, [and] Vidhreśa. (7.2)
Mandara, Odanayuta, Subhadra, Aprameyaka, Gadadhvaṃsa, Viṣṇuśīrṣa, Varuṇa, and Ādisaṃyuta;
then Saṃprasāraṇasaṃyukta and Ekanetra follow after that. 7.3.
One should then invoke Ananta, joined with Ādideva;
Śrīdhara, together with the Full Moon; Atri, conjoined with Mādhava;
and Madhusūdana, who is the essence of nectar and is highly honored.
O best of sages, O observer of noble vows, one should extract the conch [mantra] consisting of immeasurable millions from this most excellent twelve-syllable mantra of Viṣṇu,
which is joined with the staff; this is proclaimed to be its seed-syllable.
To Kruddholka, Maholka, and likewise Vīrolka;
to Vyulka, Sahasrādī, and Ulka as the fifth;
Tejolka shall be the sixth; and these last ones are Digrajā and Antima.
These six, beginning with the heart mantra, are the supreme mantras;
or else, they may be applied to all twelve locations of the twelve-syllable mantra.
This arrangement is proclaimed specifically for the Supreme Vāsudeva.
Furthermore, that Bhāskara, the abode of qualities, is the seed of liberation and so forth.
Again, there is the arrangement of the limbs joined with the half-moon;
having extracted the twelve-fold self, it is conjoined with Varuṇa.
One should recite these six— Ādideva, Pañcabindu, Hṛṣīkeśa, Godhana, Aniruddha, and Aurva— as the staff-bearers (daṇḍins).
In the ritual arrangement of the limbs (aṅgakalpanā), these should be joined in sequence with the word "namas" at their end.
In the case of the *vyūha* and other forms, Viṣṇu’s [mantra] should be joined with the seed-syllable and the staff-syllable (7.13).
Alternatively, the seed-syllable may be the "Furious Meteor" (*kruddholkā*) and so forth, or else the twelve syllables.
In the case of the seed-syllable, the king of mantras has twelve limbs; for the other, it has six limbs (7.14).

Among the three groups, Vāsudeva himself is traditionally remembered as the Brahmārṣi; the metre is the Gāyatrī of the Goddess, and the deity is he himself. His color is white, his principle is intellect (buddhi), and his field is the supreme ether.
In the method of the seed-syllables (*bījapakṣa*), there are twelve seed-syllables corresponding to the twelve limbs and twelve skin-layers.
Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) starting with the *praṇava* (OM) and ending with "namas," joined with the name at the end of each seed-syllable,
one should subsequently recite the mantra as before, accompanied by meditation.
Having placed [the mantra] pervading the two hands, sequentially upon the ten fingers,
and having assigned the ten syllables, one should place the remainder upon the head.
(7.18) The preceptor, likewise, having assigned the syllables as before, [should proceed].

Having placed four [syllables] upon the head in the four directions, starting from the east as before, one should place the remaining three syllables, O twice-born one. However, the distinction of this from the previous is that the deity is like crystal in appearance.
The omnipresent Lord himself should sit comfortably upon the vast coils of the serpent Śeṣa,
accompanied by the two goddesses stationed at his sides.
He should recite the mantra twelve lakhs of times, and half of that amount should be for the libation (tarpaṇa).
And half of that should be the number of oblations; in this way, the king of mantras is perfected.
There exists no mantra equal to this twelve-syllable one at any time. I shall now declare the Saṃkarṣaṇa-mantra; listen with focused attention.

O twice-born one, having extracted the first seven syllables from the twelve-syllable mantra and having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), one should indeed recite one's own name ending in the dative case;
this same procedure is prescribed for Pradyumna and Aniruddha as well.
All [the mantras], like those consisting of twelve syllables, have their seers (*ṛṣi*) and other attributes proclaimed.
Listen now in full to the procedure for the mantra of the foremost enclosure (*agrimaprākāra*):
having first prepared the altar (*vedi*), one should place the fire together with cow dung (*gopana*).
Having extracted Bhadrapāṇi together with Ādhava from the half-moon,
this twelve-syllable mantra is designated as the "Outer Wall.
At the commencement of all mantra practices, one should hold the hand raised with the index finger extended.
Having lifted up the *mūrdhra*, one should whirl it three times clockwise.
Listen now to the sequence for extracting the syllables of the *gāyatrī* preceded by Viṣṇu:
having first extracted the *udgrīva* of the eight-syllabled mantra. || 7.28–29 ||
From the first [vowel], one should then utter the five syllables, followed by the jar (kumbha) together with Viṣṇu;
one should pronounce the Vairāja [syllable] joined with Mandara, which is immeasurable.
One should extract that which is endowed with *saṃprasāraṇa* and is radiant.
One should recite five leaves of the twelve-syllable mantra.
Having uttered the word "dhīmahi," one should then recite "Vijaya" joined with "Viṣṇu," followed by "Bhadrapāṇi," and then "Vīrasena."
Immediately after placing the *piṭhī*— which is accompanied by a kinsman, peaceful, joined with a vessel facing upward,
endowed with Śrīdhara, and possessed of the *sarga*—
one should extract the *pavitra* for Agni and Viṣṇu, having first raised up the leader of the deceased (*pretanāyaka*).
Having released Atri, who is preceded by the first [syllable] and joined with Vāsudeva,
one should extract the Vairāja;
thus the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī-mantra is extracted in its entirety.
O high-minded one, its seer is Brahmā, its meter is Gāyatrī, and its deity is Viṣṇu;
its six limbs are Krūḍholkā and the others, located respectively in the head, the forehead, the pair of eyes, and the pair of ears. (7.36)
In the mouth, the throat, and the heart; in the pair of armpits, the two elbows, and the two wrists;
in the hands, the belly, the private parts, the thighs, the shanks, and the pair of feet.
One should place the letters in their proper sequence; now hear from me the colors of those letters:
golden, red, smoke-colored, white, black, and very pale;
then white, yellow, crimson, dark, white, and resembling the color of blood, respectively.
Then [he saw] what was like crystal, gold, and a fine complexion, equal to the rays of the moon;
resembling the filaments of a lotus, with the color of molten gold;
likewise having the luster of stars, red, the color of the stars, and ruddy.
"O Great-minded One, these colors have been described as resembling the orb of the sun.
The deity is to be meditated upon as previously stated; the distinction is that he is seated upon Garuḍa.
Having meditated in this way, one should recite [the mantra] at dawn; at midday, [one should meditate on him with] a radiance dear to crystal."
Thus, evening and morning, one should meditate upon [the deity] who resembles a fresh rain cloud.
There should be twenty-four hundred thousand recitations for the rites of libation (tarpaṇa) and fire-oblation (homa);
this is declared to be the measure for these lords of mantras, which is also the standard for the sacrificial fees.
When these four are accomplished, Viṣṇu himself becomes manifest.
I shall now declare the extraction of the eight-syllable mantra that bestows prosperity (*śrīkara*).
To the north is Śrīdhara, and to the east there should be two *māyā* seeds. 7.45.
Then there should be *Ugrātman*, followed by *Kaustubhayuta* and *Viṣṇuśīrṣī*.
After that, one should recite the three syllables *Śrīkara*; following this, one should utter the pair [of syllables] *Yuga*. This is the supreme eight-syllabled mantra (*aṣṭārṇa*). || 7.46–47 ||
They declare that the seed-syllable (bīja) of this mantra is joined with the first [syllable], accompanied by fire (anala), consisting of twelve parts, and endowed with the Great Illusion (mahāmāyā).
O twice-born one, the six limbs begin with "kruddha," and Prajāpati is the seer (ṛṣi).
"Know, O Queen, that this is the Gāyatrī metre; the deity is Śrīpati (the Lord of Fortune).
All [the syllables] consist of eight letters each, preceded by the word 'muni' for every syllable.
He wears all ornaments, standing in the shadow of the Kalpa-tree. || 7.49-50 ||
Seated upon the shoulder of the four-armed Garuḍa,
he has eight arms and is adorned with all ornaments such as a crown;
he is constantly embellished with divine perfumes and unguents.
In his right hands he holds a discus, a mace, an arrow, and a goad;
and in his left hands he bears a conch, a club, a bow, and a noose.
He wears yellow garments and is as pleasing to behold as the full moon.

One should meditate upon him as being seated atop Garuḍa, holding the lotus-feet of the God of gods with his two arms, and bearing with the pair of his remaining hands a jar of nectar placed within them. 7.54.
And the goddess Lakṣmī, born from the left thigh of the god—
golden-hued, auspicious, clothed in silk, adorned with divine ornaments,
and perpetually embellished with divine flowers and the anointing of celestial perfumes.
One should meditate upon her who holds a noose and a goad, possessing a gentle form, while reciting the mantra.
Established in the vow and with senses restrained, one should mutter it twelve thousand times.
O you of noble vows, listen as I shall declare the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa mantra.
It is said: [Regarding] the first of the two groups of six syllables, one should extract the names of the forms in the dative case and join them;
likewise, the seed-syllables are simply the initial letters, conjoined with the *tāra* (OM) and the bindu. || 7.58–59 ||
[Of the others consisting of twelve syllables, four have been mentioned previously];
now listen, O observer of good vows, to the other eight known as the *vyūha* forms:
Nārasiṃha, Adhokṣaja, Acyuta, and Puruṣottama.
Janārdana, Upendra, Hari, and Kṛṣṇa—these eight are proclaimed.
These eight, along with those previously mentioned for the castes as before, are [to be addressed] with their own names in the dative case, followed by the seed-syllable as before. (7.61–62)
And the limbs are as before; the meter is said to be Gāyatrī.
All [details] such as the seer (ṛṣi) and so forth are as previously stated, and the ritual practice (caryā) is likewise as before.
Having first uttered the seven syllables for the ten incarnations beginning with the Fish (matsya), [one should proceed].
"And having uttered the names of the forms, with the word 'rūpāya' as the final term,
the seed-syllable shall be the very first letter, generally accompanied by the bindu"—
thus it is stated in the *Pañcarātra*, in the *Mahopaniṣad*, in the *Viśvāmitra-saṃhitā*.
Chapter Seven: The Ritual for Extracting the Mantra Beginning with Twelve Syllables.
Chapter Eight: Kāśyapa.
O Blessed One, you yourself have proclaimed the extraction of all mantras;
yet, O bull among sages, I do not understand all those various names of the syllables that you have spoken—you ought to instruct me in them. (8.1)
O best of sages, if you will direct your mind toward me with favor, I,
Viśvāmitra,
shall describe the castes in their proper order.
When these are known, the extraction of mantras becomes easy.

On a perfectly level plot of ground that is pure, secluded from people, auspicious, free from drafts, and sprinkled with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), [one should perform the ritual]. 8.3–8.4.
Having fashioned a square measuring two cubits, four fingers high, and resembling the surface of a mirror,
one should prepare the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) using clay from a pure location, mixed with cow dung and water.
Having sprinkled the pedestal with water and smeared it with [sandalwood paste] while reciting the *praṇava*,
and having consecrated it ten times with the twelve-syllable mantra,
one should place within it the wheel of the *mātṛkās* endowed with sixteen spokes.
Having joined it with the hub and the rim, and having sprinkled it with sandalwood water during an auspicious conjunction of stars and at a favorable moment, O best of the twice-born, he,
well-adorned, should put on a pair of white garments himself.
With his limbs smeared with auspicious sandalwood paste and adorned with white garlands,
and having, as instructed by his guru, projected the goddess Mātṛkā upon his own body,
he appeared, O best of the twice-born, like many jewels strung upon a single thread. || 8.9–8.10 ||
In that very same manner, one should fashion a garland of syllables within that form;
having brought the wheel of syllables to mind as "Sūta," one should draw it.
Having written the *praṇava* (oṃ) in the center, [one should place] the vowels upon the grounds of the consonants.
Likewise, one should draw these two— the Nādinī and the Sparśā— in the middle of the navel.
She has her limbs fashioned from the vowels, is adorned with the ornaments of the consonants,
has a lotus-face formed by the vowels, and possesses the two hands [represented by] the *ka*-group and the letter *ka*.
The goddess, whose feet are formed by the pair of *ṭa*-class consonants, whose belly is fashioned from the *pa*-class,
who consists of the letters beginning with *ya*, and who possesses the radiance of a white heart;
she is the goddess holding a noose and a goad, adorned with a white complexion.
Having thus meditated upon the Goddess Mātṛkā, one should worship her with offerings beginning with the *arghya*,
using the sixteen types of service (*upacāra*) and the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*).
One should also worship the Person whose nature consists of the phonemes (*varṇātmā puruṣa*) in the center of the wheel.
Thereafter, one should extract the mantras as desired, preceded by devotion.
O twice-born one, listen attentively to the names of the phonemes:
the Praṇava, the Brahmakośa, the Brahman, and also the Udgītha.
The *tāraka* [mantra] is the beginning of the Vedic meters; these are its designations: *oṃ*, *ā*, and *syā*.
The letter *a* is immeasurable and is called the first Viṣṇu; the letter *ā* is the primordial god, the protector Madhusūdana. (8.18–19)
The letter *i* is conceived as *iṣṭa*, *indhana*, *rāma*, and *bandhu*;
the letter *ī* is *pañcabindu*, *mahāmāyā*, and *vāmana*.
The letter *u* and the others are *udaya*, *uddāma*, *śrīdhara*, and *bhuvana*.
The letter *u* is the Lord of the Upper World (*ūrdhvaloka*), Hṛṣīkeśa, and the one who dwells in the cave (*guhālaya*).
The letter *ṛ* is Ṛtadhāman, Satya, and likewise Aṅkuśa.
The letter *ṝ* is Viṣṭara, Jvālā, Yogin, and Dāmodara as well.
The letter *la* is the name of Goptṛ, and Keśava is Maheśvara;
the letter *lṛ* is Dīrghaghoṇa, whose appellation is Nārāyaṇa.
The letter *e* is Mādhava, triangular in shape, and is known by the name Saṃprasāraṇa.
The letter *ai* is Godhana, Vīrasena, and he who is known as Govinda.
The letter *o* is Otadeha, Vāsudeva, and likewise Audana. The letter *au* is Auṣadha, Aurva, and he who is called Saṃkarṣaṇa.
The syllable *aṃ* is Anu (or Sva), Pradyumna, and Kapilākṣaka;
the syllable *aḥ* is Kalānta, Upasarga, and Aniruddhaka.
The letter *ka* is Karāla, Kamala, and the one designated as Brahma.
The letter *kha* is named Cakrin, who is dwarfish and has Garuḍa as his vehicle.
The letter *ga* is remembered as Gadadhvaṃsin, the wielder of the mace, and the destroyer of the five.
The letter *gha* is Gajavāha, the fivefold self, and the five-handed one.
The letter *ṅa* is Ekadaṃṣṭra, Śārṅgapāṇi, and Kapidhvaja;
the letter *ca* is Vakratuṇḍa, Khaḍgadhṛk, and Pretanāyaka;
the letter *cha* is Chhalavidhvaṃsī, Svacchanda, and likewise Kuṇḍalī.

The letter *ja* is the destroyer of birth, as well as [the wielder of] the mace (*musalī*) and the quarters of the sky; 8.30 The letter *hma* is the consumer of *hmaṣa*, the Sāmaveda, and the golden one (*suvarṇaka*);
the letter *ña* is remembered as the noose-handed one (*pāśapāṇi*), Bhṛgu, and the white moon. 8.31
The letter *ṭa* is Hṛdayāhlādī, Parvata, and Kheṭakī;
the letter *ṭha* is Tomara, Meghī, Kaustubha, and is remembered as Duṣprabha.
The letter *ḍa* is Puṇḍarīkākṣa, Bhūmi, and Vahniniketana.
The letter *ḍha* is *Ṭṛḍhakarma*, *Puṣpabhadra*, and *Prardana*.
The letter *ṇa* is *Sumukha*, *Vanamālī*, and *Pracaṇḍaka*.
The letter *ta* is *Ekanetra*, *Vairāja*, and likewise *Vijaya*.
The letter *tha* is Supratiṣṭha, the essence of taste, and the destroyer of all.
The letter *da* is Vaidhara, Tṛṣṭi, Atri, and the ender of all cities.
The letter *dha* is Subhaga, Puṇya, Dhanada, and the [deluder...destroyer].
The letter *na* is Mānuṣeśa, Vighneśa, and Bhadrapāṇika.
The letter *pa* is Pāpahanana, Pavitra, and Paścimānana.
The letter *pha* is Phalgunayana, Śikhaṇḍin, and Vikarman. (8.36–8.37)
The letter *ba* is Matimān; the short [letter *va*] is Vanemijṛmbhala, [and the long *va* is] Kālanemijit.
The letter *bha* is Bhallātaka, and the letter *bha* is Subhadra Sūkṣmalocana.
The letter *ma* is Māghavī Dakṣa, Mandara Pāṭalapriya. 8.38.
The letter *ya* is the self of the Puruṣa, the conch, the wind, and the four states of existence.
The letter *ra* is fire with its great flame, the self of the universe, and the burner of all.
The letter *la* is Pulaha, the son of Mahendra, and is yellow in color.
The letter *va* is Varuṇa, the water-pot, the essence of nectar, and the juice of immortality.
The letter *śa* is the bestower of auspiciousness, Lakṣmī, the Śrīvatsa mark, and the increaser of wealth.
The letter *ṣa* is of the nature of wrath, fierce in spirit, and the burner of enemies.
The letter *sa* is the full moon, the self of time, and is named Śūla;
the letter *i* is the twelve-fold self, the sun, refined by radiance;
the letter *la* is the *ḍuṇḍubha* snake, the embryo, the *viṣkambha*, and is designated as poison.
The letter *kṣa* is Nṛhari; *kṛt* is Ananta; the *anusvāra* is Garuḍa, the Self-possessed; *dhruva* is the *bindu*; and the half-moon (*candrārdha*) is known as the staff (*yaṣṭi*).
The form *svā* is Hutānta, and it is proclaimed as *ṭhaṭha*.
Salutation is declared to be bowing; these are known as the designations of the syllables.
(8.45) Listen now to the deities of the syllables situated in the center of the wheel in their respective order.
For the *praṇava*, the Supreme Brahman is established as the deity. (8.46)
Because he is the form of all causes, Viṣṇu is its presiding deity (adhidevatā).
The deities beginning with those of two syllables and ending with Madhudeṣya are proclaimed;
those beginning with nine syllables and ending with Keśava are remembered as the four deities.
"I shall proclaim to you the deities beginning with the letters ending in the thirteenth.
These sixteen, beginning with Vāsudeva, have been proclaimed.
O bull among sages, hear now the deities of the consonants (sparśas) in their proper order."
Vidhi, Sudarśana, Vāṇī, Śārṅga, and Nandaka are desired;
likewise Gadā, Yamadaṇḍa, Musalī, Aṅkuśa, and Bhṛgu;
Mumeru, Kaustubha, Bhūmi, Vāmana, and Vanamālikā.
Daṃṣṭrin, Rasa, Atri, Dhanada, Vighnarāja, Pavitraka, Śikhaṇḍavān, Jṛmbhala, Subhadra, and Dakṣadevatā;
these are remembered as the deities of the letters ending in *ya*, *tha*, *va*, *ya*, *ga*, *na*, and *ra*, respectively. (8.51–8.52)
Śrī is the deity of the *uṣman* sounds; Candra and Sūrya are the deities of the *krodharūpa* letters.
Bhadra and Nṛsiṃha—these are declared to be the deities in their respective order.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Rule for the Designation of Phonemes," in the *Viśvāmitra-saṃhitā*, a Great Upaniṣad within the *Pañcarātra*.
The Ninth Chapter.
Kāśyapa said: "O Blessed One, please describe the characteristics of initiation out of your grace for me."
"O you who are affectionate toward your devotees, tell me everything in full detail.
Viśvāmitra replied:
"I shall describe the initiation in brief; listen to that, O bull among the twice-born."
When the sun is situated in Pisces, Aries, Taurus, or Gemini, during the auspicious bright fortnight,
under a favorable lunar mansion, on the eleventh day, and at night;
having caused a pavilion to be constructed in a pure and pleasing location— || 9.2–9.3 ||
Having smeared it with cow-dung, one should encircle it with a garland of *darbha* grass.
One should construct an altar in its center measuring four cubits;
others say it should be one *tāla* in height, while its width and length are equal to that.

O Sage, one should construct a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) according to the prescribed rules on the western side of the altar. In due order for the Brāhmaṇas and the other castes, it should possess these characteristics:
for the twice-born (Brāhmaṇa), it should be quadrangular, measuring two spans (tāla), and favorable.
One should fashion the [funeral] mound for a Kṣatriya as circular, joined with the shape of a cow’s ear;
for a Vaiśya, it should be in the form of a bow, measuring two spans (vitasti);
and for one born of a Śūdra womb, it should be triangular, measuring two cubits (prādeśa).
One should construct it with a measurement equal to its width and length,
and likewise provided with three girdles, adorned with a *yoni* on the western side.
On the tenth day, being composed, one should collect all the sacrificial fuel sticks (*samidh*) and other materials.
At midday, having bathed and being pure, he should subsist on a single meal;
on the eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī), having bathed and wearing a pair of clean garments,
with his limbs anointed with white sandalwood paste and adorned with white garlands.

Adorned and fully decorated with whatever ornaments have been obtained, when evening has arrived, he should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana). At the four doorways and on both sides, two kalās each should be established. || 9.11–12 ||

Having placed [the materials] in the center of the Vedavikā, one should fashion a maṇḍala of a lotus within a wheel. One should prepare a pitcher made of gold or other precious metals, filled with filtered water, into which gems and gold have been placed; it should be equipped with a tuft of kuśa grass and wrapped with a thread.

Clothed in a pair of garments and adorned with sandalwood paste and garlands, it is strewn on all sides with unbroken grains and flowers. The water-pot (*kumbha*) should be made of the same material as the *karkarī*. || 9.14–15 ||
The preceptor should consecrate the water-jar (*karkarī*) one hundred times with the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*) and sprinkle it all around the altar with an unbroken stream.
He should then perform the installation of the ritual jar (*kumbha*) in the northeastern quarter of the lotus-diagram.
Having placed very beautiful rice grains, one should set a water-jar upon them.
Inside the jar, one should place its fruit, and around that fruit, one should arrange fruits. One should place a large jar on the right side and a small water-pot on the left.
Having invoked Hari into the pitcher, one should worship him with the root-mantra;
and in the mandala, one should worship the deity with the sixteen services,
together with all his retinues, according to the path enjoined by the scriptures.
And having spoken of the god Hari from the mandala by the prescribed path in the west,
and having visualized Hari reclining with Lakṣmī and Bhūmi,
one should worship him with all offerings, beginning with the arghya and ending with the naivedya.
Having churned the fire with the root mantra, the Guru should place it within the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
There, having prepared the *caru* offering from pure, white rice,
he should offer one-fourth of it to Viṣṇu residing in the mandala.
Having offered one portion, he should present it to the one residing in the water-pot (kumbha).
He should offer a portion as an oblation into the fire and consume a portion himself.
He should offer one hundred and eight pieces of fuel-wood with the root-mantra (mūlavidyā).
The wise man should offer oblations with the *Puruṣasūkta* that many times;
then, having performed the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), he should [initiate] the disciple who has bathed, whose senses are subdued, and who is wearing two new,
bright garments and the finest ornaments.
Having summoned him who is adorned, whose limbs are anointed, and who is decorated with pure garlands,
the Guru, remaining silent, should seat him facing east on his own right side while tying a new cloth around [his head]. || 9.26-27 ||
With him [the disciple] holding on, he should offer twelve oblations separately and in sequence with both ghee and *caru*. Having offered,
he should then sprinkle [the disciple] three times on the head with sesame seeds and flowers.
Having taken the sacrificial ashes with the white eight-syllable mantra,
and having applied the vertical *puṇḍra* mark and tied an amulet on the wrist,
one should have him consume the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) with the [appropriate] mantra.
Afterwards, for the sake of self-purification, he should cause [the disciple] to eat the sacrificial oblation (caru) with the syllable Om (praṇava).
Having cleansed his teeth with a tooth-stick, he should discard it;
then the Guru should carefully observe the place where its tip falls.
Whatever is inauspicious in the southern, southwestern, or northwestern [directions] is indeed inauspicious;

one should declare that which is in other directions to be auspicious. One should pacify inauspiciousness by means of a propitiatory oblation (śānti-homa), offering eight hundred oblations with the Nārasiṃha mantra.
Having looked at the feet of the Lord, he should cause the disciple to sip water from sesame seeds;
then the Guru, bowing with his head, should address the Lord:
"For the liberation of the fetters of these bound souls (paśus) who are tied by the noose of saṃsāra..."
O God, you alone are our refuge; no other resort is found.
(9.35) That very means for the release from the bonds—which consists in the propitiation of you—[is used] for these beings born as animals, who are bound by the snare of birth. (9.36)
"I purify [the disciple], O Lord of Gods; you should grant permission for that.
Having thus informed the Lord of Gods, one should wrap the disciple with a thread.
Having made it firm, [the thread] should be black in color and tripled by means of three threads.
Having tripled that [mantra] again, one should wrap it twenty-five times around the body of the disciple, starting from the feet and ending at the head. Then,
having touched that [body], one should offer oblations with clarified butter one hundred and eight times.

Then, having performed the *pūrṇāhuti* for the sake of attaining the vision of his own [deity], the Guru should offer oblations as many times as that number with the mantra of the presiding deity of dreams. Being composed, he should also present an offering of black gram and boiled rice (*māṣaudana*) to the spirits (*ūta*).
Having loosened the disciple’s blindfold and removed it from his body, O best of the twice-born,
he should then take that thread of illusion (māyāsūtra), place it in a shallow bowl,
cover it, and set it down beside the jar.
Having spread darbha grass, he should place him upon it like one entering a cave;
then the Guru should not remove the deity residing within the pitcher and mandala. In the morning, he should inquire of that disciple regarding the auspiciousness or inauspiciousness of his dream.
If [the omen] is auspicious, one should initiate him; if it is inauspicious, one should not initiate him.

Having performed the pacification of that [inauspiciousness] through a *śānti*-oblation and having bathed, being thus pure, he should then enter the pavilion prepared for the sacrifice together with his disciples.
Having worshipped the banner and the arch according to the prescribed rite,
and having devoutly honored that deity seated within the water-pot and the basin,
one should offer milk-rice and other foods, and then perform prostrations and circumambulations.
Having bound the eyes of the disciple and seated him at his side, the preceptor, with focused attention,
offers sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, and sesame seeds separately one hundred and eight times each with the root mantra, concluding with the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti).

Having taken that thread of illusion and cut it according to the number of principles (*tattva*), the Guru, recollecting the principles beginning with *prakṛti*, should offer them into the fire by means of the yoga of the sequence of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*). Thus, there are twenty-five [offerings]. (9.49)
One should offer oblations eight hundred times separately, or perhaps eight times [each].

Having meditated upon the Lord Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Self, the Infallible One, as being perfectly established within the pericarp of the lotus of his own heart, the Guru [should perform the rite]. (9.50–9.51)
Having recollected the *jīva* of the disciple, the preceptor should cause it to enter into that very [body];
then, having performed the rites of drying and so forth upon the body of the disciple,
