he should again transfer the *jīva*, together with his own heart-lotus, into it.
One should assign the principles (tattvas) according to their nature through the process of emanation (sṛṣṭikrama).
At the time of emanation, one should offer oblations to the principles in their proper order.
Having touched the body of the disciple, one should [visualize] the disciple situated within that [body].
Having meditated upon the deity stationed there, he should perform the binding of the eyes with a cloth while reciting the root-vidyā; then, having put on another garment,
he should wash his feet, cause the deity to sip water (ācamana), and then [open] his eyes.
Then, having tied it with a cloth and placed it at his side,
he should clear the path for one who is seated facing east;
[he should clear] the path of time, the path of space, and subsequently the path of the worlds.
Then, having purified the path of reality (tattvādhvan), followed by the path of mantra (mantrādhvan), and the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan) through his own wisdom,
he should first perform an oblation of clarified butter (ājyahoma) with the Great Utterances (mahāvyāhṛtis).

Having offered oblations, the Guru should touch the feet of the disciple with the remaining clarified butter (ājya). Then, having likewise offered oblations with sesame seeds, he should touch the disciple's navel.
Having performed the lotus-oblation (padmahoma), he should also touch the disciple's heart.
Having offered oblations there with the *caru* rice, he should touch the disciple's head.
There should be a separate hundredfold oblation with the *mahāvyāhṛti* formulas.
Then, taking the right hand of the disciple into his own, [he should perform the rite].
Having performed a circumambulation with his right hand alone,
he, with one-pointed mind, [beheld] the god Nārāyaṇa situated within the circle of the water-pots; then, remaining in that very doorway adorned with gold, jewels, and other such things.
The wise one should fill his joined palms with flowers alone;
he should cast them into the maṇḍala where that handful of flowers falls. On whichever part of the ground it has fallen, he should designate that as the location for the respective deity’s image.
At the end of that disciple’s name, there should be the word *Keśava* and so forth;
or else *Bhāgavata*, or likewise *Bhaṭṭāraka*.
For a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya, the word *deva* should be at the end of the name.
Thus, the names for the Vaiśya and the fourth [caste] should end with "Pāladāsa.
Then, having performed the ritual of releasing the directional bonds (digbandha), one should show the mandala using the established jars—
either nine or thirteen.
Having bathed him and caused him to put on new garments, and having washed his two feet and then made him sip water, O best of the twice-born,
the teacher, together with the disciple, should meditate upon the Lord with a concentrated mind.

Into the right ear of the disciple, he should impart the eight-syllable mantra, beginning with the *praṇava* and joined with its limbs (*aṅga*), together with its seer (*ṛṣi*) and other components; thereafter,
he should give the twelve-syllable mantra and the mantras of the [divine] forms (*mūrti*) in their proper order.
Just as a guru might bestow a single [syllable] by the power of that mantra,
so too may a Śūdra and women born of the anuloma [castes] [receive] a syllable;
it should be devoid of *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *huṃ*, *phaṭ*, and the like, and accompanied by the *praṇava* (oṃ).
One should cause him to recite the name of Viṣṇu alone, ending in the dative case;
and the Brāhmaṇa should undertake the chanting of the Gāyatrī, the fire-oblation, and the mantra.
Then the disciple himself [should worship] the Lord Hari, who resides within the pitcher and the maṇḍala.
Afterwards, he should propitiate Ruru for the disciple who has prostrated and then risen; while the disciple stands with palms joined in reverence, the teacher himself,
having meditated upon the mandala of the wheel and lotus within his own hand as the "hand of Viṣṇu," [should place it] upon the head of that disciple.
Having first deposited [the disciple], the teacher should thereafter instruct him in the rules of conduct:
"The mantra must not be spoken to anyone else, nor should the rosary be shown;
one should not display the mudrā to another, nor speak of the accomplishment of the mantra."
One should not utter the name of the guru; one should not transgress his command. One should always remain near him, maintain respectful conduct, and likewise not step over his sandals.
One should not speak ill of the guru, nor should one do anything unpleasant to him.
One should practice devotion toward one's teacher, children, wife, and others as if they were the teacher himself.
One should worship the mantra, the teacher, and the deity with an equal mind.
One should not touch atheists, nor should one converse with them.
One should never stretch out one's feet in the presence of the Guru, the deity, or the sacred fire.
Without having performed the worship of the deity, one should not consume anything at all.
During the *sandhyā* periods, one should perform the recitation of mantras, hymns of praise, prostrations, and other such rites.
Upon seeing Vaiṣṇava ascetics, one should prostrate oneself on the ground like a staff. Whether walking, standing, sitting, eating, or devoted to sleep,
one should meditate upon the Lord Nārāyaṇa with an inner self directed toward Him.
The Guru should thus instruct the disciple in such conduct and observances.
Then, having performed the *śānti*-oblation, he should offer the *pūrṇāhuti*.
Having performed the dismissal of the fire, [he should dismiss] Hari who resides within the jar and the maṇḍala.
Having dismissed him, the guru should cause the prostrate disciple to prosper with blessings;
and the disciple should give to the guru a cow, land, ornaments, an elephant, a horse, a palanquin, and a large number of male and female servants. (9.85)
Without practicing deceit regarding his wealth, he should offer himself [as a servant];
he should feed the Vaiṣṇava Brahmins according to his ability, having fully satisfied them.
After they have eaten, he should remain right there, restrained in speech, until the remnants of the meal are consumed.
After sunset, having anointed himself and being well-adorned,
he should go home accompanied by his relatives with the permission of his guru.
Thus, one who performs the initiation in the presence of the *cakramandala* [attains success].
He alone is truly a wise brāhmaṇa; he alone is the best among those in the stages of life (āśramins). He is not to be addressed by these titles:
Ekāntin, Pāñcarātrika, Sūri, Bhāgavata, Sāttvata, or Pāñcakālika. || 9.89-90 ||

This [path] is not to be described by other names, just as an ordinary person is not. It is considered to be eightfold: convention (*samaya*), then custom (*samācāra*), the study of one's own texts (*svādhyāya*), the collection of requisites (*dravyasaṃgraha*), purification (*śuddhi*), worship (*pūjā*), praise (*stuti*), and meditation (*dhyāna*). || 9.91 ||
He who abides by this rule is considered a Bhāgavata.
O twice-born one, the collection of the six qualities beginning with knowledge is called *bhaga*;
he in whom that [collection] exists is the Blessed One (*bhagavān*), and he alone is Hari, the Blessed One.
"He who is well-established in that [path] is entitled to the name 'Bhāgavata'.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Rule for Initiation," in the Viśvāmitra-saṃhitā of the Mahopaniṣad within the Pañcarātra.
The Tenth Chapter: Kāśyapa said:
"O Brahmin, you ought to tell me the method of propitiation."
"By performing which correctly I shall cross the ocean of existence.
Viśvāmitra said:
O son of Kaśyapa, listen; I shall describe the method of propitiation."

For those bound by the snares of saṃsāra, the act of propitiating Viṣṇu must be performed with absolute purity as the direct cause for liberation. O wise one, even through bathing, the purification of the body may be achieved. || 10.2–10.3 ||
Therefore, I shall proclaim the ritual bathing; listen with a one-pointed mind.
Bathing is said to be of seven kinds:
that of water, that of earth, as well as the divine, the Vāruṇa, the Āgraya, the mental, and the Mātra.

One should bear upon one's head the dust raised by the hooves of cows as they walk, or that which is carried by the wind; for it is said that this white clay is worthy of being worn because it originates from a sacred field of Viṣṇu. || 10.5–10.6 ||
The application of the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* on the forehead and other parts of the body, preceded by the utterance of the names of the deities such as Keśava and others,
constitutes the "earthen bath" (*pārthiva-snāna*) practiced by the best of yogis. (10.7)
When rain falls upon a cloudless sky accompanied by sunshine,
that which results from such a deluge is called divine bathing (divya-snāna).
As for the immersion performed by all [others] in rivers, ponds, and the like— || 10.8–10.9 ||
That bathing which is performed according to the prescribed rule is declared to be *vāruṇa* (pertaining to Varuṇa).
When the offering of one’s own fuel-sticks, *bhargas*, and cow-dung has been performed in the fire,
one should take that ash in the hand and consecrate it with the mantra alone.
The application of the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) on the forehead is indeed a form of bathing.

Having washed one's feet and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), putting on a pair of clean garments, and sitting upon a pure seat, one should control the breath while remaining silent. || 10.11–10.12 ||
Furthermore, the remembrance of Hari residing within the lotus of the heart—
that constitutes a mental bath, which is honored above all other baths.
This is preceded by the recitation of the mantras beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā."
The sprinkling that is performed with pure water using the tips of *kuśa* grass is called the "mantric bath. These seven have been described to you;
even after performing the preceding *vāruṇa* bath, the procedure for the others may follow.
Therefore, O twice-born one, listen as I describe that Vāruṇa bath.
Having gone to a river, stream, pond, or similar body of water, and having stood upon its southern bank,
one should first cleanse the bank there with handfuls of water.
Having placed bathing water and a pair of washed garments there, he should then bring clay from a pure spot and divide it into two parts;
with one part, he should perform the cleansing of his body. || 10.17–10.18 ||
One should cleanse the head and other parts with bathing powders and other substances. Having bathed, one should divide the remaining portion of the earth that was set aside into three parts.
Placing one part in the left hand, one should perform the binding of the directions (*digbandha*) with another.
One should then smear one’s own body with another portion,
and with what remains, one should fashion the pedestal for the sacred site (*tīrtha*).
There, one should meditate upon the Gaṅgā as having issued from the lotus-foot of Viṣṇu’s left foot.
Having offered the *arghya* and other oblations, and then having gathered handfuls of water,
one should recite the mantra three or seven times and pour it over one's head; then,
meditating upon the Lord Nārāyaṇa in the heart, [one should contemplate] his feet and the crown of the head.
Having placed his head downward, he should recite the mantra as much as he is able.

(10.23) Then, having emerged and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), putting on a pair of clean garments and having applied the vertical sectarian mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra), [he should worship] that which has the form of the gods, sages, and ancestors. (10.24)
Having offered libations to the deity according to the path prescribed in his own Sūtra,
and having completed the remainder of the daily rites (āhnika) and performed the ritual attendance (upasthāna) to the Sun,
he should return to the sacrificial hall and wash his pair of feet.

Having washed both hands from the wrists down to the knees, and having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should stand at the door while performing the ritual placement of mantras on the limbs (aṅganyāsa).
Then, facing the door, one should strike it with both hands. || 10.26–10.27 ||
Having formed a foremost enclosure with the index finger held upwards,
and having opened the door with the Vāyu-mantra,
one should enter within while reciting the Devavrata Sāman, preceded by the right foot.
Having recited the Varuṇa mantra accompanied by perfumes and other offerings,
and having performed worship of those stationed at the gate, one should proceed to the pavilion,
which is endowed with all auspicious things and possessed of a floor inlaid with jewels.
It was further adorned with *sauvīra* stones, reeds, and banners;
it was richly endowed with garlands of jeweled bells and featured a variegated pedestal of gems.
It was joined with strings of rubies and shone with hanging garlands.
If one is unable to act in this way, the wise person should meditate thus with the mind alone:
having gone before the Lord, [reciting] the Puṇḍarīkākṣa-vidyā, prostrating like a staff upon the ground, and rising with palms joined in reverence. || 10.32–33 ||
Having set down the lamp-stand and cast aside the garlands and other offerings,
and having performed the washing of the bowl when the attendants had departed,
he put on a pair of white garments and was adorned with all his ornaments.
His body adorned with garlands and white unguents,
having applied twelve vertical marks (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*) with white clay,
[he should place the deity] on an auspicious seat such as a grass mat on the right side of the Lord. || 10.35–10.36 ||
Once purified by the *uṣṭra-mantra*, he himself should remain silent,
having assumed either the *padmāsana* or the *svastikāsana*.
Then, having caused the sound of musical instruments— the resonance of conchs and trumpets— to resound.
Having closed the door with a curtain so that no gap remained,
he visualized a wall of fire around himself using its mantra;
and with the *cakra* mantra, he performed the protection of his own self by means of a wheel of waters.
Having performed [the preliminary rites] in this manner, one should then perform three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) in succession.
Having thus ensured self-protection and having formed the yoga-mudrā,
[one should focus] upon the navel-center (nābhikanda), which is a four-cornered mandala known as "wind" (vāyu).
Having meditated upon that seed-syllable with the mind,
one should dry up the impurity residing in the body by means of the smoke-colored wind arising from it;
then, one should contemplate the fire-seed-syllable situated within a triangle inside the heart-lotus.
One should burn away impurity with the flames of fire arising from that [red-colored seed].
Then, having placed the yellow-hued Māhendramantra in the region of the throat, which is square in shape,
one should visualize the seed-syllable as rising up together with the wind.
One should stabilize [the body] with the *kumbhaka* breath alone, visualizing a circular mandala resembling crystal at the crown of the head. Occupying its center,
one should wash [the body] with nectar-water flowing forth from that seed-syllable.
Then, from the feet up to the head, one should—
with an attentive mind— dissolve the body and the principles beginning with the earth into their respective causes by means of the yoga of the process of withdrawal.
From the feet up to the knees is said to be the location of the earth element.

Situated there, it is fivefold, yellow in luster, and square; it is associated with the sense of smell and the organ of generation, and from it the subtle element [of smell] is perceived. (10.47–10.48)
Having withdrawn the sense of smell, one should subsequently dissolve it into water.
The wise know that the region of the waters extends from the knees up to the navel.
Therefore, water possesses four qualities; it is white and situated in the crescent of the moon.
Having withdrawn the tongue, which is connected to the anus, together with the subtle element of smell into taste,
one should subsequently withdraw that [taste] into fire, O twice-born one.
The region from the navel to the heart is proclaimed to be the seat of fire.

Having dissolved that fire— which is situated therein, consisting of the three qualities, triangular, pale-red, and intensely blazing— along with its essence, into the two feet within the form [of the body],
and having then dissolved it into the wind from the heart up to the middle of the eyebrows, [one realizes] the abiding of the wind.
Having withdrawn that wind situated there—smoky-colored, double-folded, and characterized by the notion of form—one should then bring it back into the ether, which has touch as its quality.
The region of space is said to extend from the middle of the eyebrows up to the crown of the head. || 10.53-54 ||
Therein, one should then withdraw the blue quality of sound, together with hearing and speech,

from the midst of the subtle element of sound (śabdatanmātra), which is conjoined with touch. Having withdrawn the subtle element of sound into the ether (ākāśa), one should likewise withdraw that into the ego-principle (ahaṃkṛti).
One should contemplate that [Self] within the intellect, that within primordial nature (prakṛti), and that within the individual soul (jīva) along with its latent impressions;
that subtle one, situated at the navel-center, possessing a splendor equal to the sun,
by means of the subtle Suṣumṇā channel which is as slender as a lotus fiber.
Then, by means of the wind through retention (*kumbhaka*), one should slowly cause it to ascend;
having pierced the aperture of Brahman, it emerges upward from the body. Having entered the solar orb, it rises upward as a bodiless entity. (10.58)
Having meditated with a concentrated mind upon that individual soul (jīva) as having entered the Supreme Brahman,

and having contemplated his entire body born of a womb as being completely consumed by the seed-syllable of fire (vahnibīja), which stands at the tips of the feet and possesses brilliant luster; || 10.59-10.60 ||
One should meditate in the sky upon the seed of cessation, possessing a radiance equal to ten million moons;
and within the ocean of nectar arising from that, one should visualize a white lotus.
O Sage, having thus meditated, one should contemplate the individual soul (jīva) as having arisen from the Supreme Brahman.
From the individual soul (jīva), one should contemplate Prakṛti; from that, the intellect (buddhi); from the intellect, the ego-sense (ahaṃkṛti).

From that, the mind (manas) has arisen, and from it, the subtle element of sound (śabdatanmātra). One should discern that from which speech and hearing arise, together with space (ākāśa). || 10.62–63 ||
From ether, which has sound as its sole quality, the subtle element of touch (sparśa-tanmātra) arises;
it is endowed with sound, touch, and form, and is equipped with the eyes and feet.
From fire arises the subtle element of taste (rasa-tanmātra), and from that, water, which possesses four qualities.
From those two, the subtle element of smell (gandha-mātra) indeed came into being.
One should contemplate the earth as having arisen, endowed with sound, touch, form, taste, and smell, and joined with the sense of smell and the organ of generation. 10.65–66.

Having thus assumed a body composed of the five elements from that previously mentioned lotus, he bathed his own body— which was pure and non-material— with the floods of nectar that had arisen therefrom. (10.67)
Reflecting that he was worthy of propitiating Hari,
and having recollected either the eight-syllabled mantra or the sixteen-syllabled one,
he performed with devotion one of the three types of nyāsa, namely the *aṅganyāsa*.
Having performed the *praṇava* for the ṛṣis and others, or likewise ending with *namaḥ* and *svāhā*,
one should worship Vāsudeva, whose essence is the letters, in due order with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings; thereafter, [one should worship] the Lord residing within the lotus of the heart.
One should worship in sequence with mental offerings ending with the fire oblations (homa).
Then, having requested the Lord of Gods, one should perform the Brahma-sacrifice (brāhmayāga),
[preparing] the articles for propitiation and a vessel for washing filled with water.
Having placed the *galantikā* (water-dripper) on his left side while standing to the right,
the wise man should wash the vessels for the *arghya* and other offerings with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī.
Then, he should place a golden seat in front of the deity.
Having washed them, one should place one's feet upon them again;
then, one should gradually set down the vessels upon those feet. One should place the *arghya* vessel in the front corner and the southern rear corner.
Having placed the vessel for water for the feet (pādya), one should place the vessel for sipping water (ācamana) in the northwest corner;
furthermore, one should place the vessel for bathing water (snānīya) in the northeast (śāṅkara).
One should then place the vessel for sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) and the arghya offering in the very center of all.
Siddhārtha, unhusked grain, the tips of kuśa grass, sesame seeds, barley, fragrance, fruit, and flowers—this is said to be the eightfold arghya.
Also dūrvā grass, piṣṇupaṇī, śyāmāka, and lotus. || 10.77–78 ||
Having first placed these substances for the water for the feet (*pādya*),

the wise one should thereafter prepare the substances for the water for sipping (*ācamanīya*)— namely cloves, nutmeg, and *kola*— and for the bathing water (*snānīya*)— namely white mustard seeds and so forth— as previously described. (10.79)
One should fill all these vessels with filtered water.
Having meditated upon a twelve-spoked wheel together with the sun in the right hand,
one should burn those substances with the mass of its rays.
Having meditated upon a bright moon within a white lotus in the left hand,
and having visualized those [flowers] being sprinkled with the nectar-water arising from it,
one should meditate upon the Lord Nārāyaṇa in both hands.
Having touched the substances in all the vessels with those two [hands], with a mind focused on nothing else,
he should recite the Viṣṇugāyatrī over them, consecrating them once each;
then, having displayed the Saurabheyī mudrā arising from that [mantra].

Having visualized that those [vessels] have been filled with a stream of milk, one should touch the vessel for the *arghya* offering while reciting: "Oṃ, I prepare the *arghya*. Having touched the other vessels in the same manner, one should likewise utter: "I prepare [them]."
Having drawn a little water from the arghya vessel into another vessel and placing it in the left hand, one should consecrate it with the root mantra;
one should recite it seven times, and then, taking that water again— || 10.86–87 ||
Having sprinkled those substances and himself with the *kūrca* grass,
he should, with a concentrated mind, fashion the Yoga-pīṭha for the God of gods;
first the Ādhāra-śakti, then Kālāgni, and then the Tortoise.
Above that, [one should visualize] the infinite [space] endowed with a thousand hoods.
Having meditated upon the Goddess Earth above that as being square,
one should then fashion the eight feet, beginning with Dharma, above her.

Dharma, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty are in the intermediate directions; these four, beginning with Nara, are also in the cardinal directions starting from the east. The four in the east are white, and those in the west are red in color.

All of them are to be meditated upon and worshipped as having human forms, lion faces, and four arms. O best of the twice-born, the mantras should be fashioned with their names preceded by the *praṇava* (OM) and followed by the word "namaḥ" in the dative case. 10.92–93.
These four [directions] begin with the east; within them reside the four deities.

The threefold ego (ahaṃkāra) constitutes the nooses, as do the qualities (guṇas), namely sattva and the others. Above that, the soul (jīva) consisting of the five elements is the mattress (tūlikā). || 10.94 ||
One should meditate upon the maṇḍalas of Fire, Moon, and Sun as the spreading carpet before the fire,
in their proper sequence. Above that, one should meditate on a twelve-petaled lotus,
filled with smiling filaments and joined with a central pericarp.
The twelve forms should be known, in order, as being upon the twelve petals; and the fifteen powers, beginning with Mohinī, are in the filaments.
At the base of the pericarp, O Sage, there are three qualities and three negations.
One should contemplate the triad of qualities and powers in this sequence in the center.
Having thus prepared the Bhadrasana posture, one should worship the Lord therein;
on the right side of the pedestal, one should sacrifice to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should likewise worship Sanatkumāra, Sanaka, and Sananda on the northern side;
and on the western side, one should sacrifice to Durgā, Vināyaka, and Nārada.
Having worshipped one's own lineage of gurus according to the prescribed rite,
one should take [the water] from a certain washed vessel filled with arghya-water and,
using the root mantra, lift it evenly with both hands to the forehead.
Having invoked [the deity] from the root-form, like a lamp from a lamp, unswerving,
one should recite four times the mantra joined with the word "āgaccha" (come).
One should then place that water, consecrated by the root-mantra, upon the head of the recipient.
With the *kūrca* [grass-bundle], one should visualize the deity before oneself and prostrate on the ground.
Rising up, one should say "Welcome" and subsequently display the mudrās.
One should then pray for the presence [of the deity] there until the conclusion of the worship.
Having performed the rite of facing [the deity] by means of the Puṇḍarīkākṣa-vidyā,
and having prepared its seat with the root-mantra, the knower of mantras should perform the ritual placement of the mantra upon the image [and the body].
However, one should perform the ritual placement of the hands (*karanyāsa*) and display the conch-gesture (*śaṅkhamudrā*).

When Hari has been installed and remains motionless, one need not perform the invocation (*āvāhana*), for it was already performed by the gods, the *siddhas*, and the sages established in goodness. || 10.107–108 ||
O twice-born one, the invocation (*āvāhana*) of this [fire] is its bringing face-to-face;
when the time for the *homa* has arrived, one should raise the fire situated in the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*),
and likewise awaken it at the time of the worship of the gods.

O Kāśyapa, when the yoga-pīṭha has been prepared and the placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*) performed— O Great-minded One, while the image is being made stable— the deities should be offered arghya, garments, ornaments, flowers, perfumes, and ointments. 10.110–111.
One should meditate on him standing when he is standing, and likewise seated during the rites of water for the feet and the sipping of water;
one should meditate on him seated during the consecration, seated upon a lotus throne;
and during the offering of incense, lamps, and food, one should meditate on him seated upon a svastika seat.
In other ritual services as well, one should remain consistent with the requirements of those specific rites.
While meditating upon and propitiating the deity, one should perform each respective action.
At the beginning of the *sāmgraha* and other rites, thinking "I am worshipping," one should scatter a handful of flowers.
Standing with palms joined in *añjali*, he should address the Lord with this verse:
"O Lord, sovereign of all the immortals, Viṣṇu, Jiṣṇu, Lord of Śrī!
I worship you with offerings such as the *arghya*; be pleased with me through your compassion. (10.115)
Having thus made this request and prostrated with the head, one should offer the *arghya* upon the [deity's] head;
one should cast the first portion of the *pādya* into the vessel for receiving the foot-water;
then, during the offering of the *ācamana*, one should meditate on the Lord as being filled with water.
Furthermore,
while he sips water, one should present incense rich with the fragrance of agallochum for the acceptance of the God of Gods;
one should also present a lamp with camphor before the God of Gods.
One should ring the bell during the invocation, the offering of water (arghya), the incense, and the feeding of the retinue;
however, one must not ring it when showing the lamps.
Furthermore, one should scatter handfuls of flowers at each offering before the lotus feet.
Having presented the madhuparka, he should grasp the Lord's lotus feet with both hands and bow down before them with his head, preceded by devotion.
Having prostrated himself like a staff upon the ground, he should then address the Lord.
"I am your slave, O God, together with my sons and my possessions. Command me as you wish in whatever duties must be performed, O Teacher of the World.
Having made this request, he should thereafter arrange his retinue. (10.122–10.123)
On the petals of the lotus-throne, one should worship in sequence starting from the east:
Śrī, Kaustubha, Vanamālā, and the Vaiṣṇavī Yogamāyā;
likewise Vimalā, Sṛṣṭiśakti, and Utkarṣiṇī.
Jñānaśakti, Satyaśakti, Īśānī, and Anukampakā;
Pitāmahī—these are remembered as the twelve Śaktis in sequence, located in the directions starting from the east in the first enclosure (prathamāvaraṇa) according to their order. || 10.125–10.126 ||
Pervasion (vyāpti), splendor (kānti), contentment (tṛpti), faith (śraddhā), knowledge (vidyā), compassion (dayā), and forbearance (kṣamā)—
these eight, ending with Śakti, hold chowries and fly-whisks;
having worshipped them in the second enclosure, one should worship those bearing the conch, discus, and other emblems.
One should worship these Puruṣas in the four directions starting from the east:
Śrīvārāha, Nārasiṃha, Śrīdhara, and Hayānana.
In the corners starting from the southeast, one should worship the two Rāmas, Bhārgava and Rāghava.
Vāmana and Vāsudeva—these eight are remembered in sequence;
and in the third enclosure, one should worship the eight weapons:
Pāñcajanya, Musala, Cakra, and Nandaka.
One should worship the mace, the Śārṅga bow, the discus, and the forest garland in sequence.
Then, in the fourth enclosure, one should subsequently worship Kumuda and the others in order.
And in the fifth enclosure, one should worship the guardians of the directions, beginning with Indra.
Having thus fashioned Garuḍa standing facing the deity,
with his two hands joined in *añjali*, one should worship him with offerings such as water for the feet (*arghya*) and other ritual requisites.
One should also worship the goddess Śrī on the right side of the deity.
On the left, one should worship the ground according to the respective deities here with water for honor (*arghya*) and other offerings.
(10.134) Outside the second enclosure, in the intermediate direction between the north and east, one should worship Viṣvaksena, who has four arms and holds a conch and a discus. (10.135)
Afterwards, one should inform the Lord that it is time to go to the bathing seat;
once the Lord has risen, one should place the sandals before him.
With the two verses beginning with "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," one should cause him to step upon them.
With the mantra "uttiṣṭha brahmaṇaspate," he should lead [the deity] to the bathing altar;
with "bhadraṃ karṇebhiḥ," he should seat [the deity] upon the altar.
The *arghya* offering should be made with the *Viṣṇugāyatrī*, and the *pādya* with the verse beginning "viṣṇo" (or "viṣṇupade").
One should cause the Lord of the World to rinse his mouth with the mantra "āpaḥ punantu," and then,
having displayed [the offering] consisting of a measure of śāli rice, one should again offer the madhuparka with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī and with the mantra "jitaṃ te."
One should offer betel leaf and provide mouth-fresheners;
one should give a tooth-stick to Viṣṇu with the mantra "tad viṣṇoḥ," and one should offer a tongue-scraper to the Lord with the mantra "tad viprāsaḥ."
One should again offer water for washing the face with the Viṣṇugāyatrī;
having offered betel-leaf with the mantra "jitaṃ te," one should scatter flowers at the feet and thereafter anoint the Lord.
With the Vāmadevya mantra, he should cause him to receive the garland with that very same [mantra].
Having shown him the mirror, he should then perform the rubbing with black gram powder for the Lord, reciting "viṣṇornukaṃ. || 10.143-10.144 ||

One should not offer water with *viṣṇo* [as a mantra]; rather, one should offer pure *āmalaka* water for washing, reciting the *gandhatoya* mantras and the *āpo hi ṣṭhā* hymn. One should then sprinkle [the image] with seventeen jars filled with grain.
With the mantra "hiraṇyavarṇāṃ hariṇīm," one should apply an ointment of turmeric;
having smeared [the image] with saffron and adorned it with garlands of flowers,
one should sprinkle it with water from the jars and wash it with the Pāvamānī hymns.
Having clothed him in a pair of garments and anointed him with sandalwood paste,
one should worship the Supreme Lord with garlands and offerings such as the *arghya*, while reciting the verses "brahma jajñānam" and "kayā naścitra ābhuvat. (10.148)
Having performed the bath with a thousand streams accompanied by the *Puruṣasūkta*, one should wipe the limbs with a cloth while reciting the mantra "Agnirmūrdhā.
Then, having provided two clean, washed garments, one should clothe him in them. (10.149–10.150)
Having fashioned the sacred thread and the upper garment with the *praṇava*,
and having offered water for sipping (*ācamana*), one should thereafter pray for forgiveness.
Having presented the sandals, one should lead the Lord to the seat of ornaments.
When that deity is seated comfortably, one should worship him again with the arghya and other offerings.
Having dried his hair with incense made from agaru, while reciting the Ṛgvedic verse "divo dhārām," and then having anointed him with pure, fragrant sandalwood paste; ||| 10.152–153 ||
Having smeared the body thinly with camphor and snow-melted water while reciting the "Idaṃ Viṣṇu" mantra,
one should scatter unbroken rice grains on the feet while reciting the "Irāvatī" mantra.
Having adorned [the image] with ornaments such as a crown using the mantra "jitaṃ te," and having placed upon it various beautiful flower garlands,
one should apply collyrium using the mantra "tad viṣṇoḥ" and the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī. || 10.155–10.156 ||
After placing [the object] before his eyes, he should then show him even a mirror.
By means of the *vyāhṛti* mantras, that [object] is conquered; he should then fumigate it with incense arising from *agaru*.
Furthermore, with incenses of fragrant scent, he should again display lamps.
With the mantra "Uddīpyasva," one should offer sesame seeds and even rice grains,
as well as clothing, gold, betel, various gems, cooked meats, cows, and grains with clarified butter, according to one's wealth. || 10.158–159 ||
And the preceptor, having placed a cow-hide before the God of gods,
when this gift is made for the sake of the Vaiṣṇavas,
it shall become the cause of happiness for the subjects dwelling within the kingdom of the lord of the earth. || 10.160 ||
Having performed the rite of removal and dispelling obstacles out of compassion for his devotees,
he should cause all musical instruments to be played along with the sounds of conchs and trumpets,
and even with golden horns that bring delight to the ears.
One should have songs sung by singers and have dances performed by female dancers;
one should cause chariots, elephants, horses, palanquins, and the like to be prepared;
and one should display excellent vehicles and Garuḍa atop the banner.
Having established and displayed a parasol made of pearls, they then fanned the Lord on all sides with white yak-tail whisks, peacock-feather fans,
palm-leaf fans, and silken cloths.
He should have the Brahmins recite the four Vedas along with their auxiliary sciences (ṣaḍaṅga);
he should cause the chanting of hymns to be performed by Brahmins who are most proficient in the Vedas,
using lamps lit with cow's ghee placed in golden vessels.
One should also perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) for the deity with the finest offerings brought by the most excellent brahmins.
Then, one should inform the deity regarding the meal, the seat, and the vehicle.
After offering the sandals, one should then lead the deity to the place of the meal.
To the deity seated there, one should offer water for the feet (pādya) along with the respectful offering (arghya);
thereafter, one should present water for sipping (ācamanīya) and the honey-mixture (madhuparka).
Then, with the syllable Om (praṇava), one should offer a roll of betel leaves.
One should present a cow with its calf, adorned with golden hooves and horns,
along with a measure of eight kinds of grains placed in vessels; and one should give her to the worshipper for the sake of completing the ritual worship.
One should present the prepared food, consisting of the fourfold varieties of milk-rice (pāyasa),
prepared as appropriate with fruits that are neither undercooked nor overripe, produced in all seasons, and endowed with sweet and other flavors. (10.172)
Having sprinkled [the offering] with the Astra-mantra and protected it with the Varma-mantra,
and having offered worship with the Praṇava, one should perform the rites of burning,
moistening, and so forth; then, for the sake of pacifying defects in the sacrificial food (haviḥ), one should cause it to be circumambulated clockwise.
Having formed and displayed the *saurabhī* mudrā with devotion,
and having placed the flower situated in the *arghya* vessel in due order,
one should form the so-called *viṣṇuhasta* with the left hand.
While [the disciple] maintains contact with his right hand, which is joined in the *grāsamudrā* gesture,
he should, with a mind full of devotion and careful attention, pour [the offering] into the right hand of the Deity while reciting the mantra "devasya tvā. (10.176–177)
One should ring the bell during the three offerings of *arghya*, incense, and food.
Having offered the purifying food and well-prepared water for drinking,
one should offer water for sipping (*ācamanīya*) and rub sandalwood paste upon the hands.
One should offer betel-leaf accompanied by camphor;
and one should cause a handful of rice mixed with gems to be given to the Ācārya.
O best of the twice-born, the entire collection of rites prescribed for the ritual worship (karmārcā) should be performed. || 10.179–10.180 ||
The wise one should perform all of that for the *dhruvabera* (the permanent image) and so forth;
having asked the Lord of Gods for forgiveness with a mind bowed in devotion,
O twice-born, he should worship the attendants with the four [substances] beginning with fragrance.
Having offered the hymns of praise, the wise practitioner should again recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times, or half of that, or half of that again. Then,
holding the vessel of *arghya* in his hand, he should exit to the front pavilion.
Having thus performed the fire sacrifice and then gone into the presence of the deity,
he should report that ritual [which has been completed] at the pair of the god’s lotus-feet;
then, according to the procedure for a great festival, he should offer the oblation to the retinue.
One should worship Viṣvaksena with the offerings remaining after they have been enjoyed by the deity;
having made a petition to the God of gods, one should prostrate on the ground like a staff,
taking up all the remaining articles of worship in their entirety.

Having gone home and worshipped the Lord of the Universe, who resides within the lotus of the heart, with those materials, one shall always be one who has accomplished all that was to be done. Thus, in the *Pañcarātra*, in the *Mahopaniṣad*, in the *Viśvāmitra-saṃhitā*.
The tenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Sequence of Constant Worship.
The eleventh chapter: Kāśyapa.
"Having performed the fire sacrifice," so it was said by the Blessed One; "that which was ordained for me, its procedure has not been instructed. Tell me that, even in brief.
(11.1) — Viśvāmitra.
O Sage, listen attentively to the procedure for the fire-pit (agnikārya) during initiation rites, consecration, installation, and festivals;
likewise, in all expiatory ceremonies, and especially during ritual ablutions. || 11.2 ||
In these and all other such rites,
O observer of noble vows, listen now to the general procedure for the oblation.
Having approached the kitchen, wash both your feet.
Having sipped water, he should construct a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) with the proper characteristics in the portion of the ground intended for sacrifice;
it should be one cubit in length, square, and provided with three tiers (mekhalā).
It should be equipped with a rim and a navel, and its depression (avaṭa) should be equal in width [to the pit].
The head is in the eastern direction; the two arms are in the northeast and southeast corners; the pair of feet is in the southwest and northwest corners;
the belly should be in the center of the pit, and the yoni is prescribed as the [central] yoni.
Having occupied an excellent seat situated to the west of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa),
wearing an upper garment and with his sacred thread over the right shoulder, he should perform the fire-oblation (homa) facing the east.
Having swept the pit and smeared it with cow-dung mixed with water, [he should proceed].
Having swept with those very *kuśa* grasses, one should sprinkle [the site] with the root mantra (*mūlavidyā*).
Alternatively, one may perform the fire-oblation (*havana*) according to the rules upon a bare sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*).
One should place a vessel of flowers on the right side of oneself.
One should cause the other sacrificial materials to be placed on the left side:
fuel-sticks together with *kuśa* grass, the cooking-pot for the *caru*, the vessel for the clarified butter,
the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), water, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and the stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*).
Having set aside the fans, the ladle, the heap of dry wood,
the preparation for moving the fire, the fragrant substances, and the aromatic powers— these pairs of items— he should employ them if they are available.
One should draw three lines extending eastward in the center of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa),
and likewise three lines extending northward, while reciting the root mantra (mūlavidyā).
Having removed those two blades of darbha grass and washed one's hands with water, [one should proceed].
One should place either churned fire or even ordinary worldly fire there;
having established the fire with the syllable *praṇava*,
one should fan it and then surround it with three sets of three darbha-blades each, with their tips pointing toward the east and the north.

Having placed the *praṇītā* vessel— filled with water, honored with unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and containing a *kūrca* of *darbha* grass— with its mouth facing north in the midst of the primary sacrificial materials;
and having fixed a cutting blade (*chedana*) made of three *darbha* blades, measuring one span (*prādeśa*) in length, upon it.
With those very *darbha* strainers, one should offer the *praṇītā* water in the hollowed palms;
one should then place the *prokṣaṇī* vessel together with its *kūrca* grass before oneself.
Holding that *kūrca* between the thumbs and the tips of the ring fingers of both hands, one should [use it]. || 11.18–19 ||
With a *kūrca* made of three-stranded grass, he should again sprinkle all the materials for the oblation with that water, accompanied by the *āghāra* formula;
and he should touch those materials while pronouncing their respective names.
One should cause the water from the *prokṣaṇī* vessel to flow in a clockwise direction all around.
Having filled the *praṇītā* vessel with water, one should honor the deity there.
Then, having spread out a seat of *darbha* grass on the southern side of the fire, [one should proceed]. || 11.21-22 ||
Having meditated upon Brahmā within the *kūrca* and offered it before him,
and having worshipped again with substances such as perfumes while reciting the Viṣṇu-Gāyatrī,
one should place an *āḍhaka* measure of rice in a cooking pot and purify it.
Having placed it upon the edge of the fire-vessel, one should quickly cook the sacrificial porridge (caru). Then, having poured the strained and melted clarified butter (ājya) into the butter-pot,
one should place a pair of darbha-grass tips there with the root mantra.
Having placed it over the embers to the north with fire,
and having performed the circumambulation of the fire three times with a blade of *darbha* grass, he should lower it [the vessel] and,
having cast the *darbha* into the fire, place clarified butter before himself.
Having purified that *kūrca* grass three times and touched it and the fire with the *ādibha* [mudrā],
one should strike [the oblation] and render the clarified butter immortal (*amṛtīkuryāt*) by means of the *surabhi* mudrā.
Thereafter, one should honor the guardians of the directions, headed by Indra, in their proper order.
Having washed the *sruc* and *sruva* ladles with hot milk using a bundle of *kuśa* grass,
one should wipe those two ladles— at their base, middle, and tip—
with the root, middle, and tip of the *kuśa* bundle respectively, O best of sages. (11.29)
Having heated the two *amra* fruits and placed them to the north of himself,
and having taken clarified butter with the *sruc* ladle, he should sprinkle it over the objects of the oblation.
Having sprinkled the *sarū* with the clarified butter and having set it down in the vessel, [he should proceed].
One should prepare four kinds of sacrificial porridge (caru)— made of milk-rice, jaggery-rice, and rice with mung beans, as well as rice alone— or one may cook the caru on the hearth.
Whatever is offered to the image, all of that should also be offered as an oblation (homa).
Having begun from the west, one should have the enclosing sticks (paridhis) placed in a northward orientation.
Then, having sprinkled water all around, one should place a fuel-stick (samidh) in the northeast direction;
furthermore, one should place another fuel-stick upon the *praṇītā* vessel.
Mentally fixing his mind upon the Lord, the manifest husband of Lakṣmī,
he should offer oblations of clarified butter from a single vessel, even if it is only once.
Having placed the clarified butter in his left hand, which is spread over a bundle of kuśa grass, he should perform the offering.
Then he should perform the oblation for Prajāpati and the oblation for Indra as the foundational offerings (ādhāra-huti).
He should offer the portion of clarified butter (ājyabhāga) in the southern half of the eastern quarter;
the portion for Soma in the northern part; and in the center, he should offer with the Vyāhṛtis.
At the time of the fire sacrifice (homa), one should meditate upon Agni as having seven hands and two heads,
endowed with three feet, and possessed of seven tongues;
he is the granter of boons, holding a spear in his hand, and also bearing the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles.
He holds a shield that grants fearlessness and a vessel of clarified butter in his left hand.
That which is called Kālī is said to occupy the middle position on the tongue;
she should be known as dark-colored, while Karālī is red in color.
Then, in the eastern quarter of that place, there is one yellow in color and swift as thought;
she should be known as red, with the hue of fire, in the southern direction.
She would be situated in the western direction, smoky in color, and bearing a name corresponding to her appearance.
Established in the north, she is white in color and emits sparks; she resides in the southeast corner. Then the seventh is Viśvarūpā;
she has the luster of the bimba fruit and her abode is in the northeast.

In the Kālī [flame], there should be a fire-oblation for pacification; in the Karālī, victory shall be attained. Manojava brings about nourishment, and in the Lohitā, there is the power of subjugation. In the Dhūmrā, one should perform killing; in the Sphuliṅginī, there are prosperities.
In the rite called Viśvarūpa, there shall be the great fruit beginning with atomization (aṇimā).
For the pacification of water, one should offer sesame seeds mixed with honey;
one should perform eight hundred oblations with the mantra consisting of thirty-two syllables.
At the conclusion of the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should establish the Vaiṣṇava fire;

then the Vedic rites for the fire, beginning with the impregnation ceremony (garbhādhāna), must be performed. In the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), one should visualize Lakṣmī, having bathed after her menses and adorned with all ornaments.
Having meditated upon the god Nārāyaṇa, who is beautiful in all his limbs,
one should perform the rite of conception (*garbhādhāna*) with the first seed-syllable,
and then perform the rite for ensuring a male child (*puṃsavana*) with the second seed-syllable.
The practitioner should perform the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana) in the third month;
the birth-rite (jātakarma) in the fourth, and the naming-rite (nāmakarma) in the following month.
The first feeding of solid food (annaprāśana) is in the sixth month, the tonsure (caula) in the seventh, and the initiation (upanayana) in the eighth.
By means of the eighth [syllable], this eight-syllable mantra should be established. The procedure should be performed in due order; now hear the procedure for the twelve-syllable [mantra].
One should perform it according to the rule by means of the four seed-syllables beginning with the ninth. || 11.51–52 ||
The Prājāpatya, the Saumya, and immediately after that the Āgneya;
these four [oblations] are offered in the sequence of the Vaiśvadeva, according to order.
One should offer the fuel-stick and the seed-syllable with the twelve-syllable vidyā-mantra.
Then, having offered one hundred and eight oblations with the mantra complete with its ancillaries (sāṅga),
he should worship the foremost deity with all the substances such as perfumes and so forth.
In the midst of that, he should prepare the yoga-pīṭha for the God of gods.
One should offer oblations repeatedly with cow-derived ghee while reciting those mantras.

In the midst of that, having brought down the Lord of Śrī from the heart-lotus and having performed the entire ritual of mantra-installation (*mantranyāsa*) and so forth according to the rules, || 11.56 ||
Having thus offered sixteen oblations in sequence for the sixteen enjoyments, beginning with the *arghya* and so forth,
for each of the attendants one by one,
one should likewise perform the offering to the Blessed One in the seven-flamed fire along with the vessels.
And immediately thereafter, if there is a rite of worship for Bimba and the others,
one should perform the oblation with palāśa fuel-sticks and so forth, as will be described hereafter.
Those fuel-sticks should be the size of a palm tree, or even as small as the little finger.
A sacrificial fuel (samidh) that is thick and causes agitation leads indeed to a lack of rain;
one that is short causes excessive rain; one that is skinless brings about the destruction of wealth;
one that is split causes the ruin of the family; and one that is scarred brings about the destruction of the wife.
One with branches causes agitation; one that is old brings about the destruction of sons;

one that is wet causes the loss of kinsmen; and one containing an insect brings about total ruin. O Sage, fuel-sticks that are flawless and smeared with clarified butter should be offered as oblations.
One should offer the *caru* mixed with clarified butter in the measure of a mouthful according to the *grāsamudrā*.
One should offer clarified butter with the *sruva* ladle, and offer fuel-sticks (*samidh*) with the hand.
One should offer the *caru* with a leaf of the *palāśa* tree, or with the hand alone.
O twice-born Kāśyapa, one should offer unbroken flowers and fruits,
as well as grains, sesame seeds, and rice,
using the tips of the fingers as the measure, quickly and with great purity.
The knower of mantras should offer oblations of that same measure, having anointed them with clarified butter.
Having thus performed the oblation according to the prescribed rule, the most excellent of preceptors should then perform an expiation with clarified butter using the five Upaniṣads.

Taking a sacrificial ladle (*sruc*) filled with clarified butter (*ājya*) along with fuel sticks (*samidh*) made of *sadarbha* grass, one should lift it up as far as the tip of the nose while covering it with the *struva* spoon; then, one should offer it into the fire with the root-mantra. This shall constitute the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
Having gathered all the darbha grasses as prescribed in their proper order,
he completely burned them without remainder—
likewise the after-offerings (anuyāja), the supporting fuel-sticks (ādhāra-samidh), and the enclosing sticks (paridhi). || 11.69–70 ||
Having offered the oblation upward, one should again set down the *praṇītā* vessel before oneself;
then, taking water from the *prokṣaṇī* vessel and pouring it over the *praṇītā*,
one should sprinkle water upon the ground starting from the east and ending with the north (the direction of Soma).
Having cast off his body toward the west and sprinkled himself with water,
having also dismissed the Brahman and performed the ritual sprinkling (pariṣeka),
he should then offer the deity situated between the fires into the lotus of his own heart.
Having filled the *sruc* with water and sprinkled it outside the sacrificial pit in a clockwise direction,
and then having sprinkled himself with the remainder,
he should apply a mark (*tilaka*) with ashes, take the *arghya* offering, and enter. || 11.74 ||
Having offered that oblation at the lotus feet of the God of Dhāmri,
[he said]: "O God, O Supreme Lord, please accept this worship as it was performed by me according to my ability, which has been placed before You."

Having thus informed the Lord of Gods and having prostrated before him like a staff, one becomes one who has fulfilled his duty; thus has the fire-ritual been described by me to you. (11.77) Thus [ends] the Viśvāmitra-saṃhitā within the Mahopaniṣad of the Pañcarātra.
[The Ritual for the Agnikārya], the Eleventh Chapter.
The Twelfth Chapter. Viśvāmitra.
O Brahman, listen as I shall explain the procedure for the perpetual festival (*nityotsava*).
In this Tantra, three types of festivals were previously proclaimed by Brahmā.
In the morning, one should invoke the Supreme Lord into the rice grains placed within the vessel.

O Sage, he should circumambulate accompanied by the twelve Śaktis. O twice-born one, at the time of dawn, at midday, and in the evening when flowers have gathered, or else at these three times, he should cause [the image] to move for the sake of the offering.
O best of the twice-born, for the sake of offering the bali-oblation, one should install the Lord of Gods within the bali-image at Dhruva and all other enclosures,
and then worship Him with services beginning with the arghya offering.
Then [he saw] a pure, excellent brahmin, wearing white garments,
with an upper cloth and a turban, bearing the twelve sectarian marks (*puṇḍra*),
a Vaiṣṇava of pleasant count, self-controlled, young, and devoted to the recitation of prayers.
Having meditated upon Garuḍa, one should place him upon his head (one should deposit the *bali* offering upon his head).
Rich with the sounds of conchs and *kāhala* trumpets, preceded by the resonance of musical instruments,
another person should hold a golden water-pot together with its handle.

Another should hold a vessel filled with offerings for the *bali*. Then, on the side of the door of the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*), near the threshold (*udumbara*)—specifically on the right—is Vāstunātha, two-armed and holding a red vessel. || 12.8–12.9 ||
O best of the twice-born, the Lord of the Site (Vāstunātha) should be meditated upon as wearing white garments, taking refuge in the gods, with his right hand raised holding a mace.
The Lord of the Field (Kṣetranātha) has a staff in his hand and resembles a dark blue cloud.
O twice-born one, having meditated upon the two [deities]— one holding his left hand in the *muṣṭika* gesture and positioned on the left side, gazing at the face of the Lord,
and the other situated in the middle of the *udumbara* tree above, adorned with all ornaments— one should worship them both.

One should worship Dvāraśrī (the Goddess of the Door’s Splendor), who resembles molten gold, whose lower lip is like coral, who holds a lotus and a water-pot in her hands, and who dwells upon a lotus;
she is to be worshipped at the base of the right door-panel of the inner sanctum.
O twice-born one, he has his turban bound and an upright sectarian mark (urdhvapuṇḍra), wears white garments, and is adorned with necklaces, armlets, bracelets, earrings, and other ornaments;
he possesses the radiance of the rising sun and has four arms, with [one] on the right. || 12.14-12.15 ||
In his two arms, he holds a discus in the upper hand and a mace resting upon the surface of his hip with its tip relaxed;
in the left [hand] he bears a blazing conch, and in the upper [hand] a rosary.
Having thus meditated upon Caṇḍa below, O best of the twice-born, one should worship him;
and one should also worship Pracaṇḍa, whose pair of arms are crossed.
One should worship Garuḍa, who resembles gold and is radiant with a pair of curved eyebrows.
One should properly worship the god of gods, who has a protruding belly and round eyes, adorned with all ornaments,
clad in blue garments, resplendent with a pair of wings,
and standing with palms joined in reverence before him.
Then, one should worship the two leaders of the Gaṇas, who are well-situated upon the two door-panels of the front pavilion,
who resemble the interior of a lotus, who possess arms like those of Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa,
and who are adorned with red garments and other ornaments.
Likewise, both Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ are in the first enclosure;
Kumuda is in the eastern direction, adorned with various garments and ornaments,
four-armed, and holding a white chowrie in his pair of right hands.
One should worship him who holds the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya-mudrā*) in his right hand, as well as a necklace and a garland;
he bears the sign of silence and has lotus-like eyes, with his pair of arms crossed in the southeast corner.
In the south, one should likewise worship Puṇḍarīka, who has the luster of gold and bears the banner of Garuḍa;
and in the southwest (Nairṛta), one should worship Vāmana. In the west, one should worship Śaṅkukarṇa, whose body is the color of the five precious gems.
O bull among the twice-born, one should worship according to the rules the deity Sarpanetra, who stands in the northwest corner and holds a fly-whisk made of peacock feathers. And in the north,
one should devote oneself to the dark-complexioned deity named Sumukha, who carries an umbrella.
Having thus meditated upon Supratiṣṭha in the northeast, one should offer praise.
O Kāśyapa, whatever remains unmentioned regarding these [deities] is like that of Kumuda.
All [the deities] are adorned with an upright *puṇḍra* mark situated on the forehead.

One should worship Jaya and Vijaya, who stand at the sides of that outer gate. O Sage, both of these resemble Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa; they are four-armed, wear yellow garlands and garments, and have yellow turbans upon their heads.
O best of men, one should place Upendra in the western part,
Tejo-dhara in the southeast, and the one named Duratikrama in the south;
likewise, Mahākarma and Mahāhrada in the southwest and the west.
One should place Agṛhya in the northwest, Vasu-retas in the north; likewise Vardhamāna in the northeast, Sākṣin above the sky,
and Ādhāra-nitya at the base of everything, in due order.
One should worship these [deities], who possess the luster of crystal and grant boons and fearlessness with their hands;
or else, those holding a rosary, a discus, a conch,
and a mace in their four hands, and adorned with crowns and other ornaments.

Then, one should worship both Abhadra and Subhadra, who stand at the sides of the door of the third enclosure, just as one worships Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa. Following that, one should worship Indra, who is dark-complexioned and four-armed.

One should worship Agni, who is red in color, mounted upon a goat, holding a sharp-edged thunderbolt (*kuliśa*) and a spear (*śakti*) in his hand; and one should worship Yama, who is black, mounted upon a buffalo, and holding a staff (*daṇḍa*) in his hand. 12.37.
[He saw] Nirṛti, who has a corpse for a seat, who holds a sword, and possesses a black luster;
Varuṇa, mounted upon a crocodile, white as a pearl, and holding a noose;
and Vāyu, mounted upon a deer, marked with a black banner on his foot.
One should worship the Moon, white and mounted upon a hare; Śiśira, white and mounted upon a bull, holding a trident and possessing three eyes, with the luster of coral;
and beneath him, the King of Serpents, mounted upon a tortoise and bearing a plow. || 12.40 ||

One should worship Brahmā, seated upon a swan, possessing four faces, while meditating [upon him]. All of these [deities] have four arms; remembering that they hold rosaries and contemplate the Supreme Lord, one should worship them with hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Having worshipped Amareśa and Virūpākṣa, who stand at the sides of the gateway,
as well as the collection of weapons beginning with the discus in the fourth enclosure—
the thunderbolt, the spear, the staff, the sword, the noose, and likewise the banner— (12.43).
One should worship these in sequence: the Śiśirāstra and the trident (triśūla).
[Then] both the Śaṅkhanidhi and Padmanidhi, situated at the sides of the great gateway (mahāgopura), resembling Śaṅkha and Padma respectively, and clothed in white garlands and garments.
One should worship these two [deities] mounted upon treasure-vessels, with short hands and feet,
holding conchs and lotuses, or alternatively, with treasures in their hands.
Having worshipped the weapons of the Blessed One, one should then offer worship to them in the eight directions.
One should worship, in due order, the conch, the mace, the discus, and the sword Nandaka; the mallet, the Śārṅga bow, the lotus, and the forest garland.
Having placed the Lord upon a palanquin, one should pray for the offering of oblations.
At the time of offering the oblation, one should have the singers sing various songs and have the dancers perform their respective dances,
accompanied on all sides by the sound of musical instruments such as conchs, trumpets, and kettledrums.
Deafening the quarters with the sounds of drums, he performed the ritual of offering oblations;
the space between the directions was completely covered by various banners, parasols, clusters of palm-leaf fans, and yak-tail whisks being waved.
It was filled on all sides with various maidens adorned with ornaments and wearing garments made of fine silk;
it was also accompanied by throngs of singers resembling the kings of the Gandharvas.
Attended by the best of the twice-born both in front and behind,
he recited the four Vedas in groups,
each being served separately at various stations with betel and diverse kinds of food.
Having offered well-ripened fruits and cakes, and having gratified the knowers of the Vedas, the singers, and the dancers with gifts,
he proceeded thus everywhere until his departure from the gate of Gopapura.
Having silenced the sound of musical instruments and such, one should cause the conch alone to resound.
Having gone out near the great pedestal and facing the temple,
one should have it proclaimed in every direction by means of various musical instruments.
Having washed the top of the pedestal with pure fragrant water and having worshipped the lords who are the attendants of Viṣṇu there as well,
one should place the remainder of the offering upon the head of the pedestal and leave nothing behind.
Having had singers sing various kinds of melodies,
and having been danced around by dancing girls from all sides,
he should circumambulate three times and then enter the interior of the sanctuary once more.
Having reached the portico and helped him descend from the palanquin,
and having offered him his sandals and seated the Lord upon the throne,
he should worship Him again with all the ritual offerings, beginning with the *arghya*.
Having presented various kinds of offerings appropriate for the occasion,
and reciting the *Śākuna-sūkta*, he led the God of gods into another chamber, seated him as before, and served him with food.
Then, having offered the arghya and other ritual gifts according to tradition, the best of worshippers should display various kinds of song and dance before the deity outside [the shrine].
In the event that disturbances such as excessive rain or intense heat should occur, [he should perform these acts].
One should not perform a regular festival; one should merely offer a bali-oblation.
Or, one may simply cast the bali-oblation before Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa, preceded by the root mantra for those two.
Having said "Namo bhūtebhyaḥ" (Salutation to the beings), one should cast the bali offering along with water.
At the time of giving the bali, one should release it with their own names,
ending in the dative case and followed by "namaḥ," preceded by the syllable Om.
"Only after displaying one's own respective mudrā is the rite ordained; it is not performed otherwise.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Daily Festival," in the Viśvāmitra-saṃhitā of the Mahopaniṣad within the Pañcarātra.
The Thirteenth Chapter.
Kāśyapa said: "O Blessed One, please explain to me the classification [and application] of mantras and mudrās."
"O Omniscient One, if you have compassion for me, you ought to explain [this]. Viśvāmitra says:
'The various ways of joining the fingers together are called *mudrās*.'"

Because it causes the dissolution (*drāvayate*) of delusion (*muda*) in an instant upon the mere sight of the wicked, it is therefore called "Mudrā" by those expert in mantra and tantra. It serves as the expulsion of those who would cause harm and the propitiation of the gods. || 13.2-13.3 ||
Because these [mudrās] are seen at the beginning of ritual actions and so forth, one should therefore display them.
Just as the enumeration of the collection of mantras is prescribed according to what has been received,
in that very same way, one should display the mudrā in secret and not before the public.
Having washed both hands and purified them with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya),
and having anointed them with auspicious fragrances, one should subsequently display the mudrā:
with the middle and ring fingers held together, the thumb is extended between them.
Having inserted the fist into the heart and fixed it there,
this Heart Mudrā should be employed during the ritual of the placement of the mantra-limbs (mantrāṅganyāsa).
Having turned it face-downward and placed it upon the head, [one should proceed].
One should strike the index finger with the tip of the thumb; this is the *śīrṣamudrā*.
Having formed a fist with the thumb pointing upward, one should touch the tip of the thumb above the crest-lock (*śikhā*);
this is declared by the wise to be the *śikhāmudrā*.
Having formed the thumb-mudrā and bound a raised fist,
with the forefinger slightly bent at its tip— by means of this fist-mudrā,
one should meditate upon the binding of armor at the heart; this mudrā is of the nature of the armor (kavaca).

Having formed a fist by joining the thumb and index finger with three rows [of fingers], one should place the thumb and index finger at the top like a circle on the outside and snap them in all directions;
this is the mudrā known as the Weapon (astra). || 13.11–13.12 ||

One should place the *śikhāmudrā* with its tip facing downward between the eyebrows; this is declared to be the *cakṣurmudrā*. O Sage, one should perform these [mudrās] on the limbs in sequence, using the right hand.
Having raised the index finger and joined the three [middle fingers] together,
one should place the thumbs against them and rotate one's own body outward in a clockwise direction; this is declared to be the *sagrīva-prākāra-mudrā*.
The wise one should perform the protection of his own body with this mudrā:
having placed the left hand extended below the navel,
he should turn it palm upward and place the right hand upon it.
It is renowned as the *yogamudrā*. Then,
O bull among the twice-born, one should place the right palm above the navel according to the prescribed method, and further, place the hand with the thumbs joined together upon that [other hand].
This pair of mudrās is indeed the Yoga-sampuṭa-mudrā.
It is prescribed for yogins during the rite of the withdrawal of reality (tattva-saṃhāra) and in the act of generation;
it is recommended for the practice of yoga and should be employed in that very ritual.
The *kumbhamudrā* is said to be the *yogasaṃpuṭa-mudrā*.
It is shaped like a jar with a perforation, and likewise positioned facing upwards.
With it, one should perform the ritual bathing; [one should touch] the navel and the head with the index finger.
Having placed them in sequence, one should likewise join the thumb and the little finger;
this shall be the Saṃhāra-mudrā for the rite of the withdrawal of the principles (tattva).
One should display this mudrā during the dismissal of the deities.
When the four fingers are drawn together, it is the *saṃhṛti* (withdrawal) mudrā;
when the index finger is released, know that to be the *sṛṣṭi* (creation) mudrā.
It is intended for the invocation of the deities and for the creation of the *tattvas*.

The joining of the index finger and the thumb is declared to be the *jñānamudrā*; the ancient masters, however, know this as the *tattvamudrā*. [This is performed with both hands raised and turned upward.]
One should touch the two middle [fingers] with the two middle [fingers]; this is the *nyāsamudrā*.
This mudrā is known as "divine" (*devātmikā*) for those two in the ritual placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*).
Now hear, O Brahman, about the *japamudrā*: with both thumbs of both hands... 13.27.
One should touch the middle parts of the two index fingers while the others are extended;
during all times of recitation, one should display this *japa-mudrā*,
O best of the twice-born, with all the fingers of both hands joined together.

This is declared by the best of the twice-born to be the Brāhmī mudrā, which has the shape of a casket. Having joined the pair of thumbs and the pair of little fingers and index fingers of both hands together, one should bring their tips into contact; this they know as the Viṣṇu-mudrā.
O noble one, when the thumbs are joined with each other, it is called the Rudramudrā;
that is described to you as the Ubhayāṅguṣṭha-mudrā. Having covered the two ears with both hands, one should extend [one hand].
That same [gesture], when performed with the right hand, is the mudrā for saluting the ancestors (pitṛs).
Likewise, having placed the fingers of the left hand upon the left ear, one should extend the other hand; this is the mudrā of Vidhṛtarāja.
One should join the pair of thumbs between the two index fingers;
this, O bull among the twice-born, is declared to be the Bhāgavatī mudrā.
When the hands are formed into a hollowed casket, it is declared to be the Vārāha mudrā.
Then, having touched— or rather, having visualized— a red lotus in his right hand,
he should place upon its center a blazing triangular seed-syllable of fire,
written in reverse order, and cast it into the head of the molten metal.
This shall be the mudrā of Agni, which purifies all substances.
Having visualized a white sixteen-petaled lotus in the left hand,
one should meditate upon the moon in its center, endowed with its sixteen digits.
Therefore, having recollected the flowing nectar, one should sprinkle that ash. Then, having meditated upon it as having arisen again, this is known as the *āpyāyanī* (nourishing) mudrā:
[the two thumbs and the two index fingers, likewise the pair of little fingers]. 13.38–13.39.
Having joined [the hands] and extended them, one should contract the middle finger of the right hand;
then, having contracted the ring finger of the other [left] hand, one should extend the remaining fingers.
This is the Saurabheyī mudrā, which purifies all things.
Having formed the añjali with both hands, one should slightly open them.
This mudrā brings about invocation; O best of Brahmins, having seen this, the host of deities comes into close proximity. Therefore, one should display it.
Accompanied by expansion, this very [mudrā] is situated in the heart and at the head;
it is known as the *praṇāma-mudrā*, which quickly propitiates the gods, O Kāśyapa,
as well as the forms of Vāsudeva and others, and Viṣṇu and others.
O best of beings, for the deities beginning with Satya and likewise for those beginning with Mīna,
this very same mudrā is indeed the one that brings about nourishment for all.
Having joined the wrists together, one should likewise extend the fingers.
Having formed a hollowed space in the middle and likewise joined the two thumbs,
one should then turn them back, touch the backs, and extend them;
this shall be the *padma-mudrā*, which causes the [deities] such as Lakṣmī to become present.
Having placed the thumb of the left hand into the fist of the other [hand], and having joined the thumb and forefinger of the right hand while they are extended and held level,
one forms a fist-binding with the three remaining fingers of the left hand. || 13.47–48 ||
One should perform this conch mudrā, which bestows knowledge and liberation;
having placed the two hands horizontally, reaching as far as the wrists,
they should be turned toward one another and formed into a circle, O Kāśyapa.
This is the Cakra-mudrā, which destroys all malevolent beings.
Having formed two fists with both hands and bent the two thumbs, one should quickly extend the pair of middle fingers straight upward. (13.50–13.51)
One should form a mutual binding even with the other fingers;
joining the pair of elbows is proclaimed as the *gāḍha-mudrā*. One should touch the tip of the index finger with the middle finger; that is considered the *dhanur-mudrā* (bow mudrā).
Having straightened the left thumb and formed a fist with the other fingers,
one should bind that thumb with the [right hand] in sequence;
then, extending that thumb, this is the mudrā called Musalā.
Forming a fist with three fingers while excluding the thumb and the index finger,
one should again bind the bent tip of the index finger with that thumb;
this shall be the sword mudrā (*khaḍgamudrā*), which destroys the host of the wicked.
Having lowered the pair of hands so that they touch one another with their stainless palms, and having bound the pair of thumbs together, the Vanamālī [mudrā] is formed;
then, touching the right hand (apasavya-kara) while it is turned away from oneself, one should withdraw it. || 13.56–13.57 ||
One should fashion the left hand turned away and hanging down;
O twice-born one, these two gestures are known as the Varada and the Abhaya.
These two gestures should extend from Indra to Īśāna.
Having joined the two backs of the two hands together and interlocking the two little fingers,
one should extend the pair of index fingers so that they resemble a trunk;
the pair of thumbs should be hung downward like a pair of feet.
One should move the pair of other fingers like wings;
this shall be the Garuḍa-mudrā for the rite of destroying poison.
Having withdrawn the three fingers beginning with the little finger by means of the thumb, [one extends] the index finger.
This very mudrā, which propitiates Viṣvaksena,
is as follows: having extended all the fingers with their tips slightly bent and spaced apart,
and making them point upwards, one should perform this mudrā of Ananta.
Having placed the index finger of the left hand upwards and then the thumb at the tips of the [other] three fingers beginning with the lips, one forms the Caṇḍa-mudrā;
likewise, one should form the Pracaṇḍa-mudrā with the other hand.
One should raise the middle finger of the left hand; this is the *jayamudrā*. Likewise, one should form the *vijayā* mudrā with the other hand.
Similarly, one should form the *grāṅga* mudrā from the ring finger of the left hand.
This mudrā of that sage (the son of Yamunā) is proclaimed as being other than the former:
for Śaṅkha, the Lord of Nidhana, the little finger of the left hand [should be raised upward while remaining in one's own secret state]. 13.67.
In the same manner, one should form the *vastra-mudrā* with the ring finger and the thumb.

The *muṣṭi-mudrā* occurs when the fist is formed with the thumb wrapped around. The *snāna-mudrā* consists of the fingers released from the fist, with the tips of the little fingers touching the tops of the thumbs. || 13.68–69 ||
The wise know that same gesture with the middle fingers released as the *gandhamudrā*;
when the middle fingers are released, it is likewise celebrated as the *puṣpamudrā*. The *yajñopavītamudrā* occurs when the tips of the middle fingers rest upon the base of the thumbs.

The joining of the tips of the fingers at the tops of the thumbs and little fingers, according to the previously described arrangement—this is the *mudrā* of the ritual manual (*kalpa*). Having raised both hands with the thumbs extended, one should position the remaining group of fingers. (13.71–72)
Having performed the supreme *vyatikara* gesture, she should form the incense mudrā (*dhūpamudrikā*).
Having drawn back the little finger of the left hand and placed it facing upward, she should then position the middle finger and likewise withdraw the thumb. (13.73)
One should join the little finger with the ring and middle fingers;
likewise, when performed with the right hand,
the wise know this as the lamp mudrā, which brings pleasure to the Lord.
Among the various secondary rites, this mudrā consists of palms joined in añjali;
having placed the thumbs upward, with the fists formed by the other fingers,
it is known as the Pratimā-mudrikā, which brings delight to the gods.

Having raised the hands and gradually formed the añjali gesture, one should then separate the two thumbs; this is the *svāgata-mudrā* (gesture of welcome). This same gesture may also be the *prārthanā-mudrā* (gesture of supplication) and the *dhyāna-mudrā* (meditation gesture). || 13.77-78 ||
With the other hand placed upon the tips of the five fingers of the left hand,
one should offer the supreme food;
the wise know this as the "mudrā of the morsel," which always propitiates the gods.
Having lengthened both the little finger and the index finger,
one should also join the thumbs with the tips of the middle and ring fingers;
this is the *vrīhimukha* mudrā, used by the wise for the offering of grains.
Now the group of mudrās, beginning with the Ādhāraśakti, is described. Having formed two fists with both hands,
one should cast the left fist over the middle of the thumb [of the right hand], while the other [the right fist] remains above.
