This mudrā, born of the *ādhāra-śakti*, is declared to be *aspṛṣṭā*. When reversed, this same mudrā becomes *kūrmakālāgni*; it is the *priyaṃkarī*. Having placed the left hand face-downward, both [thumbs] should rest upon the back of the middle fingers.
One should make the index and ring fingers curved, while keeping the middle finger straight;
having done so, one should extend the little finger and the thumb as well. This is the Anantāsana mudrā, because one does not apply [the breath] into the mouth. || 13.85 ||
Having formed two fists with both hands while keeping three fingers grasped, one should join the pair of thumbs and index fingers and close them;
this is the *pṛthivīmudrā*. Now hear the *kṣīrābdhimudrā*.
O Sage, having joined the two wrists together, one should bring the thumb and the group of fingers face-to-face with each other, forming a hollow space at the tips of the nails;
within that, one should move the pair of thumbs without support.
This is that mudrā of the lotus which was previously described:
having joined the two hands together with the index fingers against each other, one should form it in such a way that the head is bound without the middle fingers. (13.89–13.90)

Then one should withdraw that pair of ring fingers; likewise, one should join the two little fingers together and bind them individually. One should clasp the pair of thumbs; this is the *dharmādimudrā*.
Understand these in sequence with a mind free from hesitation:
one should join the pair of the index finger and the thumb on the right hand,
and afterwards, very gradually, perform the unfolding of that bond.
Furthermore, from the re-emergence of the Śākhā-śaṅkha [Saṃgha], it becomes distinct.
One should manifest the mudrās of the three abodes; this is called the Haṃsatya. With both hands extended and touching, one should form them like the añjali gesture.
This is the pure mudrā of the Bhāvāsana for the Supreme Self:
O Sage, having taken all the fingers and so forth from the mouth [of the hand], one should take the middle finger of the right hand with the remaining three fingers. 13.95–13.96.
Having formed a fist, the wise one should cause the thumb to stand upright;
this mudrā is named Jayā by those most proficient in mantras.
When the left hand is positioned face down and placed upon the back of that [right hand], [this is the next mudrā].
With the right hand in a clenched fist, one should meditate upon Viṣṇu, the Lord of Śrī.
This mudrā, which accomplishes all aims, is also celebrated as "Victory" (Jaya);
it is dear to the God who is seated upon Garuḍa. || 13.98-99 ||
Listen now to the description of the mudrā of the God who is joined with Śakti, which is of the nature of Śakti herself:
Having extended the left hand with the palm facing upward, one should spread the fingers so that their tips are slightly curved; it should be like a bridge. (13.100)
The thumb should face forward and the fingers should be joined to it;
one should bind this [mudrā] facing the heart. O bull among the twice-born, this indeed is the [method for] other mudrās as well that have not been mentioned. || 13.101–13.102 ||
"Or one should perform the *prahva-mudrā*, or else one should make the *añjali*.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Rule for the Characteristics of Mudrās," in the *Viśvāmitra-saṃhitā* of the *Mahopaniṣad* within the *Pañcarātra*.
Chapter Fourteen.
Viśvāmitra said: Listen, O brahmin-sage, to the manifestation of the god of gods, the wielder of the horn (Śārṅgin).
Whatever object exists in all the worlds, whether stationary or moving— ||| 14.1 ||

O best of the twice-born, what could be the nature of the installation of that Blessed Viṣṇu, who exists as the pervasive reality both within and without all those things that can be seen or heard by everyone?
For it is thus stated for the sake of inspiring confidence in those of dull intellect:

"The pavilion (maṇḍapa) should be constructed in the eastern direction from the light [of the fire], or in the south, or the north, or even in the west, or in the intermediate directions. || 14.3–14.4 ||
O twice-born one, the construction of the pavilion should be carried out within the cleared spaces,
provided with thirty-six pillars— or sixteen—
along with four doors, and encircled by garlands of *darbha* grass.
Richly adorned with canopies of fine linen cloth and hanging garlands of pearls,
O twice-born one, it had water-filled jars placed at both sides of the entrance,
was smeared with cow-dung and water, and was variegated with lines of white plaster.
Surrounded by a garland of lamps and adorned with hanging garlands of flowers,
one should divide that [area] into eighty-one equal squares in the center.
In the middle of that, one should construct an altar according to the rules using nine squares.
O best of the twice-born, one should construct sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) all around the altar;
square, bow-shaped, and circular, located in the four directions.
Having fashioned eight auspicious objects from sacrificial wood, one should place them there.
The mirror, the bull, the elephant, the chowrie, the lion, as well as the banner, the flag, and the lamps— these are the eight auspicious signs, O Kāśyapa.
They should be placed on the ninth or even the seventh day prior to the day of the consecration.

O best of the foremost of the twice-born, O most excellent of sages, on the fifth day— or even on the night preceding the day of consecration— one should perform the ritual planting of auspicious sprouts according to the prescribed rules.
O twice-born one, for the purification of the image, the preceptor and the patron, together with the idol and the ritual vessels, should perform the consecration by water;
having bathed, wearing white garments, well-anointed, and well-adorned. (14.14)
When a lunar mansion favorable to the sacrificer and an auspicious moment have occurred,
one should perform the declaration of the auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*) with Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas;
having performed the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) of the site with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) for the sake of purification.
Having entered the workshop and beheld the image,
he washed both the pedestal and the gemstone with water infused with weapons;
then, placing that image upon a chariot accompanied by all auspicious things, [he set out].
Having reached a sacred ford or a river flowing nearby,
one should recite a purifying mantra three times for the sake of purification.
Then, having meditated upon that water as the Ocean of Milk, one should [place] a wooden [image] therein.
Then one should place a couch covered with a new cloth;

upon it, the deity should be laid down with the head facing east by the twice-born image-makers. Prior to the laying on the bed, one should place eight water-pots in the Brahma-square, beginning from the east.
Having worshipped Indra and the other deities among them, one should then offer the bali-oblation.
Having caused a water-shed (prapā) to be constructed there on the bank, one should have the Vedas and so forth recited;
and with songs, dances, and the like, the twice-born should pass the remainder of the day. || 14.21-14.22 ||
Having lit lamps at night and performed the protective rites there,
O bull among the twice-born, one should go to that mandala and arrange it;
O twice-born, [it should be] a wheel, a lotus, or a svastika, in the northeast of each respective [mandala].
With ten loads of *śālī* rice and half as many of husked grains (*taṇḍula*),
and with sesame seeds numbering half again, having formed a heap with cloths spread at intervals,
one should place an excellent water-jar upon it.
Having encircled it with a web of thread and wrapped it with two linen cloths,
and having placed a *kūrca* grass-bundle, nine gems, and likewise a golden lotus;
and having arranged sprouts within the vessel and covered its opening.
One should invoke the deity and worship him both in the pitcher and in the mandala.
Having properly performed the worship of the doors and the archways as before, and having offered milk-rice and other foods to the deity residing in the pitcher and the mandala. || 14.27–14.28 ||
Having established the fire in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and offered eight thousand oblations of sacrificial wood and boiled rice (caru),
and having performed the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti),
one should consecrate the entire collection of ritual materials that have been set out.
Having gone thereafter to the one who reclines upon the waters (Viṣṇu), accompanied by all auspicious rites,
she should have him recite the four Vedas, have songs sung,
and have rivers (or courtesans) dance; thus she should pass the night with a vigil.
Then, at the time of dawn, the Guru, accompanied by the mūrtipas,
having bathed, wearing white garments, and having performed his morning rites,
adorned with ornaments as before, entered the pavilion.
Then, having worshipped the door-arches, the water-pots, and so forth according to the prescribed rite,
he should worship Viṣṇu residing in the central pot and Sudarśana residing in the ritual vessel.
Furthermore, he should worship Indra and the other deities surrounding the eight pots.
Having worshipped the Lord of Gods, who resides within the mandala, together with his limbs and retinue, by means of offerings ending with the food offering (naivedya) and a multitude of enjoyments;
[one should then worship] the God stationed in the midst of the fire with seven types of sacrificial fuel (samidh) in sequence.
Having performed sacrifices and scattered offerings, and having presented a *bali* oblation before the reservoir, when the afternoon had arrived, he placed that image upon a chariot;
and having adorned it, he had the twice-born priests, stationed on both sides, recite the Vedas. (14.36–37)
Having had the Brahmins recite the Ekāyanī branch before us,
as well as the Śrīsūkta, the Bhadrasūkta, the Śākunasūkta,
the Puṃsūkta, the Viṣṇusūkta, and other hymns dedicated to the Blessed One; || 14.38 ||
The preceptor, together with the guardians of the images, recited the mantras while accompanied by Vaiṣṇavas who were absorbed in the Lord;
preceded by the sound of trumpets, conchs, and kahalas,
he scattered white mustard seeds over which the mantras had been chanted.
Scattering [flowers] before him as he proceeds for the pacification of all obstacles,
one should have him circumambulate the village and enter the temple. Having slowly brought down the image from the vicinity of the chariot-circle, [one should place it within].
Having established the mantra of the Japanese Nṛsiṃha before him, one whose mind is fixed upon that deity should make this petition to the Lord who resides within the maṇḍala:
"O God of gods, O Lord of Śrī, for the sake of propitiating you... (14.42–14.43).
"This image has been fashioned out of a desire for the welfare of those who are not your devotees.
O Supreme Lord, be gracious; I wish to perform its consecration.
Having made this petition, he prostrated himself with the eight limbs of his body.
Having obtained permission and placed the image upon the pedestal,
the most excellent Guru should perform the *puṇyāhavācana* rite, worship the door-keepers as before, and likewise worship the pitcher and other vessels while offering oblations into the fire.
Having appointed the image-protectors (mūrtipās) in the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) to perform the oblations on all sides,
and having approached the vicinity of the image— which wards off all evil—
he should meditate upon the thousand-spoked [wheel] blazing with light, consecrated with its respective mantra.
Once the images have been completed, one should place them upon their heads with that mantra.
To pacify defects arising from the artisan's workshop, the preceptor should perform a ritual ablution (snapana).
The preceptor should then arrange eight water-pots (kumbhas) around the image.
Having wound them with threads and having wrapped those [vessels] on the outside with a pair of cloths,
one should place milk, pure water, jewel-water, golden water, fragrant water,
fruit-flower water, and seed-water in the directions starting from the east.
Having consecrated eight water-pots with the Hetirāja mantra,
one should sprinkle him [the image] with those mantras in the eight directions beginning with the east and ending with the northeast.
By this very ablution, the defects of the artisan are destroyed.
Then, having wrapped the *kautuka* with two new garments complete with their fringes, one should prepare a bed of cotton wool (*tūl*).
Having scattered ten *bhāras* of rice upon the altar (*vedikā*), [one should proceed].
Having placed the cloth upon that [altar], he should scatter rice grains of the same measure;
and having scattered ten *bhāras* of sesame seeds upon that,
and having scattered sesame seeds upon the cloth itself.
Having placed kusha grass with its cushion and having laid the image upon it with its head facing east,
the best of the twice-born, O Sage, should prick the eyes with a golden needle consecrated by the Astra-mantra and the syllable Om.
Meditating with his mind upon the Supreme Self within himself as possessing two eyes,
the best of artisans— having bathed, wearing white garments, and being pure—
should then, being wise, reveal the two eyes with the mantra-consecrated instrument.
He should have the Sāmavedic brahmins recite the *Sāman* hymns dedicated to Candra and Varuṇa.
Afterwards, he should present ghee and honey placed in a golden vessel;
with these two, he should fill the eyes while reciting the twelve-syllable mantra.
Having meditated on the lunar orb above the head, one should contemplate the liquid nectar [flowing] from the heart-mantra ending with *vauṣaṭ* situated above; then,
one should meditate on a stream of nectar [falling] from a pair of cows with their calves.
One should display [the image] before the deity, adorned with golden hooves and horns.
Then, O twice-born, one should bathe the Lord with nine jars.
Having thus decorated the Lord of Gods and worshipped him completely up to the Mothers, [one should proceed].
Having offered milk-rice and other foods, and having presented betel-leaf,
one should place that image upon a chariot and lead it around the temple,
covering it from above with a tiger skin containing all auspicious marks.
Having likewise spread out a linen cloth and performed the recitation of the heart-mantra and so forth,
and having visualized the bed as the form of the Residue (Śeṣa) with a one-pointed mind,
and having worshipped it with the water-offering (arghya) and other rites, he should place a water-pot at the head of the bed.
Clad in fine linen and seated upon a cushion of śāli rice,

having sprinkled the bed with arghya water, one should likewise offer incense while reciting his own name preceded by the prostration-syllable (namaḥ) and the praṇava (oṃ), as he lies there endowed with splendor.
Having honored the image, one should lay it upon the bed with its head toward the east.
Having worshipped it with offerings beginning with the *arghya* and ending with incense, and having prostrated,
one should place the pedestal and the *brahmaśilā* upon a seat of rice strewn over a cloth.
Having laid [the image] down as before and having honored it with the *praṇava*,
one should cover it with a cloth that has been consecrated with the *kavaca* mantra and perfumed with incense;
likewise, one should cover the pedestal with the cloth used for the worship.
Having recognized the marks situated at the feet and sides of the image by means of their respective mantras,
one should place the twelve-syllable [mantra] upon the head;
from Dāmodara up to Keśava, it should be placed in twelve locations starting from the feet.
Having likewise deposited that collection of powers as pervasive once more,
one should contemplate the twelve-syllable mantra up to the crown of the head by means of what is called "dissolution.
Then, having visualized that curiosity as the immovable form of knowledge, [one should proceed].
Having prostrated before that image near the sacrificial pit,
the preceptor, with his mind restrained, should perform twenty-five oblations each of clarified butter, cooked rice, and sesame seeds, and then offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti). || 14.73–74 ||

Those belonging to the single Vedic school (ekāyana) should offer oblations in the four cardinal directions with the Vyūha-mantras; likewise, those belonging to the Vaiṣṇava tradition should perform the Vaiṣṇava homa in the corners with Vaiṣṇava mantras. Furthermore, being composed, one should perform the fire-ritual in the southeast corner and the others with the mantras prescribed for their own specific Vedic branch.

Then, having meditated upon the Supreme Brahman— the desired goal— within the heart by means of one's own power, through those whose bodies are composed of all powers, and having visualized the twelve-syllable mantra joined with the heart-lotus as a blazing form; ||| 14.76–77 |||
Having performed the ritual of elemental purification (bhūtaśuddhi) up to its conclusion, the withdrawal (saṃhāra),
and having contemplated the supreme form and assumed it for himself,
he [placed] Kumuda, Āgīneśa, and the others in those positions in succession for the sake of protection.
O best of the twice-born, having invoked and worshipped [the deity] with their respective mantras, the officiant,

accompanied by the guardians of the images (mūrtipas), should then go into the interior of the temple and sprinkle it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) for the sake of pacifying all evils.
One should worship Hetiśa and Kṣetranātha with incense and other offerings;
one should perform worship using the mantras beginning with Ādhāra up to the Yogapīṭha.
Then, the preceptor, having mentally conceived eight sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) all around as before, [should proceed].
One should perform the fire-oblation for the sake of pacification with the Cakra-mantra or the sixteen-syllable mantra (14.82).
The guardians of the forms (mūrtipās) should likewise offer oblations in sequence according to their respective mantras as before.
Having thus quelled all defects, one should then consecrate the temple (prāsāda) (14.83).
The temple of the God of gods is declared to be his essential body.
One who performs the consecration of the principles (*tattvādhivāsaka*) should deposit the principles upon the pedestal;
thus it is proclaimed that all principles ending with *prakṛti* are to be placed within the image of the Puruṣa.
Having likewise meditated upon the six paths and the syllable situated on the peak,
the preceptor, O Lord of Sages, having performed the pervasive placement (*vyāpakanyāsa*) with the mantra consisting of the fourfold self preceded by the *praṇava*, ending at its head; 14.85–86.
Then, having worshipped thoroughly, offered oblations, and sprinkled with water for pacification (*śāntodaka*),
the image-protectors (*mūrtipā*) should sprinkle the interior of the house and the courtyards with the mantras beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā*, as well as with the *pavitra* mantra. || 14.87 ||
Having reached the place of rest and prostrated with the eight limbs,
and having offered the arghya water at the head of the image and performed worship up to the incense,
the Guru, having tied a lotus-seat at the side of the feet of the image, [proceeds]. || 14.88–89 ||
Listen attentively as I describe how one should practice the dwelling in meditation:
O son of the best of the twice-born, the body is pervaded by ten channels connected to the *mūlādhāra*, as well as by other channels. || 14.90 ||
Likewise, having visualized the Goddess as pervading the image,
one should withdraw the ears and other senses from their respective objects into the Self alone;
and having visualized her in the form of light situated within the lotus of the heart.
Having meditated upon the Lord residing within the orb [of the heart] inside the lotus of one's own heart,

and having visualized the subtle, beautiful Suṣumṇā— possessing the radiance of the sun, moon, and fire— situated within oneself, both in the external image and within one's own self, [one should draw it out] from one's own body through the right [nostril].
Having entered the lotus of the heart through the left side of the image,
one should contemplate Him in such a way that the Lord is experienced within one's own body during the time of yoga, by means of unwavering meditative absorption (samādhi). || 14.94–95 ||

Thereafter, O best of the twice-born, one should effect their unification until it truly occurs; then, having created a duality, one should enter the heart with the right [hand] while the image [is held] by the left. || 14.96 ||

Then, O best of the twice-born, having meditated upon oneself by means of the self as being situated in the center of the heart-lotus— pure and consisting of the nature of knowledge— one should, by the mere utterance of one's own mantra, proceed through the middle of the channels to the *dvādaśānta*.
Once established in that, having become all-pervasive and himself of one flavor (sāmarasa),
and having attained a state of motionless vibration, he should enter the interior of his own heart. Thereafter, he should return to the heart of the image just as it was before.
Having established unity there as well, one should then proceed to the *dvādaśānta*.
Having understood that point also as before and having entered the heart,
one should emerge from the heart and enter again by the previous path.
Having contemplated the Self situated within the maṇḍala of the heart,
and having likewise contemplated this consciousness situated in the midst of the curiosity [of the senses],
one should reflect upon the connection of their splendors, like that of Indra and his enemies.
O best of the twice-born, this contemplation of Brahman has been told;
now hear, O twice-born one, the contemplation of the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman) which follows. It is fourfold: supreme, subtle, gross, and very gross. 14.104–14.104½.
O best of sages, just as the body is imperishable, so too is the fourfold sound;
indeed, O most excellent of munis, the sound itself is one's own body and the *bimba*.
One should dissolve it into *vaikharī* by means of the process known as absorption (*apyaya*).

O twice-born sage, that sound is the manifestation of the Supreme Brahman; having first reached the state of being waveless within the Supreme Brahman, one should then personally contemplate that reflection of the Word (Śabdabimba) as the Supreme Brahman itself, according to the path of creation previously described. 14.106–107.
Having thus made one's own body verbal [in nature], one should rest right there;
then, for the sake of bringing about presence (sāṃnidhya), one should perform the conjunction with the mantra.
[One should contemplate the deity] situated in the middle of the lotus of one's own heart, possessing the brilliance of a thousand suns and moons.
In the form of a continuous resonance of one's own mantra and tantra, like sparks from a fire,
it exits through the aperture of Brahmā at the crown of the head; then,
exiting the body once more, it enters its own body again by that same path.
Having meditated upon that and having clearly visualized the deity within the consciousness residing there,
one should likewise contemplate the entire form of the image as pervaded by it.
Then, one should visualize the pedestal made of precious stone as permeated by the mantra of the Earth element.

One should contemplate the identity of the reflection with the power of the substratum (ādhāraśakti) through the mantra. O Brahmin, having contemplated thus, one should then perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the mantra;
or even if devoid of [prior] nyāsa, one should perform the placement of the mantra.

Having prostrated like a staff, one should then perform the surrender of the self (ātman) and worship [the deity] in due order with offerings beginning with the arghya and ending with food offerings (naivedya). Then, one should [invite] the Brahmins, such as Ekāyana and others, around the altar.
Having stationed [the reciters] in the various directions and intermediate points, one should cause the mantras to be proclaimed in sequence.
Having placed the Vaiṣṇava reciters of the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and hymns all around, one should perform the proclamation of each respective work.
He should cause the twice-born to recite the four Vedas in the four directions;
he should cause the sounds of lutes and flutes, as well as the sounds of songs, to resound;
and he should arrange for the viewing of dances by those stationed all around.

O twice-born one, one should cause the oblation to be performed by those bearing physical forms in due order; for the sake of purifying each of the performed actions and the principles (tattvas), it is prescribed that one should cause the oblation to be performed numbering one hundred for each.
One should perform the oblation for the jewel-base-stone with the Ādhāraśakti mantra,
and the ritual fire-offering for the pedestal according to the rules with the Bhūta mantra.
At the conclusion, having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should perform the sprinkling with the water of peace (śāntitoya).

Having performed the rites for the image and other objects in that manner, and having again performed the worship with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī and the offerings of the Adhvaryu and others, he placed his hands at its feet and said:
"O All-pervading Lord, this form has been fashioned for the sake of attaining the privilege of serving You."
O Lord of Gods, remaining here until the dissolution of all beings,
accept this worship offered by those who are not your devotees, O Supreme Lord;
you alone are the supreme goal for those sinking in the ocean of worldly existence.
Having made this announcement, one should prostrate like a staff upon the ground.
O twice-born one, having then worshipped the deity residing within the circle of the jar, one should likewise specifically perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the mantras. || 14.124-125 ||

O twice-born one, for the sake of unifying with the All-pervading Lord even when He has entered into an image, one should touch the navel, the heart, and the head in succession with curd, milk, and honey respectively. (14.126)
Having offered oblations with the mantras beginning with Aniruddha, one should sprinkle [the deity] in sequence at the end;
having touched all the limbs with the entire [mantra],
and having sprinkled all the limbs from every side, one should perform the fire-oblation with the sixteen-syllable mantra.
Then one should offer the *pūrṇāhuti* oblation, pronouncing the name [of the deity];
they should offer the *bali* with that same mantra while facing the directions beginning with the east.
The guardians of the forms (*mūrtipās*) should worship Kumuda and the others on all sides.

Having bathed at dawn, the Ācārya went to the sacrificial hall; having entered and worshipped the deity, and having informed him, he obtained his permission. Then, taking with him the vessels for the *arghya* offering and other requisites, he proceeded to the temple of the Blessed One.
O best of the twice-born, having performed the worship of the Lord of the Field with his own mantra,
and having offered oblations of clarified butter into the fire, one should then perform the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
Then, those who have assumed the forms [of the deities] should offer oblations in the various directions of the temple using that very mantra.
Having gone to the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) afterwards, O twice-born one, it should be divided equally into seven parts.
The central portion is for Brahmā; next to that are the portions for the gods and humans;
the outermost station is for the Piśācas, consisting of the three positions beginning with the Piśācas.

O Brahmin, having set aside the single-liṅga (ekabera) for worship at the front, one should place the jewel-stone (ratnaśilā) upon the Brahma-pada; or else, in the case of a multi-liṅga (bahubera) image, one should place it between the Brahma and the deities. Listen now to this supreme installation, the most excellent installation.
In that place, O best of the twice-born, the Lord grants the desires of his devotees, as well as all forms of prosperity—
whether pertaining to the divine, the human, or at the junction between the two, O sage. (14.136–14.137)
Whether it be a temple with many shrines or a simple bed and seat,
one should construct a pit slightly larger than the measurement of the *brahma-śilā*.
O best of the twice-born, in the center of that [pit], [one should place a stone] twelve finger-breadths in width.
Having fashioned a vessel of that same size out of gold or other materials,
elevated and wide with four fingers [in measurement],
and having consecrated a golden vessel filled with gold, jewels, and so forth; || 139–140 ||
One should perform the ritual placement (vinyāsa) with the Gāyatrī mantra preceded by Viṣṇu, situated at the beginning and end with the Praṇava; one should fill the pit with nectar and make it firm.
One should place the stone upon it, situated with the other [mantras] starting from the Brahma-mantra.
One should fashion a nine-petaled lotus in the center and dig a cavity within its pericarp.
A wise person should place gems therein: he should set a diamond in the eastern lotus, a sapphire in the southern lotus, and a pearl in the western lotus.
One should place a ruby in the north, crystal in the southeast corner,
sun-crystal (sūryakānta) in the southwest, and a blue gem in the northwest lotus; a topaz (puṣyarāga) in the northeast, and a kaśyapa stone in the center lotus.
Having placed a lotus fashioned entirely of iron above that,
[one should place] gold in the eastern quarter, sun-crystal (sūryakānta) in the southern quarter, sapphire (candranīla) in the southwest, and topaz (puṣyarāga) in the northwest. 14.145–146.
One should place vaidūrya in the northeast lotus and crystal in the central lotus; silver in the eastern [lotus], and likewise tin in the southern lotus;
lead in the northern [lotus] and iron in the western lotus, and one should deposit copper in the southeast.
The lotus in the south-western direction should be made of iron, and that in the north-western direction of bronze;
the lotus in the northeast should be of bell-metal, and the central lotus should be of gold.
A lotus made of all types of metal should be placed in the center of the middle lotus.
Having placed upon it a tortoise fashioned from gold,
and having established the goddess Earth and the king of serpents made of silver,
one should then install the entire collection of objects with the syllable *praṇava* alone.
O best of the twice-born’s sons, having placed yellow orpiment (haritāla), powdered *chinnā*, collyrium from Surāṣṭra,
and *māṃsī* in the directions starting with the east and at the heart,
and having further placed *vacā* and *bilva* in the corners, and *rajanī* [in the remaining places].
One should place Sahadevī, preceded by Viṣṇu and followed by Aindrī, in sequence;
one should place Śaṅkhapuṣpī in the center and deposit their roots there.
With the mantras beginning with Vāsudeva, one should deposit them in the cardinal directions and the corners.

One should place all the substances in the corners, beginning with the northeast. O twice-born one, if gems and the like are unavailable, one should place pearls, gold, or silver, and having offered oblations, perform the recitation of mantras.
Having taken [the materials] with the *praṇava* mantra, having entered the middle and western [sections],
and having covered it with a new cloth, the preceptor should smear it with lime (*sudhā*),
worship the pedestal (*pīṭha*) with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, and then place it upon that [spot].
Having had a well-fitted golden lotus fashioned for the pit,
and having placed upon it a small golden image of Garuḍa,
one should deposit the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), fruits, flowers, and medicinal herbs.

Furthermore, one should worship the deities of the Paiṭhīya rite, such as Kāla, Kūrma, and others, in their proper sequence with their respective mantras using the twelve-syllable mantra. Having offered oblations with those very mantras, one should then go into the presence of the marriage canopy (kautuka).
Having bowed with the heart-mantra and cast aside the veiled cloth,
and having meditated upon the Lord as awakened, one should then address him:
"O Lotus-eyed One, O Blessed One, for the welfare of all the worlds..."
I shall install you, the imperishable one in the form of an image, especially within the temple for those who are not your devotees, such as the high-souled Brahmins and others.
O Lord of Gods, be present here, forgive me, and show compassion.
Having thus addressed the Lord of Gods with the mantra beginning with "Arise," he should raise the reclining image together with the guardians of the forms (mūrtipās),
place it upon a vehicle while reciting the Śivasaṃkalpa hymn before him.
Having circumambulated [the site] clockwise, accompanied by the chanting of the Vedas and other hymns,
the twice-born man should enter the interior with the mantra "ato devā," and having performed the *puṣyāhavācana* rite, he should recite the *puruṣasūkta*.
With the twelve-syllable vidyā situated between two *praṇavas*,
when a most auspicious moment has arrived, having placed [the mantra] within the heart as a vessel,
one should meditate upon Viṣṇu, the supreme beyond the supreme, the abode of Śrī.
Having established that image upon the pedestal in the pit,
and having positioned it level with a plumb line while discerning its specific inclinations and elevations,
the knower of mantras should subsequently exhale the breath with the *vāṅmantra* alone.
Having offered the *arghya* with the twelve-syllable mantra, and with the *astra* and *hṛdaya* mantras,
one should bring that adamantine image to a state of absolute immobility.
Then, from the source of one's own mantra, [one should visualize] the form of the full moon.
Having meditated and bathed the image with a continuous stream of excellent water,
one should then bathe the Supreme Lord with nine jars.
Then, having rendered the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) completely devoid of water on all sides, [one should proceed].
And having wrapped that image firmly with two pieces of cloth, one above and one below, in a manner that was beautiful, O Kāśyapa,
that image situated within the heart possesses the radiance of a hundred suns.
One should contemplate the supreme form and consider it as pervaded by that very [form],
from the womb up to the pinnacle, both externally and internally, O Sage.
One should install the threefold group of six limbs upon the Brahma-stone and the other [architectural elements].

That form of the mantra which is gross should be visualized as having the appearance of a foundation stone (ādhāraśilā). One should then remember that subtle form, endowed with qualities such as knowledge and associated with the sacred seats (pīṭha).
Furthermore, one should contemplate that supreme image (bimba) situated within the portion of the gurus.
O best of the twice-born, one should install all the seat-mantras (pīṭhamantra) at the location of the seat, and all the mantras residing within the body of the image,
including all those beginning with the deposition of the principles (tattvanyāsa), so that they appear like shimmering stars.

Then, having meditated upon the Teacher of the World and performed the rite for absorption (laya), one should support the pair of his lotus feet with both hands. Placing the head there as well, the disciple should address the Lord, the Guru. || 14.178–179 ||
O Blessed One, lotus-eyed one, compassionate toward those who have sought refuge, accept, O Lord, this consecration of the mantra-form given by me.
O God of gods, Lord of the universe, grant your presence here.
"O Lord, whether through knowledge or through ignorance, whatever offense has been committed by me,
forgive it out of compassion, O God, with supreme mercy toward me. Then the Vaiṣṇavas standing nearby should speak while clapping their hands.

Thus, O best of the twice-born, one should praise [the deity] with hymns of praise consisting of words of eulogy, accompanied by the powers such as Lakṣmī and others. O Kāśyapa, if there is an installation,
one should perform the entire rite together with the image.
One should cause the installation of the retinue and the establishment [of the image] according to the proper location.
Furthermore, the installation of the Enemy of Madhu (Viṣṇu) should be performed during the months of Vaiśākha, Jyeṣṭha, Phālguna, or Pauṣa. || 14.184–185 ||
On days favorable to the sacrificer, even those that are most auspicious—
namely, under the asterisms of Punarvasu, Uttarā-phalgunī, Rohiṇī, and Śravaṇa,
as well as Revatī, Puṣya, Hasta, and Aśvinī, O best of the twice-born.
But on the site, O twice-born one, one should have it constructed on the fifth or even the tenth lunar day, or on the thirteenth or the full moon;
and the days of the Moon, Saturn, Jupiter, and Venus are auspicious, O twice-born one. (14.187–14.188)
O Lord of Sages, the installation of the Consort of Śrī is commended when Jupiter and Venus have not set;
likewise, the consecration of the Enemy of Madhu (Viṣṇu) should take place during fixed zodiacal signs. || 14.189 ||
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Consecration," in the *Viśvāmitra-saṃhitā*, within the *Mahopaniṣad* of the *Pañcarātra*.
Chapter Fifteen.
O Kāśyapa, you should now tell me the procedure for the mandala,
wherein the worship of the God in all rites is described. (15.1)
Viśvāmitra [constructed] a square [altar] with four pieces of wood from the sacrificial tree, each six fingers thick and twelve fingers wide. || 15.2 ||
O Sage, one should fashion the circumference of the maṇḍala as twice its width;
at its corners, one should establish four circles eight tālas in height,
and above them, one should place four wooden posts.

Having arranged it into a four-cornered shape, one should place it upon an auspicious ground. One should fill its center with pure clay so that the middle is elevated; O Sage, one should make it perfectly level, like the surface of a mirror.
Having smeared the mandala with cow-dung and water,
one should lay out seventeen threads there, dropping them from east to west.
In this way, there will be exactly two hundred and fifty-six squares.
Having placed a peg in the center of exactly thirty-six squares,
one should rotate five circles with a string from their middle;
the area within those circles shall be the pericarp, and the outer circle formed by the string shall be the mandala.

One should divide those [sections] into three parts: the first is the region of the filaments (kesara), the second shall be the region of the petals (dala), and the third is the region of the pericarp (nābhi).
One should fashion it in two or three ways according to the path of the cord (sūtra).
O twice-born one, there should be two mandalas outside the region of the navel;
the position of the spokes outside the neck would constitute a single mandala.
The seat, consisting of twenty-eight squares, should be all around on the exterior.
A square should be formed by eighty squares as the pathway;
outside that, by two rows, there should be another square.
Above that, there should be twelve squares, and by two further rows, there should be one hundred.
O Kāśyapa, one should construct four doors in the four intermediate directions within the separate sets of four squares by means of two rows; furthermore,
for the purpose of piercing the conch-patterns, one should again [mark] each of the four corners.
O Kāśyapa, one should clear away the pair of squares within the two rows;
O Mahāmati, near each door on both sides,
for the sake of providing upward beauty to the outer and inner pathways.
Two squares are to be erased from the outer rows, one each in the next [rows] inward;
furthermore, for the sake of beauty, one square each is to be erased from the outside again. O best of the twice-born, three squares are to be erased individually in each case.
For the sake of ornamentation by way of inversion— one [square] within and two outside—
the application of the squares for sweeping has been demonstrated.
Alternatively, one may sweep even without constructing the surrounding [pedestal and so forth].

O son of Kaśyapa, having constructed the first lotus with two hundred and twenty compartments, one should fashion three enclosures with four gates in the four directions, O son of Kaśyapa. (15.9, 15.20)
Alternatively, one may fashion a single door according to one's desire in each cardinal direction; and for each enclosure, one should arrange twelve lotuses—
one in each corner and two on either side of each door.

It should be endowed with twelve petals and provided with a pericarp and filaments. One should fashion the other lotuses using half the size of the first lotus. O Kāśyapa, one should place twelve dots upon the central lotus.
Having drawn one hundred and ninety lines upon the pericarp and the ground of the filaments, and then four [lines] on the ground of the petals in the cardinal directions,
there shall be a pair of fourfold lines in the corners and on the petals.

One should place the tip of that needle in the center and also [draw] the half-petals; O best of the twice-born, there would be two spokes in each direction and two in each intermediate direction within the field of the spokes, making exactly twelve spokes for it.
They are like lotus petals, equal to the covers of blue water-lilies; or else they have the appearance of the interior of a barley grain, or the shape of a citron;
they have the size of an ant’s belly and are not visible to one another.
The central parts of these [images] should also be equal to one another.
Such is the recommended form for the worship of Vāsudeva.
Previously, the various types of images and so forth were described by me for the worship of Nārāyaṇa.
"Eight by eight, however, the field with its seed should be made;
thirty-six squares of the threads must be swept out, O Kāśyapa.
Without the center and so forth, O best of the twice-born, the lotus is not to be made."
Having fixed a peg, one should divide [the circle] equally into two parts with a cord.
The first part shall be the ground for the pericarp; one should then divide the second part into three.
Among those, the first is the field for the filaments, and the second is the ground for the petals.
The third [space] should be the intermediate area between the two petals and the pedestal;
O son of Kaśyapa, one should fashion twelve or eight [deities], beginning with Bindu.
This maṇḍala, by name Bhadraka, grants all desires.
O best of the twice-born, if one desires to construct a svastika or a maṇḍala,
one should erase thirty-six squares in the center and cast down eleven threads running east-west and north-south, O wise one.
Having cleared away two by two among those [squares], one should arrange a path in the middle;
one should also make an exit toward the east, the north, and the west.
In the eastern pair of squares, within the row of paths facing north, [one should place the deity].
One should fashion it facing south from both the east and the west;
likewise, O twice-born one, there should be water in the north, and it should also face west.
In the east, the tips [of the lines] should point south; in this manner, the Svastika maṇḍala is formed.
Kāśyapa, the previously mentioned field of thirty-six squares is of two kinds.
One should place a lotus in the center and divide the remainder into three equal parts.
Of those [three], the orb of the sun is surrounded by two parts.
The intermediate space should be one part less than the outer portion;
thus, this is the solar mandala, and the lunar mandala is likewise.
And for all the mandalas, the external pedestal and so forth are as previously described.
Or, O twice-born one, one may arrange the seats and so forth without the lotus of the wheel;
or, O twice-born one, there may be a lotus alone, devoid of the wheel.
One should adorn the mandala with five-colored jewels, such as white and the others.
Or else with powdered gems, or with metals and minerals;
or indeed with sandalwood, saffron, musk, and the like; or else with small packets of fragrant substances ground from the remains of sacrificial bodies.
With black, white, or dark-blue powders; with crushed kusumbha or pāṭala flowers; or with ground turmeric, or with five-colored flowers;
or with the husks of rice and the like, or with ground grains of rice. || 15.45 ||
O Brahmin, son of the best of sages, one should create the beauty of the forms everywhere using colors corresponding to the color of the pericarp;
the filling of the intervening spaces should be done with black or dark-colored pigments. (15.46–15.47)
One should adorn the pericarp with yellow [squares] and adorn the joints with white ones;
the line of the pericarp with red, and the area of the filaments with black.
Having divided the eastern portion into two parts, one should then [fill] the northern part with white.

One should make the intervals between the filaments with yellow and red, and the filaments themselves with white. O twice-born one, one should adorn the tips of the petals with red alone, and further embellish the areas from the base to the edge of the petals with white and red.
The entire circumference [of the wheel] is white, or else it is surrounded by red spokes;
in the case of two hubs, they are dark blue and yellow, while in the case of a single hub, they are pale red.
The tips of the spokes are black, and their junctions are pale red. || 15.51–52 ||
O twice-born one, one should also divide the circle situated between the spokes into three parts with black [pigment].
Having divided the portion near the nave into two, the wise man should decorate the front portion with colors other than white, and the remaining portion near the nave with white in various patterns.
One should adorn the pedestal with yellow, pale-red, or white [flowers];
and one should decorate the walkway, which is provided with canopies of creepers and leaves, with pale-red, red, white, and yellow [flowers]. 14.54–55.
One should adorn the doors with white, red, yellow, and black [pigments] respectively;
then, the corners starting from the north should be decorated with colors other than white.
One should fashion conch-shells with white [pigment], and the svastika should be pale-red.
Then the solar disc should be yellow, and the lunar disc white;
the space between them should be made with colors as desired, within a circle measuring one cubit. || 14.57–58 ||
One should make the height of the lines equal to the little finger;
in the case of a double [measurement], it should be the size of the navel; in the case of a triple [measurement], it should be equal to the middle finger;
and in the case of a fourfold or fivefold [measurement], it should be equal to the index finger or the thumb.
Having thus prepared the mandala, one should then worship it as desired:

the path of mantra (mantrādhvan) in the pericarp (karṇikā), the path of principles (tattvādhvan) in the filaments (kesara), the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan) on the petals (dala), and the path of words (padādhvan) in the navel (nābhi). || 15.60–15.61 ||

O twice-born one, one should contemplate the path of time (adhvan) within the spokes, the path of the digits (kalādhvan) within the spokes, and the path of the worlds (bhuvanādhvan) within the rim, the pericarp, and the bindu; furthermore,
one should honor each of the twelve syllables individually.
O twice-born one, having invoked the Supreme Self and performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa,
one should worship Lakṣmī and the others upon the filaments, the twelve forms upon the petals, Śrīvatsa and the rest, and Vyāpti and the others all around. 15.63–64.
In the circle at the edge of the petals, Viṣṇu is to be worshipped, situated at the first navel;
Brahmā at the second navel; and Tryambaka (Śiva) at the third.
In the twelve lotuses, there are the twelve Māsapas, and in those following them, the incarnations beginning with Matsya.
In the first circle, that of the navel, the weapons beginning with the conch (śaṅkha) are to be worshipped in the four corners of the pedestal;
likewise Vārāha, Narasiṃha, Ananta, and Hayānana. || 15.66–67 ||
The deities beginning with Āgneya are to be worshipped in the [four] directions, and Indra and the others in sequence along the pathways.
At the four gates and corners, Caṇḍa and the other gatekeepers are to be honored.
On the thoroughfares and in the corners of the quarters, one should worship Viṣvaksena.
In the region outside the eastern gate, Garuḍa is stationed;
Sudarśana is at the southern gate, and the mace is at the western gate;
and the Pāñcajanya conch is at the northern gate in the first enclosure. || 15.70 ||
O twice-born one, in each of the twelve months, Viṣṇu and the others reside within the twelve lotuses situated in the surrounding enclosure;
O twice-born one, these forms begin with Vāsudeva and end with Kṛṣṇa.

O Kāśyapa, O highly fortunate one, in this maṇḍala, worship of the twelve Ādityas should be performed during the removal of the final enclosure; thereafter, one should sacrifice to Vāsudeva and then to Nārāyaṇa.

In the eight *bindus*, the eight syllables should be worshipped, and upon the filaments, the powers (*śaktis*) beginning with Vyāpti; likewise, Lakṣmī and the others should be worshipped upon the petals. On the spokes, Pāñcajanya should be worshipped individually.

In the three groups of eight Pāhmas and the three [inner] enclosures, the twenty-four forms are to be worshipped individually. In this mandala being thus constituted, one whose mind is focused on no other than Nārāyaṇa— || 15.75–76 ||
Having invoked him, one should worship this Hari, the Lord of all gods.
Thus, O son of Kaśyapa, the ritual of the mandala has been described by me.
If there is anything further to be said, you should speak it.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Ritual of the Mandala Sacrifice," in the Viśvāmitra-saṃhitā of the Mahopaniṣad within the Pañcarātra.
Chapter Sixteen.
"O Blessed One, son of Gādhi, if on the special day of the god Harimedhas, O Teacher, an offering was performed by me," || 16.1 ||
O Omniscient One, O Mine of Compassion,
you should now explain the special day of worship for Viṣṇu, the God of gods, as performed by Viśvāmitra. || 16.2 ||

"Listen, O bull among the twice-born: my wealth is bestowed upon you with favor. On the tenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Śuci, having performed your morning duties, bathed, and clad in white garments," (16.3)
Having applied the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) and gone to the abode of the Blessed One, he should bow down and address the Lord of the World, the God of gods, the Consort of Śrī:
"O Blessed One, abode of all worlds, ocean of compassion! (16.4–16.5)
O Vāsudeva, beloved of Śrī, support of all, pervading the universe!
O Janārdana, I desire to undertake that worship of you which has been specifically prescribed by you for the Cāturmāsya period.
"Be pleased with that [offering] and be gracious, O you who are compassionate toward those who have come for refuge!
Having thus informed the Lord of Gods and propitiated him as before, the twice-born one prostrated himself on the ground like a staff and praised him with hymns. (16.7–16.8)
When the time of midday had arrived, he went to the auspicious river;
having performed there all the midday rites and consumed the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), he proceeded to the presence of the God.
And there, having performed the worship of Hari as before,
he emerged from that pavilion, which was beautifully adorned as previously,
decorated with canopies, banners, pearls, garlands, and flower wreaths.
It was surrounded by four archways arising from the sacrificial tree,
and encircled on all sides by eight water-pots placed at its flanks;
likewise, its four gates were smeared all around with cow dung and other substances.
And in the center of a mandala of wheels and lotuses, painted with lime powder,
in the northeast portion of the mandala, it was covered here and there with rice, green gram, and sesame seeds,
and with broad, pure cloths.
When the Maheśvara-maṇḍala has been smeared, one should place a jar possessing auspicious characteristics,
wrapped with threads and free from any dark spots;
it should be encircled by a pair of very beautiful, new linen cloths.
Having placed it all around with a water-pot containing jewels, a golden lotus, a beard-like tuft, sprouts, fruit,
and a lid, one should set such a vessel to his right.
Then, having placed eight water-pots around [the deity] in the eight directions,
and having constructed a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) according to the rules on the northern side of the mandala,
one should again install Hari upon that altar situated in its center.
One should invoke and worship the deity both in the pitcher and in the mandala.
Having offered the four kinds of food to the Supreme Self,
one should [worship] the Lord of Gods residing in the sacrificial pit with seven types of fuel-sticks in due order.
Having propitiated [the deity] and himself consumed the remainder of the *caru* while remaining silent,
and having offered the sprouts (*aṅkura*), he went into the presence of the God;
and having worshipped the Lord of Gods as before, he remained unwearied.
Having gathered in the pavilion, he spent the night with recitations, hymns, and the like; then, at dawn, after performing his ablutions and keeping a vigil,
he remained self-restrained, maintaining even the deepest concentration within himself.
Having arrived there at the pavilion, and having performed the worship of the door-arches as well as that of the water-pot and the mandala,
he completed the entire collection of rites ending with the formal offering.
Having performed a special sacrifice to Hari, the God of gods,
when evening had arrived, he performed the evening rites and worshipped the eternal Lord Vāsudeva.
Having tied the *maṅgalakautuka* upon the image of the Lord reclining on the lotus-hand,
and having tied a golden *kautuka* upon his own hand,
he prayed to that God for permission to go outside.

Having placed the Lord of Gods upon the vehicle and led him to his abode, he should perform a circumambulation. Then, returning to the sacrificial hall, he should seat the God upon an excellent golden throne facing the mandala and honor him.
Having offered *paramānna* (milk-rice) into both the *kumbha* and the *maṇḍala*,
the knower of mantras, having performed one hundred and eight oblations with the root mantra,
should worship Indra and the other deities around the eight *kumbhas*.
And having offered oblations to Kumudāsada and the others, as well as to Lokekapāla,
and having assigned offerings to the lords of the eight directions, O best of beings,
he then set out twenty-five water-pots.
Having bathed the Lord of Gods, he first prepared a bed consisting of five bhāras of śālī rice, along with rice grains and sesame seeds,
as well as wide-spreading coverlets and woolen blankets. || 16.33 ||
Having spread out a tiger skin over four costly cushions of various colors, and having laid the Lord of the World upon it— upon that which is known as the *kṣauma*—
they placed the eight weapons for his protection. || 16.34–35 ||
Having established and worshipped [the deity], and having covered the face with a cloth,
one should clothe the deity and place the pitcher in the position of the head.
Then, with dances, songs, and the like, as well as the sounding of the Vedas— || 16.36 ||
Kāśyapa, one should spend the night in wakefulness without lying down;
then, having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta* and performed the morning rites as prescribed by one's own *sūtra*, one should go to the sacrificial pavilion for the purpose of the sacrifice.
Having completed everything, including the worship of the door-panels and the enclosure,
and having then established twenty-five water-pots (kalaśas),
one should propitiate the God who pervades the universe, residing within the pitcher-maṇḍala.
Having honored Sudarśana, the Lord of Weapons, who was situated in the *karakā* vessel,
and having offered hundreds of oblations of clarified butter into the pitcher with the eight-syllable mantra,
he raised from his bed the immutable God, the destroyer of worldly existence.
Having brought [the image] to the altar and bathed it with the jars that have been set out,
having wrapped it as is fitting for beauty and seated it upon a throne,
one should lead it around the temple clockwise while accompanied by proclamations.
Having led him into the house of the Blessed One, which was variegated with all kinds of jewels,
[he placed him] upon a couch prepared with soft coverings,
perfumed and scented with sandalwood and camphor.
Having laid that god upon a bed provided with pillows and covered with costly linen cloth, the quarters of which were made fragrant by sweet-smelling flowers,
he then covered him over with a linen garment.
Then, having performed a protective rite for the God with the weapon-lords stationed all around,
and having established the lords of the Gaṇas, Kumuda and the others, on every side,
he addressed that God of gods with the verse about to be spoken.
O Lakṣmīnātha, O Lord of the World, sole refuge of all people,
O Lord ever consecrated to removing the distress of your devotees,
please enter into yogic sleep for four months, O God.
"O Lord, for the sake of the welfare of the entire world, make me one who has accomplished his purpose.
Having made this petition and having prostrated, he should go home.
O Great-minded One, on that day, at dawn, he should perform the auspicious worship.
Having led him out to the assembly hall, which was endowed with every splendor,
and having provided a seat for him, he then honored him and consecrated him; thereafter,
he offered a great sacrificial oblation accompanied by all kinds of side-dishes.
Having placed Mādhava upon a vehicle adorned with every ornament,
and having circumambulated the village in its entirety— including all the dwellings and all the enclosures— they performed a clockwise procession and settled him back in his former place.
Having emerged and gone to his own home, accompanied by Vaiṣṇava brahmins,
he should eat as much as desired and give them a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to his ability.
From that day forward, [he should observe the vigil] of the slayer of Madhu.

O Kāśyapa, one should perform the special propitiation according to the rules for rising [from sleep] (utthāna-vidhi). Every month, during the bright fortnight, this should be performed for the Lord of Śrī.
On the twelfth day (dvādaśī) of the God of Gods, there should be the honoring of the four locations.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa,
having performed the turning over [of the image] in the sky-like site on both sides of the God of Gods, one should cause it to be honored;
and on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, one should likewise arrange for the [image] to be seated.
In the month of Ūrja, during the bright fortnight, on the twelfth day, having worshipped Madhusūdana in the four locations according to the previously mentioned procedure,
and having raised [the image] as before and consecrated it with water-pots; || 16.58–59 ||
Having adorned, presented offerings to, and honored the Lord of the Gods,
one should cause him to circumambulate all the streets and then enter the interior of the temple.
When the Lord of the worlds has become firm [in his resolve], listen to the vows, O Kāśyapa.
Kuśa-grass water, the five products of the cow, and the consumption of food—these are the practices to be observed.
O Brahmin, hear now what must be avoided: sleeping during the day, eating the food of others, consorting with women, using oil for massage, and eating from a vessel of bell-metal. (16.61–62)
"O bull among the twice-born, they say that these things—namely the eating of meat—are to be avoided.
One should feed Vaiṣṇavas according to one's ability and also give them a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Out of affection for them, one should give to them; thus Puruṣottama will be pleased."
Now hear the procedure for the formal worship of Kṛṣṇa:
on the eighth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Śrāvaṇa, under the asterism of Prajāpati (Śravaṇā), the Lord Hari was born to Devakī from Vasudeva. || 16.64–65 ||

For the sake of the welfare of the entire world, O Great-minded One, he appeared upon the earth at midnight in order to remove the burden of the earth. On the day of his birth, one should perform a particularly distinguished worship.
On the seventh or fifth day prior to that, having performed the rite of offering the five sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa),
one should construct the pavilion (maṇḍapa) adorned as before;
and having established the arrangement of the pitcher-circle (kumbha-maṇḍala) as before.
Then, on the seventh day, in the evening, having propitiated the Teacher of the World and having informed the God of Gods of that act of worship,
[he performed it] for Hari, who possesses the luster of a fresh dark cloud, or for any embodied being.
Having tied a thread with three gold *niṣkas* as an auspicious charm upon the hand of the four-armed one, the younger brother of Devakī,
and having placed him upon a golden vehicle and circumambulated it clockwise; || 16.70–71 ||
Having brought him there to the pavilion and seated him upon a beautiful throne made of Jāmbūnada gold, he honored him in due order;
then followed the worship of the door-arches, the water-pots, and the mandala.

Having performed [the rites] according to the prescribed method at the conclusion of the food offering (naivedya), one should duly perform the ritual for the Lord of the Pit (Kuṇḍeśa) with the twelve-syllable mantra. Then, having established twenty-five water-pots (kalaśas). || 16.73–74 ||
And having bathed the god with those [waters] as before,
they prepared a place provided with ten loads of *śāli* rice, an equal amount of husked rice,
sesame seeds, and woolen blankets of various colors. || 16.75 ||
Having laid the God, who consists of the universe, upon the prepared bed,
he sat down near Him; and while reciting the twelve-syllable mantra preceded by "Victory to You" (*jitaṃ te*), he likewise passed the time with dances and other such performances.
Having spent the night in vigil, on that very day at dawn,
having bathed, wearing white garments, garlanded, and well-adorned,
he should enter the sacrificial pavilion after first performing the worship of the door.
Having performed the ritual up to the offering of food (naivedya) for the deity of the Kumbha-maṇḍala along with the vessels,
he beheld the Lord reclining— the lotus-eyed one, dark-complexioned, with youthful hair, and Acyuta with a beautiful smile upon his lips. || 16.79–80 ||
Having raised up the Lord of the worlds and seated him within the pavilion, and having performed the worship—
concluding with the offering of the great oblation— for those situated in the four locations, and especially for the primary image (mūlabera), [the ritual was completed].
Having honored him with twice the usual offerings, beginning with food and ending with ritual oblations,
throughout the entire day and the first half of the night,
he entertained him with various kinds of songs and dances, and by making him hear the Vedas.
One should pass the nights by reciting the Itihāsas and Purāṇas;
when midnight has arrived, having worshipped the Lord of the Gods,
one should bring a bathing altar and well-prepared scented oil.
O best of the twice-born, it was placed upon a ground prepared with ten loads of shali rice grains set within golden troughs;
having poured it into a well-constructed vessel fashioned from gold, it was carefully deposited there. (16.85–16.86)
Having had the "auspicious day" (puṇyāha) proclaimed by the preeminent Vaiṣṇava brahmins,
one should sprinkle the head of the deity with the sounding of conchs and kettledrums;
and likewise, the remainder [of the water] should be poured upon the heads of all the Vaiṣṇavas.

In all my temples, there are singers, dancers, and performers of the *tāṇḍava* dance from every quarter; likewise, there are courtesans who have arrived from other lands, as well as devotees such as Hanūmat and others. (16.88–16.89)
Having placed it in golden vats, it should be poured out by attendants;
those men on earth who hold that oil upon their heads shall be free from disease and very prosperous for as long as they live. (16.90)
Having enjoyed supreme pleasures here, they go at the end to the highest state.
Having prepared a body massage for the deity with powdered black gram, and having performed the removal of oil with fragrant *āmalaka* and other substances, || 16.91–92 ||
Having bathed him and, at the conclusion of that rite, having consecrated him with the waters of eighty-one jars prepared according to the scriptures,
he— becoming one with Him— adorned Kṛṣṇa, the bull among the Yādavas, who was like a glorious elephant.
O twice-born one, one should have the worship performed, either together with Balabhadra or alone,
beginning with the Kumbha-maṇḍala and so forth;
having offered milk-pudding and all other kinds of excellent food.
Having offered a great quantity of fresh butter in a golden vessel,
one should also offer a powder beginning with ginger mixed with sugar.
One should likewise offer milk, ghee, and abundant fruits such as plantains.
O twice-born one, whatever fruits are gathered by men today, Jāmbavān should offer them all to the God of gods, the son of Devakī,
with devotion and a mind purified by faith. (16.97–98)
O best of the twice-born, at that time milk was offered to him;
for that duration, women who had bathed and were dressed in clean garments, free from hunger and filled with devotion, drank it and thereby obtained many sons. || 16.99 ||
They give birth to children who are healthy, handsome, and wise.
Having placed the deity upon a well-adorned vehicle such as a palanquin,
they circumambulate the village and the temple itself.
Accompanied by all auspicious rites and the sounding of musical instruments,
one should lead [the image] into the temple and install it in its proper place.
From that time forward, for three, five, or seven days, one should perform the rites.
A wise man should cause a festival to be celebrated according to his faith and according to his wealth.
Likewise, O best of the twice-born, during the spring season in the month of Madhu,
on the ninth day of the bright fortnight when the moon is in the constellation presided over by Aditi (Punarvasu).
And when he had appeared at midday during the moment of Abhijit, O twice-born one,
together with Queen Sītā and his younger brother Lakṣmaṇa,
one should worship the Lord of the World, the Lord of all the lords of gods.
O great-minded descendant of Kaśyapa, Rāma was born to Kausalyā from Daśaratha for the purpose of slaying Rāvaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas;
he appeared in the world of mortals as one who wields a bow and possesses arrows that strike with great force.
At that time, one should worship Rāghava, the elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa, who holds arrows and a bow, according to the previously mentioned procedure.
O twice-born one, this is the distinction from the previous [rite]; the remainder is the same.
One should worship Lord Hari in his form as Nṛsiṃha, accompanied by Lakṣmī,
together with the goddess Earth who has been lifted up from her lap along with the host of the demon Hiraṇyākṣa, for the sake of accomplishing all goals. (16.109–16.110)
O twice-born one, during the month of Āśvayuja, or likewise in the bright fortnight, one should worship Hari, the bearer of the conch and the discus,
by means of that previously mentioned ritual procedure.
And likewise, O twice-born one, in the month of Kārttika, during the dark fortnight.
On the twelfth day, having awakened Puruṣottama, the portion of the God of gods,
one should worship the Lord as before in jars and other vessels, O Kāśyapa;
and on the full moon of the month of Kārttika, one should worship Hari, the Lord of all gods.
Having propitiated the Lord of the worlds according to the prescribed injunctions,
one should indeed display the lamps at dusk for Him who lies upon Śeṣa;
likewise, they should be displayed at all the gate-towers and throughout the circular enclosures of the ramparts.
Having specially dug [holes] for pillars at all the doorways,
one should place lamps in all the pavilions for the Lord; and having constructed the peaked roof and other structures, one should place lanterns in the center and at intervals within.

Having offered it with clarified butter from a cow, one should present it to the God of gods. O twice-born one, before the primary image (mūlabera), there should be a golden vessel filled with an āḍhaka measure of cow’s clarified butter and covered with ten strands of thread. || 16.117 ||
Having placed [the image] upon a heap of grain, one should worship it with a lamp there.
One should also offer all kinds of cakes and other edible foods during all the lunar mansions of the month, as well as at the equinoxes and solstices.
On all the transits of the sun, and especially on the twelfth lunar days (dvādaśī),
as well as under the asterisms of Śravaṇa, Punarvasu, and the two Phalgunīs,
a special sacrifice to Viṣṇu should be performed for the destruction of the enemies of the gods.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Ritual for Special Days," in the *Viśvāmitra-saṃhitā* of the *Mahopaniṣad* within the *Pañcarātra*.
Chapter Seventeen.

"O Brahmin, I have heard of Kāśyapa, who is ever devoted to the performance of festivals; for me, who am intent on the ritual of the Great Festival, a desire to hear about him has arisen—you ought to speak of him to me. || 17.1 ||
O best of the twice-born, I have first described to you the threefold Viśvāmitra-mahotsava as proclaimed by me: the daily (nitya), the occasional (naimittika), and the special (kānyaka). || 17.2 ||
On an auspicious lunar day and asterism, during both the equinoxes and solstices, having resolved upon the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha), and being attended by all the deities—
these are to be known as occasional (naimittika) rites, performed when a specific occasion arises.
When there is a very long drought and a famine occurs;
when great meteors fall at night, or a rainbow appears in the direction [of Indra]; when hair and fish are seen, or when a white crow is seen. (17.4–17.5)
And upon the falling of thunderbolts, when the quarters of the sky are ablaze, during earthquakes, when temples are shattered, when sacred trees (caitya-bhūruha) fall,
and likewise when the images of deities tremble or break; || 17.6 ||
During great winds, heavy rains, or the occurrence of planetary conflicts, and during all such great portents, O observer of noble vows,
that great festival which is performed for the sake of pacifying these evils— [is described here].
That festival of the Enemy of Madhu (Viṣṇu) which is performed with a specific desire in mind by those seeking a particular fruit should be known as *kāmya* (optional),
for it bestows fruits according to one's wish. || 17.9 ||

The great festival should be arranged for nine days, seven days, five days, three days, or one day, according to the extent of one's means; having first reflected upon it in the mind for that purpose, one should plan it accordingly.
O twice-born one, whether during the solstices or the equinoxes, or during the lunar mansions of the month,
or on the full moon or the new moon, or under the asterisms of Rohiṇī or Śravaṇa,
or even on the day of consecration, one should designate it as a sacred day (tīrthavāsara). || 17.12 ||
In a village, or even in a city, or especially in a town,
one should cause offerings to be presented on the streets for the benefit of the people.
In a sacred abode devoid of villages and the like, one should not perform a festival outside.

O best of the twice-born, a festival should not be performed simultaneously in two temples, whether they are within the same village, in all the surrounding enclosures, in a branch of the village, in an independent shrine, or likewise in two separate Ālayas. || 17.15 ||
The auspicious rite for the deities of the site and the limbs may become defective.
While another festival of the gods is underway, one should indeed perform the Vaiṣṇava rite;
during a Vaiṣṇava auspicious occasion, one should never perform any other [rite]. 17.16–17.17.
For Vāsudeva is indeed the presiding deity of all deities;
while this great festival, beginning with the hoisting of the banner, is underway,
one should not perform a human festival for Keśava, the primordial god.
When there is an intercalary month and the preceptor of the gods, Śukra, has set,
one should not perform a festival for the first time; if one should do so, great suffering will arise for the king and the kingdom,
and death will occur among the people.

There would be no fault in performing it on the second day or thereafter during the festival, as previously stated; however, the hoisting of the flag should take place on the nineteenth day prior to the day of the *tīrtha-aṅkura-arpaṇa*,
or otherwise on the twenty-eighth day.
Or one should perform the raising of the banner of the son of Vinatā on the twelfth day;
or one should perform the offering of the germinating seeds (aṅkura) on the ninth, seventh, or fifth day from the lunar mansion chosen for the hoisting of the banner.
O bull among the twice-born, if due to some other cause an obstacle to the hoisting of the banner should arise prior to the day prescribed for the festival,
one should perform the festival of the banner on the very day the festival begins.
At night, during an auspicious lunar mansion, one should strike the *bherī* drum;
having placed auspicious sprouts and seeds within the *pālikā* pots,
one should thereafter raise the banner following the striking of the *bherī*.
One should then bring a fine, white, and firm cotton garment,
sixteen cubits in length, or even slightly less;
it should be ten cubits long and half that in width.
Alternatively, one should perform as previously described, according to the extent of one's means.
Having washed, smeared, dried, and polished the pedestal,
one should draw in its center Garuḍa, golden-hued and endowed with all his characteristic marks.
Nine *tala*s in height and two cubits in width, wearing a bodice,
holding a handful of flowers, with his body perfumed by white garments;
his face terrifying with fangs and marked by a frown.
From below the knees to the navel, he has a golden luster; from the navel to the neck, a snowy radiance;
and from the neck to the forehead, a hue as red as saffron.
His face is dark, his tip of the nose is blue, and his left foot is drawn up.
Seated upon his back, he bore [the bird] which was resplendent with great wings;

intent on the effort of soaring into the heights of space, his pair of round, fierce eyes were fixed, and he was endowed with a frown like a basket, while his curls hung down from his forehead. || 17.33 ||
Adorned with all ornaments such as necklaces, he possesses a form of bliss;
likewise, he wears the red Vāsuki as his sacred thread,
and bears the white Ananta as a bracelet upon his left staff-like arm.
He always bears upon his chest the yellow-colored Kārkoṭaka,
and Takṣaka, who has the appearance of smoke, as his waist-string;
and on his right ear rests the one named Padma, with the color of a red lotus.
He wears a large tawny lotus on his left ear, and upon his head he bears a conch shell white as snow;
he also wears a bee-like amulet fashioned into a bracelet. || 17.37-38 ||
Above both sides, one should draw two chowries;
in the lower portion, a water-pot filled with water and accompanied by a vessel of sprouts;
and on both sides, one should draw a pair of brilliantly blazing lamps.
Above, one should draw an umbrella adorned with strings of pearls;
on both sides, one should likewise sketch a conch, a discus together with a sword, a Śārṅga bow accompanied by arrows, and a mace. 17.40–41.
And one should draw [the design] with five colors, with the interior space being dark blue.
The banner should be half the size of the flagstaff and need not be painted.
When the time for the consecration has arrived at midnight, the Guru himself—
Having gone to the workshop of the artisan, he had the act of opening the eyes performed by the craftsman;
then, having gratified the artisan and dismissed him,
he placed that banner into a golden vessel.
Having performed a circumambulation of the temple from left to right accompanied by the playing of musical instruments,
he should lead [the image] into the interior of the temple and display it before the deity.
Then, having brought it to the sacrificial pavilion, he should proceed according to the sequence prescribed for consecration.
Having performed the opening of the eyes and other rites immediately thereafter,
one should cause his reflection to be cast upon a cauldron filled with water;
and one should perform the ritual bathing upon the image in a mirror.

O high-minded one, one should perform the worship with the *arghya* and other offerings, accompanied by the *puruṣasūkta*, using either twenty-eight or sixteen jars, together with the presiding priests (*mūrtipās*).
On an auspicious bed prepared with ten loads of śālī rice,
covered above with half that amount of rice and half again with sesame seeds, and spread over with broad, beautiful cloths; (17.49–17.50)
Having laid upon it the Lord in the form of Garuḍa, who is situated within the cloth spread over with very beautiful blankets and the like,
one should place on his right side a flawless, unblemished water-pot.
Having placed a very auspicious water-pot upon a heap of grain,
and having arranged eight jars all around in every direction,
one should invoke Garuḍa into the large jar and Sudarśana into the water-pot.
Likewise, one should worship Śakra and the other deities in the eight jars;
and having spread out Garuḍa on the cloth facing the temple,
one should invoke the Lord of Birds into his image with the Vyāhṛtis.
O best of Brahmins, one should pray for his presence there with this verse:
"Salutations to you, O embodiment of the Veda! O mighty Vainateya, O great-armed one, be present upon this cloth; salutations, salutations to you! (17.56)
"O Lord of Birds, being thus invoked, grant us the accomplishment of our task;
for the successful completion of the god's festival, perform the invocation of the world.
Having thus addressed Garuḍa, [he did so] again with his own Gāyatrī mantra.

Having worshipped with offerings beginning with the *arghya*, and having presented the entire variety of food offerings (*naivedya*) in its fourfold form, one should worship that which is contained within the water-pot.
At the conclusion of the food offering, one should then praise Garuḍa with hymns of praise.
Salutations to you, Garuḍa, the vehicle of Mahāviṣṇu, of immeasurable splendor,
the death of the king of serpents;
salutations to you, the lord of birds, whose body is sacred study.
O Lord of Birds, salutations to you, who uprooted the Kalpa tree;
to him who brought back the jar of nectar and liberated his mother from her curse;
to the conqueror of the lords of gods and demons, and who is adorned by the king of serpents as his ornament.
Salutation to You, the support of that upon which all this is supported;
