O Lord, for whom the Rathantara and Bṛhat Sāmans are both wings,
the Trivṛt Sāman is declared to be the head, and the Gāyatrī is Your eyes.
Homage to you, whose self is the *stoma* and whose limbs are the perfection of the *vāmadevya*;
salutations to Garuḍa, the lord of the vital breaths and other winds.
Dispel all defects and bring forth perfect virtues from every side.
"Destroy all obstacles and make even me one with your own self.

Having thus praised him, with a mind focused on no other, he should spend the night in vigilance, chanting the *upemantra* of Garuḍa accompanied by the sounds of Vedic recitation and the music of trumpets.
Having made the food offering into morsels and consecrated it with those mantras,
one should give what has been consecrated by the mantras to women who are barren; then,
having meditated upon Acyuta as Garuḍa, one should personally place it into their cupped hands.
Having eaten the sacrificial cakes, the women obtained many sons;
and in the morning, having propitiated Garuḍa with oblations and offerings,
they presented him as depicted on the cloth and adorned him with garments and other ornaments.
Having placed him upon a chariot, or on the back of an elephant, or even in a palanquin,
one should lead him to that abode and around the village,
preceded by the sounding of mṛdaṅgas, paṭahas, and bherīs.
Amidst the various sounds of conchs and trumpets,
the chanting of the Vedas by the twice-born, and manifold songs,
they should lead the gods forward on their mounts after proclaiming it aloud.
Having caused various songs to be heard at appropriate places,
and having displayed dances as well as edible fruits,
O twice-born one, all those excellent brahmins placed the pots containing sprouts in the center. (17.73–74)
The Vaiṣṇavas, who are self-controlled, should indeed lead [the image] on foot;
they should also lead the festival image following right behind Garuḍa.
According to the desire of the patron, one should perform auspicious rites on all sides.
Either in front of the sacrificial altar or even outside the gateway,
one should dig into the ground for the flagstaff (dhvajastambha), which should be made of wood free from defects.
Among trees that have hollow cores, they consider the betel-nut tree (kramuka) to be the best.

O Kāśyapa, among those with inner core, sandalwood and the like are praised; however, a pillar made from sapless wood should be avoided for the Lord of the World. Its height should be one hundred tālas, or perhaps twenty less.
O bull among the twice-born,

O high-minded one, the Garuḍa-pillar is said to be equal in height to the pillar itself measured by the *mānāṅgula*, or equal to the height of the temple, or equal to the height of the gate-tower (*gopura*). || 17.79–80 ||
O Mahāmati, the bases for the staffs and the three types of seats should be joined at their roots and placed at the front; the seats should be two tālas in length. || 17.81 ||
They should be half as wide as that [base], and their thickness should be half of that again.
One should have them thick at the bases and thin at the tips. Furthermore, one should fashion two uneven pedestals and a *maskara* staff provided with holes.
O best of the twice-born, having pierced it and fixed the flagpole,
one should insert nine, seven, or five bamboo sections;
such is that flagstaff, which should be placed on the northern side of the pedestal.
Having had it brought by the best of the twice-born who are knowers of the Vedas, one should cause it to lie down.
One should then wash the pillar, which has its top pointing east or north, and cover the pillar with *kuśa* grass while reciting the mantras beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā. || 17.85–86 ||

One should encircle the pillar with auspicious threads having upward-pointing ends and with garlands; such a pillar, beautified by iron seeds and other ornaments, should be firmly established in a pit adorned with iron seeds and the like,
facing the temple, while reciting the Viṣṇu-sūkta.
With a cord three times the thickness of a thumb,
one should fasten it very firmly into the opening at the top of the flagpole;
or else, having climbed the pole, one should attach the flag-rope.
The Guru should hoist the banner at a very auspicious moment—
either in the forenoon, at midday, in the late afternoon, or in the evening—
having tied a bell and a flag to it with the *puruṣasūkta* mantra.
One should perform the hoisting of the banner with the mantra "suparṇo 'si.
At the time of that hoisting, the preceptor— having bathed and being well-adorned—
should place the deity, seated upon the festive palanquin, facing it.
And in the pavilion, which was decorated with canopies of beautiful pearls and draped on all sides with various hanging garlands,
the clusters of pillars were encircled with the finest silk cloths.
The ground before him was thickly treated with perfumed water and other offerings;
it was strewn on all sides with various kinds of loose flowers that filled the quarters of the sky with their fragrance, as well as with clusters of flowerpots containing sprouts.
When a golden throne had been placed in the center of a space enclosed on all sides, the Lord sat comfortably there, served by the best of the twice-born,
honored with perfumes and other offerings, and presented with cakes and other delicacies.
Various kinds of edible foods along with many sorts of fruits;
and numerous rolls of betel-leaf, white and pleasing to the sight, prepared with many areca nuts scented with oil. || 17.97–17.98 ||
Having offered [the food] to the foremost of the twice-born and having given it to his servants,
he then had various dances performed by dancing girls who resembled Urvaśī, Menakā, and Rambhā, one after another.
Having fashioned Garuḍa, the best of birds, at the base of the pillar,
and having arranged a lotus surrounding that pillar in its center,
[the officiant should perform the rite] together with the image-keepers who recite the hymns and mantras of the Lord of Birds.
Having performed the *puṇyāhavācana* rite, and having sprinkled with its waters the Garuda together with the pillar and the jar (*kalaśa*),
one should worship the pillar with Indra and the other deities, preceded by the recitation of mantras.
Having sprinkled [the image] with water contained in the ritual jars and having made a formal request to Garuḍa:
"O Lord of Birds, who wards off the exultation of all the hosts of Asuras, please remain present upon this cloth until the concluding bath of the festival. || 17.103–104 ||
"Dispel the flood of obstacles with the wind from the flapping of your wings.
Having made this request, [he offered] a heap of large cakes (*pṛthukāpūpa*),
as well as four kinds of food smeared with ghee and accompanied by fruits.
Having presented the food offering accompanied by various side dishes, he placed the Lord upon a palanquin and carried him near the flagpole;
then, having displayed him, he called out to the gods for the sake of summoning the bird. || 17.106–107 ||
O Kāśyapa, after the Lord had commanded all those situated within the cosmic egg, he bound the Lord of Birds with a noose,
raised him up, and tied him firmly to the top of a pillar with that noose so that he was motionless.
Having led the Lord inside the sanctum, one should establish him within the pavilion and other areas.
From that time forward, one should worship the Lord of Birds at the three junctions of the day,
day by day, with offerings beginning with the *arghya* and ending with the various articles of enjoyment (*bhoga*).
One should kindle a lamp that does not go out in his presence;
and having offered the great oblation to the deity residing in the pavilion,
one should then worship until the end of the fire-sacrifice and honor [the deity] even during the night.
Having smeared the ground at the base of the flagstaff with cow dung,
and having adorned it there with four eyes made from lime powder,
he fashioned a pedestal out of eight loads of śāli rice.
Having drawn the Kālacakra in the center, representing the form of Time,
and having immediately worshipped the lotus-eyed Puruṣa,
one should propitiate the deity and establish him right there, facing [the practitioner]. || 17.114 ||
Having worshipped him with offerings beginning with the *arghya* and ending with the *naivedya*,
and having performed the concluding *pūrṇāhuti*, he caused the kettledrums to be beaten. To the east of that [shrine] he placed a multitude of conch shells, and in the southeast corner, trumpets.
One should place the mṛdaṅga drum and flutes in the south, and also in the southwest;
the mṛdaṅga in the west and the jhallarī in the northwest;
and immediately thereafter, having set down the vessel joined with bronze and iron.
And in the north, one should place drums and small drums;
having thus established them in this sequence according to one's means,
one should sprinkle the kettle-drum with water and wrap it on all sides with cloths.

Having meditated upon space as the abode of sound within the drum, one should worship it. Then, having bathed, the son of a Śūdra mother by a Kṣatriya father (pāraśava), adorned with white garments and garlands, equipped with the *pavitra* grass ring and the sacred thread (*upavīta*), shall enter into the presence of the deity.
Having sprinkled it with the Astra-mantra during an auspicious moment, the Guru,
having washed the corner and sprinkled it thoroughly while meditating on Hari in the form of the horse-headed one,
strikes it three times and then gives it to a man of the Parashava caste.
Then the Pāraśava, taking up the drumstick, should visualize Puruṣottama in the center of the drum and Śrī and Bhūmi on both sides;
he should strike it at will, displaying his skill of hand.
One should cause the Lord to hear the verse that brings the deities;
at that time, for the delight of the assembly of gods, singers should separately cause various verses, melodies, and songs to be heard.
For their satisfaction, one should present dance and song;
having offered them an oblation (bali) accompanied by all enjoyments,
the preceptor— facing the east— should do so, as should his disciple or even his son.
One should recite [the mantra] with a loud voice while first joining the palms in reverence:
"O hosts of immortals who dwell in the eastern quarter—whether deformed or beautiful—come here, for this worship is prepared. (17.128–129)
"Having accepted [this offering], may you, being satisfied, protect us;
may you come joyfully to this sacrifice. Salutations be to you!
(17.130). With this mantra, one should thus invoke Kumuda along with his attendants.
Having worshipped [him] thoroughly with the arghya and other offerings, one should present milk-rice (pāyasa). Then, with conchs and the sounds of trumpets,
with the great roar of drums from elephants, and by making those musical instruments heard— 17.132.
One should please that Lord of the Gaṇas with their songs and dances;
then, standing in the southeast corner and facing east, one should cause him to hear this:
"O you who possess hosts of shimmering immortals, you who dwell in the southeast! (17.133)

May those fierce ones, whose faces are both terrifying and non-terrifying, having accepted this prepared worship and being satisfied, protect us along with their followers who have eyes like white water-lilies;
may they approach this sacrifice with pleasure— salutations be unto you!
Having thus addressed that leader of the hosts, Kumudākṣa, and having gratified him as before, [he spoke] thereafter regarding the southern quarter:
"O hosts of ancestors who dwell in the southern quarter, come hither! (17.136)
May those whose forms are as fierce as forest fires,
having accepted this offering presented to them and being fully satisfied, protect us; may they, who follow the lotus-handed Lord, approach this great sacrifice with pleasure— homage be to you!
Having propitiated Puṇḍarīkākṣa, the leader of the Gaṇas, and having departed toward the direction of the Yātudhānas,
the Gaṇas returned; they are the cruel ones who dwell in the southwest.
May those flesh-eaters of cruel intellect, the followers of Vāmana, accept this prepared offering and protect us, being satisfied;
may they approach this sacrifice with pleasure—homage be to you! (17.140–141)
Having thus invoked Gaṇeśa, one should then worship that Vāmana;
then, having gone to the western direction, [one worships] Śaṅkukarṇa, the Lord of Gaṇas. "O lords of serpents, come! You who lie upon the west. (17.142)
May the great venomous serpents, the Daṇḍaśūkas,
having accepted this prepared offering and being fully satiated, protect us along with their followers, the Śaṅkukarṇas;
may they approach this sacrifice with pleasure— homage be to you!
Having thus addressed him and worshipped him, and then having gone toward the quarter of Vāyu:
"May the hosts of Gandharvas who dwell in the northwestern region come;
they are beautiful to behold and possess terrible speed. May they accept this prepared worship."
Having taken [this], may they, being satisfied and followed by Sarpanetra, protect us;
may they come to this sacrifice with pleasure—salutations be to you!
By means of this, one should satisfy Sarpanetra together with his host. || 17.146–147 ||
Having gone to the northern quarter, the hosts of Yakṣas who dwell in the north approached the fair-faced leader of the Gaṇas;
though they were deformed and held staffs in their hands, they offered this prepared worship. || 17.148 ||
"Having taken [the offerings], may they protect us; let them not be satiated, for they are followers of Sumukha.
May they approach this great sacrifice with pleasure; homage be to you!
Having thus invoked them as before, he should then satisfy Sumukha.
May the hosts of Piśācas who dwell in the northeast come here; may they,
assuming various loathsome forms, accept this prepared worship and,
being satisfied and well-established, protect us as our followers.
"May they come to me with joy; homage be to you!
(17.152) Having invoked and worshipped the Lord of the Gaṇas with this mantra, one should then stand facing the intermediate direction and subsequently face the sky. (17.153)
One should invoke this Gaṇādhyakṣa, who is the essence of the Praśris, and recite the mantra:
"O pure ones, whose forms are pure, you hosts of Siddhas who dwell upon the sky, accept this prepared worship! (17.154)
Having taken [these offerings], may you, being satisfied and following after Praśrigarbha, protect us;
may you come to this great sacrifice with pleasure—homage be to you!
Having gratified him with this, [he restored] that Praśrigarbha to his former state.
While summoning the human beings from below, he should recite this mantra:
"O hosts of immortals who dwell upon the earth, you who possess many forms and many faces, come hither to this prepared worship. (17.157)

"Having taken [these offerings], may you, being satisfied, protect us, the followers of Manava; may you come to this great festival with pleasure—salutations be to you! Having thus invoked them in sequence, one should satisfy them, ending with dance. || 17.158-159 ||
The *samatāla*, the *mattatāla*, the *lāṅgalika*, the *mallatāla*,
the *maṅga*, the *jayatāla*,
the *bhadraka*, the *ḍhaklarī*— so named— and likewise the *brahmatāla*. || 17.160 ||
These ten tālas, ending with Anantatāla, have been proclaimed.
O twice-born one, hear also the musical notes (*svaras*) of the lords of the *kumuda* and other gaṇas:
Ṣaḍja, Ṛṣabha, Gāndhāra, Madhyama, and likewise Pañcama. (17.161–162)
Raivata, Niṣāda, Dhaivata, Madhyama,
and Pañcama— these ten notes have been declared in their proper sequence.
Gāndhāra-rāga, Kaulya, Kauśika, and Naṭabhāṣika.
Śrīkāmada, Keśī, Dakṣārāga,
as well as Śālāpālya, and Medharāga as the fifth— these ten rāgas are proclaimed to belong to the Kumuda and others. (17.164–165)
Vilāsa, Sarvatobhadra, Kheṭaka, Cakramaṇḍala, Kāntāra, Kuṭṭima, Pṛṣṭhakuṭṭima, Kaṭibandhana,
Vāmajānūrdhvanṛtta, and Ādyata— these are the two pairs [of movements]. 17.166.
These specific dances are traditionally prescribed for Kumuda and the others in their respective order.
For all other gods, the Bhadra tāla is praised;
for Bhava, the Udgara-ruḍa tāla is used, while for the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa), the Madhyama tāla is prescribed.
The musical note is *svara*, while the melody (*rāga*) is *gauḍa*; the dance is *viṣṇukrānta*.
For the enemy of obstacles (*vighnāri*), the rhythm (*tāla*) is *jayatāla*, and the dance is said to be *svastika*.
The note is declared to be *ṛṣabha*, and the melody is indeed *varālī*.
Having thus performed the invocation of the Gaṇeśas,
the Guru should then cause the invocation of the divine weapons to be performed by himself. Likewise, Brahmā should be invoked by the lords of sages residing in his own world.
Rudra, the lord of the Pramathas, together with Marīci and the others;
Indra, along with all the hosts of gods; and Gāyatrī and the primordial deities—these must be summoned with great effort for the purpose of bringing that Great Splendor (Mahas) into their presence.
Having thus addressed everyone and performed the rites, O bull among the twice-born,
he led the Lord inside along with the officiating priests, the image-keepers, and those skilled in playing kettledrums and other instruments, as well as singers and dancers. (17.173–174)
Having placed an image of Nityotsava in palanquins or similar vehicles,
or having led the Sudarśana around the village in a clockwise direction,
one should proceed according to the previously mentioned sequence through the cardinal and intermediate directions.
Having requested the presence of Indra and the other gods at that great festival,
and having invoked the four-faced Brahmā into the center of the village and honored him; and having likewise requested the presence of Rudra together with his attendants— 17.176–177.
Having made supplications, struck the drum, and performed song and dance,
the preceptor, having periodically refined the *garuḍatāla* rhythm,
entered within the vicinity of the pillar bearing the Garuda-banner.
Having caused all the deities to sound their instruments, the singer,
having had all the songs sung and the dancing performed by the female dancers,
entered within and respectfully addressed the god.

Having bowed down, the self-possessed preceptor, being pleased, should go to his own home. At the time of the sounding of the kettledrum, the people who hear its sound should not cross a river, nor should they travel more than a yojana.
One should reside in that very village until the concluding bath (*avabhṛtha*) of the festival.
He by whom the sowing of auspicious sprouts was performed during the banner festival shall remain as the presiding teacher (*guru*) of the festival until its concluding bath.
If it is not possible for [the preceptor] to come there, then his son or even a disciple—
whosoever has been authorized—
should complete [the rite] immediately on the seventh day prior to the day the festival begins. || 17.184 ||
The best of instructors should cause the sowing of the auspicious sprouts to be performed.
Having brought thirty-six *pālikās*, as many *śarāvas*,
and jars (*ghaṭikās*) of the same dimensions, the wise one [should proceed].
One should sow auspicious sprouts in these three kinds of vessels.
O Sage, the height of the *pālikā* vessels should be one cubit plus one finger-breadth;
their width and depth should be sixteen finger-breadths.
The opening should be seven finger-breadths in measure, or perhaps a palm;
the footstool should be eight finger-breadths [high], with a width of one hand and a finger.
Its face should resemble the *mohinī* flower and possess the luster of a lotus. || 17.188–189 ||
The five-mouthed vessels, however, should be twenty-two finger-breadths in height;
their shape in the middle should resemble a jar, measuring six finger-breadths [in width].
Their mouth, situated in the center, should measure four finger-breadths.
O bull among the twice-born, the measurement for those [vessels] with faces on four sides should be as follows:
the height of the shallow bowls (śarāva) shall be twenty finger-breadths, and their width shall be one span;
thus is the threefold arrangement of the vessels.

One should prepare a collection of vessels made of gold, silver, or copper, according to the extent of one's wealth; however, in the absence of all these, they may be made of clay. Thus, a set of one hundred and eight is declared to be the superior arrangement.
In the middling conception, there should be sixteen for each;
the inferior is said to be half of that, or according to what is possible. In rites for the gods, they should be even in number; in rites for humans, they should be odd.
Or rather, a *pālikā* vessel alone should be taken for the sowing of auspicious sprouts.
In a very beautiful and secluded place, one should construct an excellent pavilion (17.196),
provided with sixteen pillars for the purpose of sowing the auspicious sprouts.
It had four gates,
each adorned with excellent archways made from milk-exuding trees and encircled by garlands of *darbha* grass;
canopies were fashioned there from heaps of the most precious linen cloths.
It was adorned with pearl garlands hanging down from the canopy,
and its collection of pillars was draped in wonderful, highly precious silken cloths;
its floor was smeared with cow dung and decorated with powders of white plaster.
Its surface was adorned with auspicious lotus designs formed by lines of powder;
it was provided with clusters of lamps filled with oil and jasmine flowers, decorated with loose blossoms, and strewn with white unbroken grains of rice. || 17.200–17.201 ||
O one of noble intellect, prepare such an excellent pavilion, surrounded by rows of banners and perfuming the quarters with the fragrance of incense. Then,
at an auspicious conjunction of stars, the preceptor should perform the taking of the clay.
It resounded with the noise of musical instruments accompanied by conchs and kahalas;
it was filled with throngs of brahmins learned in the Vedas, wearing white garlands and garments,
and marked with twelve vertical *puṇḍra* lines made from white clay.

Having approached that supreme, pure, and purifying field of truth, he stood facing them— those great devotees of the Lord, whose bodies were adorned with ornaments, who were tranquil, self-controlled, and masters of their senses. (17.205)
There, being pure and composed, he should wash the spade with water and the like;
having dug [the earth] while reciting the Vārāha mantra, he should place it in a golden vessel, cover the clay with beautiful new linen cloths, and recite the Vārāha mantra. || 17.206–207 ||

Having adorned him with garlands of flowers, O twice-born one, he should have Viṣvaksena carried along by officiating priests seated upon elephants or chariots, stationed beneath the shade of an umbrella. Or else, having mounted Viṣvaksena upon a chariot or an elephant, [he should proceed].
Then, having decorated it appropriately with a palanquin or a horse,
adorned with pearl parasols and all manner of fly-whisks,
the best of the twice-born should lead it while it is being carried by the foremost of the twice-born.
O Sage, accompanied by elephants, the Bahvṛcas recited the Śākuna Sūkta;
they proclaimed the Śrīsūkta, the Puruṣasūkta, and the Sāman on all sides.
Having circumambulated the village and indeed having gone around the dwelling as well, [they departed].

Having entered the excellent pavilion previously described, O Sage, the preceptor, accompanied by the guardians of the images (mūrtipās), together with those guardians who are clothed on all sides in new linen garments,
wearing upper cloths, and well-adorned; ||| 17.212–17.213 ||
Wearing turbans, their hands adorned with jewel-seals, anointed with unguents, wearing garlands, and their faces decorated with earrings;
with sacred grass in hand, bearing the vertical *puṇḍra* marks, they were of pure mind. (17.214)
Having performed the ritual cleansing of their hands and sipped water according to the root mantra,
those twice-born ones, who were equal to the foremost sages such as Śuka, Vyāsa, and Vasiṣṭha,
sprinkled the ground with pure water for the purpose of sowing the sprouts. || 17.215–17.216 ||

Having consecrated the threads with the recitation of weapon-mantras (astramantra) and having placed them upon the tips of *kuśa* grass, one should mark [the ground] in sequence with threads sprinkled with powdered chalk (*candrakṣoda*).
First, the initial threads are [drawn] toward the east; twelve are clearly [drawn] toward the north. 17.217.

Having cast down fifteen [seeds] in that manner, one should arrange fifteen in the northern direction as well. Likewise, in the eight directions and in the center, twelve each of the *pālikā* vessels and so forth are to be placed in sequence, totaling one hundred and eight.
O Sage, a group of *ghaṭikās* should be placed for Brahmā, Indra, and Varuṇa;
one should establish *pālikās* in the quarters of Agni, Nirṛti, and Yama;
and one should arrange *śarāvas* in the quarters of Vāyu, Candra, and Rudra.
Alternatively, O Kāśyapa, one should arrange nine threads extending eastward and eleven others extending northward;
by this sequence, the installation of all [the deities] shall be performed according to the rule.
O best of the twice-born, if other vessels are unavailable, one may use earthen bowls (pālikās) everywhere;
one should wash the bowls and so forth in sequence with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī mantra.
Then, having firmly filled the roots of the pits with young grass, kāśa-grass, and ordinary grass, [one should proceed].
After that, having first filled [the pit] with clay,
one should then fill it above with sand brought from the river;
and one should fill the remainder of the cavity with powdered cow-dung.
First, having constructed eight hundred compartments,
each either circular or square, one should arrange them above with auspicious materials.
From Brahmā to Īśāna, one should first place the group of small jars.
O twice-born one, one should first establish [the vessel] with the mantra called Parameṣṭhin;
immediately thereafter, one should place the shallow bowls (śarāva) with the Viśva-mantra.
One should perform the installation of all [these items] while facing either the east or the north.
Thereafter, one should wrap each [jar] individually with cloths while reciting the root-mantra.
If one is unable [to do this for every jar], one should cover them all with cloth over a heap of grain;
the auspicious new jar should be wrapped with threads.
Wrapped in a pair of linen cloths and filled with scented water,
one should place it— having deposited the nine jewels— using the root mantra upon the image, the mandala, the pitcher, and all four fires. (17.230–231)
Having worshipped the Blessed One first at the various stations with undivided mind,
and having presented the water for the guest-offering (arghya) and other items up to the end in the presence of the God of gods,
the best of preceptors should prepare a sowing bed for the auspicious sprouts.
Or else, O best of the twice-born, having worshipped the deity in a single water-pot,
[one should offer] śāli rice, mung beans, wild nīvāra grain, śyāmāka, priyaṅgu, sesame, barley, wheat, and other grains fit for sacrifice.
Having placed [the relics] into a single, large, beautiful golden vessel,
and having set that vessel upon his head, he should perform a circumambulation of the sacred site,
accompanied by the sounding of trumpets, conchs, and other instruments. || 17.235 ||
Having entered within and shown the pavilion to the Lord,

he then led him clockwise around the site; then, upon the ground consecrated by Indra, which was prepared with grains of *bhārata* rice and fashioned into an eight-petalled lotus, [he placed] the *pālikā* vessels and other implements.
Having washed [the vessels] with milk and covered them with a new cloth,
one should announce an auspicious day accompanied by conchs, trumpets, and other instruments;
then, one should worship the presiding deities of the *pālikā* and the other vessels in their proper order.

One should perform the offering of clarified butter to Brahmā at the water-jars (ghaṭikās), to Keśava at the small bowls (pālikās), and to the Three-eyed One (Triṇayana) at the shallow dishes (śarāvas). Likewise, one should place the series of arches (toraṇas) at the doors, as well as the banners and the eight jars.
Having worshipped the lords of the Gaṇas, Kumuda and the others, according to the prescribed rite,
and having also worshipped Indra and the other gods, one should invoke and worship the Moon within the Soma-vessel and offer milk-rice mixed with ghee.
Having offered a hundred oblations of clarified butter and likewise seven fuel-sticks,
one should offer the sacrificial porridge (caru) with the Vyūha-mantras and the Sūkta.
Having performed the offering, one should place the full ladle and then offer a hundred oblations of clarified butter.
Having touched the *pālikā* with the mantra of touch (*sparśamantra*) and sprinkled it with the *saṃpāta* clarified butter,
one should pour the remainder of the *saṃpāta* ghee into the vessel for the seeds.
Then, with undistracted mind, one should recite the Soma-mantra one hundred and eight times.
When an auspicious moment has arrived, with the permission of the Brahmins, the Guru should sow seeds in the seed-vessels (*pālikā*) and other receptacles using the Root-Mantra (*mūlavidyā*).
He should sow them in their entirety, from Brahmā to Īśāna. || 17.245–246 ||
Others, with the consent of the image, should also perform the sowing of seeds;
having sprinkled it with water and milk, one should accomplish the rite according to the prescribed rules,
and having offered oblations in all directions for the sake of protection.
One should offer a bali-oblation day and night to the lords of the Kumuda and other gaṇas.
One should worship Somarāja daily with milk-rice (pāyasa),
and with a concentrated mind, one should also cause lamps to be kept burning without extinguishing them.
The patron should diligently satisfy the best of the twice-born with abundant betel leaves and areca nuts,
and he should thoroughly gratify the preceptor.
For the sake of the growth of the sprouts, he should sprinkle them with turmeric.
If the sprouts are yellow or white, it will be auspicious; if they are the opposite, it will be inauspicious. One should examine them once they have fully grown.
Whatever action was intended for which this sowing of sprouts was performed, [the result thereof shall be known]. || 17.251–252 ||
Until its completion, he alone shall remain the performer of this rite;
should he become incapable or die, his son,
his pupil, or a priest with his permission shall perform it.
At the time of consecration and initiation, during festivals and the construction of a temple;
at the equinoxes and solstices, as well as during lunar and solar eclipses;
at the rite of offering the purifying thread (pavitrāropaṇa), and during the festival of the white lotus and the damanaka flower. || 17.254–255 ||
In the Vaiśeṣika and other systems, even for one who has risen from his bed,
when there is a desire to accomplish rites for pacification or nourishment,
he should, being unwearied, perform the sowing of auspicious sprouts in this manner.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Planting the Sprouts," in the Viśvāmitra-saṃhitā of the Māhā-upaniṣad within the Pañcarātra.
Chapter Eighteen.
Viśvāmitra had already, prior to the day the festival began, caused all the village streets to be swept,
having even cleared away the refuse.
Rows of arches should be fashioned at all four corners;
plantains and betel-nut trees, bent down by the weight of their fruit, should also be fashioned there.
In the middle of the pathways, sand should be spread out so that it is level.
One should also beautify it with banners, garlands of *darbha* grass, and canopies;
having sprinkled it with cow-dung and water, one should purify the quarters.
The walls of the rows of houses should be variegated with five colors.
The railings should be adorned on all sides with full water-jars containing sprouts, clusters of *pālikā* vessels, and lamps fed with fragrant oil and wicks;
they should be beautiful, their necks decorated with fine linen cloth.

During the festival of the God of gods, for those people who are eager for service and have arrived from other lands, food and other provisions should be prepared; likewise, water-sheds should be made well-filled with scented water. (18.6–18.7)
O twice-born one, when they have assembled, if some should become afflicted by disease, then collections of all medicinal herbs must certainly be prepared for their sake. Furthermore,
very cool couches should be made for the purpose of unprecedented rest.
In all matters, the market streets within the city should be fully completed;
all wells and watering places should be provided everywhere,
either in the first enclosure or in the second enclosure.
One should construct a large sacrificial pavilion according to the available space,
provided with four doors and equal in its width and length. One should also arrange a water-shed at the four directions of the pavilion.
One should construct an altar in the middle of the pavilion, one cubit in height,
measuring two or three cubits in length and likewise in width.
To the east of that altar, one should prepare a square area.
One should prepare the *kuṇḍa* for the Āhavanīya fire as bow-shaped in the south,
the *sabhyāgni* as circular in the west of the Dakṣiṇāgni,
a triangle in the northern quarter, and a square in the northeast.
Alternatively, the *āvasathya* hearth should be established in the eastern direction.
Thus, one may perform the festival as prescribed for the five fires, or [one may perform it] with the fires situated in the four directions, excluding the *āvasathya*. || 18.15–18.16 ||
A twice-born man may establish either a fire-triad consisting of the Sabhya and Āvasathya fires, or he may arrange for a single Āhavanīya fire.
He should construct archways at the four gates using trees that yield milky sap.
He should have the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles fashioned, as well as the eight auspicious symbols (*aṣṭamaṅgalāni*) as before.
With those very items, the wise king should prepare the seats for the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*),
and he should also have various kinds of vessels made for the purpose of the fire-oblations (*homa*).
One should plaster the pavilions and water-stalls with village mud;
having decorated them with lime powder, one should also cover them with canopies. One should likewise wrap the pillars with garments of silk and linen.
He should choose four teachers from among the foremost and sixteen officiating priests;
even while performing the ritual acts, he should take various types of attendants into his service.
He should adorn them with new garments, bracelets, and other ornaments.
One should bathe [the deity] with ornaments according to one's wealth and in accordance with one's authority,
as well as with upper garments, turbans, and unguents;
likewise, on the day the festival begins, one should also bathe [the deity] with other [substances].
On the day preceding the commencement of the festival, the preceptor, having bound the marriage-thread upon the god who was endowed with all auspicious marks using eight hundred jars,
and immediately thereafter upon the two goddesses, [proceeded]. || 18.24–25 ||
One should prepare a single thread with a weight of one *niṣka* of gold;
one should also fashion three threads measuring half that amount.
[These should be placed] in a vessel made of gold or silver, equal in size to a *kalama* measure of rice.
Having first placed four golden threads upon a surface equal to a *bhāra*,
along with one hundred unbroken betel nuts and four hundred betel leaves, [he performed the rite]. || 18.27–28 ||
Having placed the pedestal together with fruits such as plantains upon the head [of the image],
and having covered it with a linen cloth, the guardian of the form (mūrtipa) should provide it with an umbrella and chowries,
accompanied by a hundred lamps and a canopy.
Having had many Brahmins recite the *Sūktas* and the *Śākuna* hymns again and again,
and having performed a circumambulation of the sanctuary including the outer enclosures,
one should enter the presence of the deity with auspicious lamps.
On the ground smeared with cow-dung water and made into a square,
the preceptor, having placed a vessel filled with a load of rice,
should perform the *puṇyāhavācana* rite according to the rules and honor the assembly.
The Guru, having taken the threads with sandalwood powder and water,
and having moistened them with his thumb and ring finger while reciting the Astra mantra,
the Preceptor should bind them upon the lotus-hand of the right side of the festive image.
Having formed the *devayu* mudrā with the left hand and the *savyetaraka* (opposite-left) mudrā on the hand of the Guru,
and having formed each of the four *savas* one hundred times,
the wise practitioner, having touched [the hands] with the right hand, should recite the *astra-mantra*.
Having worshipped the deity with the arghya and other offerings, one should present large cakes (mahāpūpa).
Having placed before the deity all kinds of cakes, flattened rice (pṛthuka), parched grain (lāja), various fruits, and everything including dance and song, [one should proceed]. || 18.36–37 ||
Having informed the deity and relocated him to another place,
and having honored him there with rites beginning from the consecration up to the offering of food (naivedya),
[one should proceed] according to the procedure prescribed for installation upon a beautiful, well-spread bed.
Having laid [the deity] down and passed the night, when the sun had risen on the following day,
the Bahvṛcas should raise the Lord with the mantra beginning "uttiṣṭha" (Arise),
while others recite the Śākuna Sūkta and the Ṛk verse beginning "sadeva dviṣṇuḥ."
Having placed the Lord upon a golden palanquin together with Prabhā,
and having had the Master carried by the best of the twice-born who meditated on Garuḍa through all the stages of the protective enclosures accompanied by every auspicious rite; || 18.41–18.42 ||
Having circumambulated it clockwise, [he sat] beneath a kalpavṛkṣa tree— which was spread with a silken cloth,
made of gold, adorned with all kinds of jewels, beautified by a collection of branches and twigs,
and supported by eight lion-legs. || 18.43 ||
Having seated him upon an excellent golden throne fashioned from a multitude of all kinds of jewels,
in the midst of a great assembly of various people,
he was brought there for the sake of a festival, accompanied by gold and gems.
It was filled with heaps of silken, linen, and cotton garments,
and provided with an abundance of fruits such as the jackfruit, mango, and plantain;
it was also furnished with all kinds of condiments, including *bṛhatī* and *kāravallī*.
Abounding with well-ripened coconuts and variegated by various kinds of excellent fruits,
it was adorned on all sides with many certain roots of shrubs situated on the ridges and with lofty heaps of sugar. || 18.47–18.48 ||
It was crowded with sandalwood trees of pure form and exquisite fragrance, beautifully adorned by vast pools of water containing cardamom and cloves;
it was filled with vessels of cool water collected within bamboo tubes. (18.49)
With floods of camphor, saffron, and heaps of vessels,
with musk and deer-essence collected by the people there, a multitude of offerings was brought forth, filled with the qualities of goodness (sāttvika-guṇas). || 18.50–51 ||
Adorned by all the kings who had assembled from various directions,
he displayed that which was worthy of being seen and a source of wonder for the people;
and having thus delighted the Lord of Gods with such diversions as these.
Having gratified Janārdana with songs, dances, and other performances,
and having bathed the Lord with eighty-one jars filled with all available ritual ingredients according to the extent of their means; || 18.53–54 ||
Having adorned [the image] with the finest ornaments gathered from a flood of jewels,
and having offered a great oblation accompanied by all the ritual ingredients,
he worshipped the God, the Supreme Person, within the mandala and the jar.
When the afternoon hour had arrived,
having taken earth from the corners and performed the sowing of seeds according to the previously mentioned rite,
the best of preceptors, accompanied by the patron, [proceeded].
Having gone into the presence of the god and prostrated with the eight limbs, he requested the festival; then,
having tied auspicious protective knots upon the two images for the sake of their bathing and offerings.
Having likewise performed the binding of the auspicious thread for Hetirāja,
and having consecrated them upon another bed prepared as before, he immediately raised them up, led them in circumambulation of the venerable sanctuary, and brought them back. || 17.59–18.60 ||
Having reached the sacrificial pavilion, having placed the beautiful bathing image upon a seat on the altar,
and having prepared a seat made of grain according to the sequence previously enjoined— || 18.61 ||
He brought nine jars that had been washed, covered with cloth, and filled;
they were set with perfumed water, adorned with gems, wrapped in linen,
mixed with all kinds of fragrant substances, and provided with gold coins.
Having prepared such pitchers, and having placed tufts of *kuśa* grass mixed with *aśvattha* shoots into their mouths,
one should cover them with creepers and deposit them upon heaps of grain on the ground.

Except for the honey-pitcher, one should provide for the others a single garment with its fringe intact—ten cubits long, fine, and well-fitting. Having placed eight pitchers in the eight directions, one should proceed clockwise. || 18.65-66 ||
Having established a water-pot (kumbha) containing a ritual vessel (karaka) in the center of a heap of grain measuring ten bhāras, one should worship the primary image (mūlabera) in the pot;
one should worship Sudarśana in the ritual vessel and Vāsudeva and the others [in the other vessels].
And in the jars situated in the principal directions in their proper order,
as well as in the corners beginning with the southeast (āgneya), one should honor Puruṣa, Satya, Acyuta, and Ananta, and then offer milk-rice (pāyasa) and other foods. || 18.68–69 ||
One should always place the fourfold oblation in the jars and upon the image for the offering;
then, having wrapped the eight auspicious signs individually with cloths,
one should subsequently deposit them in order upon heaps of grain below.
Having placed these eight auspicious symbols in their proper order— the conch, the discus, Lakṣmī, a full pitcher with water, the Śrīvatsa, the mirror, the svastika, and the pair of fish— 18.71–72.
One should cause the proclamation of the four Vedas to be made in the four directions in sequence;
having meditated upon the four [deities] beginning with Vāsudeva in the east and the other directions in order,
and finally having meditated upon the primary image (mūlabera) in the corners in succession.
Having requested the presence [of the deity] as far as the conclusion of the sacred bathing sites (tīrtha),

the preceptor, surrounded by four chosen officiants and himself making five, should perform oblations in the five fires with offerings beginning with milk-rice (pāyasa) and cakes (apūpa). || 18.74–75 ||
One should offer one hundred and eight oblations each of sesame seeds and barley grains separately with their respective mantras,
preceded by meditation on the deity;
or alternatively, twenty-eight times each in the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), beginning from the east.
Milk-rice, rice mixed with sesame, rice with molasses, rice with turmeric, and rice with mung beans—
these five should be offered separately into the fires while reciting the *Puruṣasūkta*.
In the fifth fire, the offering should be made with the finest food (paramānna), dedicated to the deities beginning with Brahmā.
Having uttered the name in the dative case, ending with *svāhā*, one should offer oblations in sequence,
accompanied by the words for the retinue and following each respective meditation:
Brahmā, Prajāpati, the Rudras, and all the gods in their proper order.
The meters, the Vedas, the seers, and the Gandharvas; the reptiles, the Yakṣas, and the Apsarases; the months, the years, and the goddesses as well;
all things beginning with sound, and even the mountains—[all these are] here. (18.80–81)
Beings, animals, trees, medicinal herbs, and forest giants;
those born from moisture, those born from sweat, those born from eggs, and those born from the womb;
the seven worlds beginning with Bhūḥ, and the nether regions beginning with Atala. || 18.82 ||

One should also offer oblations to Caṇḍa and the others with these [mantras] using the root-vidyā. Having uttered "This is Viṣṇu," one should perform the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti). One must not strike the enclosing sticks (paridhis), nor the sacrificial grass (darbhas), nor the vessel for the festival offerings.
One should not cause the gods to depart, and one should maintain the fire daily;
one should offer oblations every day according to the prescribed rule.
One may dwell among the four fires, the three fires, or even with two or one.

Beginning from the sacrificial pavilion (yāgamaṇḍapa), one should perform the offering of oblations (balidāna). Taking the Sudarśana [discus] together with the worship of the oblation (balyarcā) and the food-form (annamūrti), and having gone out, one should [place] the Kumuda and others at its door.
Having worshipped before the ground, one should then offer the *bali* on pure [ground].
One should prepare the *bali*-vessel, the flower-vessel, the *arghya*-vessel, and the scissors;
as well as the lamp-vessel, the incense-vessel, the lamps, and the attendants.
Taking them one by one, let others go before;
then Annamūrti should proceed, and after him Sudarśana.
Following that, the preceptor (deśika) should go in this sequence, accompanied by constant festivities and worship.
And one should have the bali offering presented by certain suitable attendants;
first, one should offer it at the gates and also at the enclosures to Caṇḍa and the others.
Having offered the bali as in the daily festival and having honored them, [one should proceed].
Beginning from the center of the village and extending from Brahmā to Īśāna, one should perform worship. Having offered oblations to all those respective deities,
one should cast the remaining portion at the great seat (mahāpīṭha), dedicating it to all the attendants (pāriṣada).
When an auspicious *lagna* has arrived, the Guru,
reciting the mantra "Arise," raises the one lying upon the auspicious bed; then,
accompanied by Brahmins chanting the *Svastisūkta* and other hymns, he departs from that chamber.
Reciting the Rathantara Sāman, the wise man should cause [the deceased] to ascend a chariot—
resembling a wish-fulfilling tree, like another golden mountain,
or well-yoked with four excellent elephants or the finest of horses. (18.95–96)
The guide should lead [the deceased] by means of a machine through the hands of a charioteer standing before him;
or else, while the best of the twice-born recite the Vedas,
he should pull that chariot along, having bound it firmly with great ropes.
In the absence of a chariot, one should place him upon an elephant, a horse, or a palanquin.
One should mount him upon the vehicles with the mantra "Bhadraṃ karṇebhiḥ.
[The vehicle] should be endowed with a golden luster and adorned with garlands of flowers. || 18.98–18.99 ||

Having placed the God of gods upon that most excellent vehicle— a golden celestial chariot adorned with a peaked roof— and having worshipped him there according to the prescribed rite, [he offered] to him a heap of *pṛthuka* grains and cakes.
Having offered betel-leaf, he should then have the proclamation made everywhere by the best of the twice-born, who are surrounded by multitudes of lamps smeared with ghee,
dressed in white garments, and wearing turbans upon their heads.
Elephants, adorned with trappings, held chowries and fans,
numerous palm-leaf fans, and pearl-encrusted sunshades;
they carried many incense burners on all sides.
It was attended by one mounted on a mechanical device at the front, with palms joined in reverence, and by Tārkṣya,
who had ascended the excellent banner; and behind,
it was followed by one seated in a golden palanquin, radiant as gold.
He was being served by one who held a cane staff to drive away the asuras,
and who wore sandals fashioned of gold,
upon which a multitude of jewels was inlaid.
The Lord of Gods was being attended by twice-born men mounted upon excellent elephants, who stood within the shade of parasols and bore on their heads vessels set in golden platters;
he was being served neither too quickly nor with delay.
He should perform circumambulation of the temple on all its courtyards and grounds;
meanwhile, others should study the four Vedas together with their auxiliary limbs (aṅgas) in their entirety,
and some should recite the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and collections of hymns.
On all sides there were those who sang, those who laughed, and those who danced;
and everywhere there were many kinds of speakers, eloquent men well-versed in all the scriptures, speaking in various broken dialects.
It was attended by those who know the divisions of Sāṃkhya and Yoga, by Śābdikas who contemplate reality, by groups of Sāṃkhyas and astrologers eager for mutual victory,
and by virtuous twice-born ones skilled in the meaning of the Pañcarātra.
And by ascetics clad in saffron robes, devoted to the recitation of prayers—
some carrying a single staff and others carrying three—
they wandered all around the village streets, performing circumambulations.
At the time of entering the temple as well, having circumambulated all the enclosures clockwise, one should enter the excellent pavilion; there,
one should install the Lord of Gods upon the auspicious throne within the sanctum.
Having placed Sudarśana in the center of the sacrificial pavilion,
one should offer the entire Annamūrti upon the pedestal intended for the bali offering.
Furthermore, the Dhruvabera should be worshipped with double the number of ritual articles used for the [other] deities.
One should worship every day with a mind full of vigilance.
When the night has turned to dawn, having placed the festival image upon a lion-throne within the pavilion,
one should worship it according to the prescribed method.
One should perform the bathing ceremony for that image, or for the purpose of bathing it;
and in the case of a single image, one should perform the consecration upon the primary image.
One should bathe it every day according to the extent of one's wealth.
Then, during the festive excitement of the great sacrificial festival,
the most excellent preceptor, having gone to the place of ornaments while the deity remains in the sacrificial hall by day, should adorn [the deity] with auspicious ornaments. (18.121)
Having worshipped the mandala and other elements, and having offered oblations according to one's means,

one should perform the fire sacrifice as before and offer the bali-offering according to the rules; then, having carried out the worship of the bali-offerings along the pathways, one should perform all the remaining rites.
As before, one should conduct the festive procession outside the village and other such places.
Having adorned both Lakṣmī-devī and Pṛthvī, who stand by the side of the Lord,
one should lead them together through the streets outside the village and so forth.
One should perform the circumambulation of the single deity every day;
day after day, one should also have special ornaments made for it,
and have it mounted upon artificial vehicles such as elephants and horses.
On the day of ascending [the chariot] and so forth, one should perform the immersion in a wooden water-tub;
furthermore, on the previous afternoon, one should perform the binding of the auspicious thread (kautuka).
The most excellent preceptor should perform the special worship of the Deity.
One should perform the offering of oblations (bali) everywhere, both by day and by night.
On the day preceding the festival at a sacred ford (tīrtha), one should hold a hunting festival;
on the day prior to that, one should engage in bathing in a large wooden tub filled with water.
On that previous occasion, having seated the Lord together with the two Goddesses upon a golden throne,
and having especially adorned the processional paths,
he should circumambulate everywhere and lead them to the garden grove.
In that regard as well, the wise one should cause special worship to be performed;
likewise, he should display all forms of play, such as song and dance.
In this manner, he should conduct a great festival with special distinction every day.
He should display everything brought and gathered in the assembly of people;
likewise, he himself should command the favor of the Lord for them.
Then, with a well-composed mind, he should gaze upon the lotus-face of the Lord.
And thinking "I am the Lord," one should perform acts such as bestowing grace.
Thus, when eight days have passed during that great festival,
and when the auspicious constellation for the sacred bathing has arisen, on the ninth day, [one should honor] the Preceptor.
Having mounted him upon an excellent chariot, especially adorned,
and having circumambulated all the streets of the villages and other areas on every side,
one should lead him into the temple and cause him to descend into the pavilion.
Having seated him upon an auspicious throne according to the prescribed rite, one should honor him;
having adorned the image of the Tīrtha with a pair of new linen garments and having tied the protective thread (kautuka), [one should place it] in a decorated golden vehicle.
Having mounted [the image] which follows the wheel and is attended even by devotion,
and having performed circumambulation, the festive worship, and the rightward circuit of the temple and the village,
one should then lead it to the bank of a river or the shore of a lake. || 18.139 ||
Alternatively, on the shore of the ocean or in a pavilion previously constructed,
having brought [the image] down and seated it upon an excellent throne, one should worship the *kautuka* together with the *cakra* and other [emblems] there according to the prescribed ritual.
Having placed twenty-five or seventeen jars before the image of the deity at the sacred site (tīrtha),
one should consecrate the deity with those jars according to the prescribed ritual for bathing and following the path taught in the scriptures.
The preceptor, along with the learned, should consecrate the deity Sudarśana with waters;

in the absence of rivers and such, the wise teacher should cause the invocation of those [waters] by means of a representation of the sacred ford (tīrtha-bimba) and the discus, as well as the devotees. || 18.143–144 ||
One should cause [the image] to immerse four times, then bring it out onto the bank and place it upon a seat;
having adorned it, one should lead it into the temple.
Those men who immerse themselves at that time together with the God [attain the same merit].
Having experienced all that merit accumulated throughout all their births—
attaining even that supreme state so difficult to reach which lasts as long as the moon and stars— they bring the Lord to the pavilion and honor him according to the prescribed rites.
Then, at the time of dawn, being composed in mind, he offered the great oblation (mahāhavis) in that most excellent pavilion attended by various kinds of devotees;
having constructed the pavilion complete with the enclosures of the discus and the lotus.
Having decorated [the area] in the center with flowers produced in their season, black tulasī leaves,
and all the colors beginning with white,
[one should place it] upon an auspicious throne marked with lion's feet and endowed with splendor. || 18.149–18.150 ||

Taking up the festival image (bera), the twice-born preceptor should worship it in sequence with the arghya and other offerings. Having separately recited the twelve syllables of the six-fold mantra, he should worship with the arghya and other offerings in due order.
Immediately thereafter, one should worship the Lord of Gods with all [the prescribed] flowers.
Having sprinkled the limbs, beginning with the heart and so forth, one should worship them with flowers;
then, having worshipped the ornaments in sequence, as well as the weapons such as the discus and others. || 18.152–153 ||
Having worshipped the gods stationed in the enclosure with their respective names,
and then having worshipped the twenty-four forms beginning with the Fish (Matsya),
one should recite the Puruṣasūkta according to the order of worship, verse by verse.
O Kāśyapa, one should scatter a handful of flowers at the pair of the Lord’s lotus feet with the Nārāyaṇānuvāka and the Viṣṇusūkta;
one should scatter a heap of flowers with the mantras of the five Upaniṣads.
O twice-born one, he should cause the recitation of the four Vedas in the four directions,
and in the corners, he should have the Ekāyana branch recited by those devoted to it.
O twice-born one, he should also please the Lord with songs and various kinds of dances.
One should consecrate the Lord of Gods with showers of flowers enriched with five colors.
One should likewise offer the four kinds of food to the God,
and perform oblations with sacrificial fuel and other materials using the fourfold root-vidyā.
The preceptor, the most excellent knower of mantras, having circumambulated the deity and prostrated like a staff, [performs] one hundred and eight [offerings] separately for each;
then, having placed the deity upon the vehicle, he establishes him in the first enclosure.
Having caused Brahmā and the other gods, as well as his devotees who had arrived for the festival,
to perform a circumambulation and obtain permission from the God of Gods to depart for their own abodes, [he sent them away]. (18.161–18.162)
Having circumambulated [the deity], he should return to his residence together with his permanent attendants.
Having spent the first watch of that night, he should lead [the deity] to the bathing pavilion,
bathe him with water-pots, and offer him great sacrificial oblations.
Having approached the sacrificial ground, performed the gift-giving, and offered the oblation according to the rules,
he should then perform a propitiatory oblation (*śāntihoma*) for the sake of atonement; furthermore,
he should recite each of the five Upaniṣads separately either a thousand or a hundred times.
Having offered the *pūrṇāhuti* oblation, one should thereafter dismiss the sacred fire.
Immediately after dismissing the deities stationed at the arches (*toraṇa*) and other locations,
one should go near the banner and honor the Lord of Birds (*patageśvara*).
Having offered oblations and performed a circumambulation to the right of the Lord accompanied by the Maruts,
one should withdraw that bird situated upon the cloth through the yoga of reabsorption. Having lowered the banner, one should recite [the mantra] at midnight.
The supreme preceptor should take possession of both the staff and the banner-cloth;
for upon their acceptance, Garuḍa shall indeed attain great satisfaction.
[He should then dismiss] the deities previously invoked, who were stationed in their respective places.
Having offered the sacrificial oblation (bali) and sounded the musical instruments individually,
and having performed the ritual dismissal (udvāsana) of Brahmā along with his silent attendants,
one should perform the recitation of the eight-syllabled mantra of Hari, together with the Guru-mantra and others.
Having performed the festival for the deity, having caused him to enter the inner sanctum (garbhamandira),
having made the formal announcement, and having prostrated again, one should worship [the deity] in one's own home.
When the night has turned to dawn, the patron (yajamāna) [should honor] the preceptor (deśika).
Having honored and gratified [the preceptor] by adorning him with garments, ornaments, perfumes, and the like,
and having given a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) consisting of one hundred niṣkas of the finest gold—
or half of that, according to one's ability— one should address the preceptor with these words: ||| 18.173–174 ||
To the teachers and others, ten niṣkas shall be given;

to the officiating priests (ṛtvij), half of that amount; and to others, half of that again. Having thus bestowed the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) in due order, one should also give to the singers and other such persons.
Having satisfied those who have come to witness the festival with fine garments and other gifts according to their respective merits,
he should honor the devotees (bhāgavatas) with radiant and excellent materials for the sake of their satisfaction.
Furthermore, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) must be given to all in the performance of the sacrifice;
for a sacrifice devoid of fees from its rites is indeed fruitless, and on the contrary, it results in transgression for the sacrificer. (18.178)
Therefore, the wise should bestow a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) in accordance with their means.

That noble-minded person who, with faith and accompanied by a sacrificial fee, causes a festival for the God of gods, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, to be performed along with all its primary and secondary components, [attains the highest reward]. || 18.179–180 ||
He delivers his entire lineage until the dissolution of the world at the end of the kalpa;
yet, even for one who, with a concentrated mind, performs a thousand horse-sacrifices,
there is no fruit equal to that of one who worships with the sacrifice to the Blessed One.

The fruit of the supreme sacrifice performed on the day of the flower-offering would exceed that of the previous days; then, having performed the daily worship as before, the best of teachers, in the evening, [should proceed]. || 18.182–183 ||
Having led the Lord outside and seated him upon an excellent seat within the pavilion,
beneath a canopy of pearls, and having honored him;
and having likewise seated Viṣvaksena in front of the Lord.
One should cause the worship of the deity to be performed, ending with the offering of the oblation (havirnivedana).

At the conclusion of that offering on that day, whatever food there may be—beginning with milk-rice (pāyasa), or the four kinds of grain-based foods such as flattened rice (pṛthuka), cakes (apūpa), and barley meal (saktu)—[should be offered]. 18.185–186.
The preceptor should cause all this betel to be offered to Viṣvaksena; having placed it all before Viṣvaksena and having offered everything to him,
he should cast it into deep water.
Afterwards, one should cause the Lord, accompanied by the Commander of the Army, to enter his place.
This sacrifice to the Blessed One has been described by me to you in brief;
having understood it thus, O son of Kaśyapa, you shall be successful.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Rule for the *iṣṭasava*," in the *Viśvāmitra-saṃhitā*, within the *Mahopaniṣad* of the *Pañcarātra*.
[Now begins] the nineteenth chapter.
"O Teacher, you have previously stated that bathing is to be performed many times;
O Blessed One, explain its method to me in brief. (19.1)
O Brahmin, being composed, I shall proclaim the ritual for Rūpana;
you ought to listen to this with an attentive mind. (19.2)
O best of the twice-born, [one should perform this] at the equinoxes and solstices, during the eclipses of the moon and the sun, during the Vyatīpāta yoga, under Rohiṇī, and under the two Punarvasus;
as well as when portents have been observed, during famine, and when afflicted by disease.

During the birth-star (janmarkṣa) of the sacrificer, as well as during rites for peace (śāntika) and prosperity (pauṣṭika), the wise man should cause the ritual bathing (snāna) and the ceremonial sprinkling (strapana) to be performed at the beginning and end of the festival. This ceremonial sprinkling is said to be of three kinds: superior, middling, and likewise [inferior].
The wise one should have one of these three performed according to his means and in accordance with the rules, as prescribed by those learned in the scriptures.
On the preceding day, he should perform the offering of the germinating seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa).
Having tied the auspicious thread (kautuka), one should thereafter perform the consecration (adhivāsana).
One should arrange the bed and other furnishings according to the procedure prescribed for festivals;
or else, one may perform everything immediately, including the ritual bathing of the image.
O twice-born one, if the original image is unavailable, one should consecrate an image of a non-Buddhist (tīrthika),
or a festival image, or a ritual offering image,
or a work-of-merit image; yet even among those, a brush (kūrca) should not be used.
One should construct a pavilion for the purpose of the ceremonial bath in front of the temple;
it should be twenty cubits in length and half that in width.
There shall be doors on all four sides, and a toraṇa arch over each door.
One should place a pair of full water-pots on either side of the entrance;
or, if space permits, one may construct a pavilion in the east. Therein, when the area is divided into three parts, one should designate the eastern portion as the *paścima* (the western part).
One should construct a pedestal four cubits high for the purpose of bathing;
in its center, there should be a platform either square or circular, four finger-breadths high,
three *tāla*s in height, and equal in both width and length.
One should arrange the horse-trench, the ground, and the water-channel upon the altar-platform (*vedī*).
However, if there is no space for another image within the structure, one should not arrange the external altar-platform.
One should cover the pavilion, which faces all directions, with silken cloths as a canopy.
Having encircled it with *darbha* grass and having hung these pearl garlands;
having smeared it with cow-dung water, one should draw lines with white powders.
Having placed earthen vessels containing sprouts, one should also set up lamps.
One should place a basin and a water-vat in the northeast corner and fill them with pure, filtered water that is well-scented. (Chapter 19, Verse 18) Chapter Twenty.
Having brought about the destruction of Vṛtra, Viśvāmitra was overcome by the sin of killing a Brahmin; Indra, the Lord of the Gods, fell from his own station along with his splendor. || 20.1 ||
O best of the twice-born, having propitiated Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the worlds, with single-minded devotion through the rite of bathing with a thousand jars, he regained his own station;
I shall now describe that procedure.
Many others as well, having propitiated the Lord of Śrī according to this ritual, obtained even those desires that are difficult to attain;
[they did so] by means of an ablution with thousands of jars containing one and a half [kumbhas]. || 20.3–20.4 ||
This propitiation of the Blessed One dispels all sins,
bestows victory, brings about nourishment, and grants the wealth of sons.
O best of the twice-born, it measures sixty-four cubits in length through its exertion.
O Sage, one should construct a pavilion half as wide as that [mandala];
the arrangement of the doors, arches, and water-jars should be as described previously,
and the sowing of auspicious sprouts should be performed according to the method stated for consecration.

Having tied the sacred thread (kautuka) and prepared the bed, one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) there. One should divide the area designated for the pitchers into twenty-five sections by means of laying out the ritual lines, with the central point being the location of Brahmā.
Then, one should arrange eighty-one water-jars;
having placed ten jars in each of the eight directions within the divine portion to be taken out, the wise man should proceed. || 20.9–20.10 ||
In the outer human portion, having divided it into sixteen parts, one should again establish forty-nine pots for each division;
the wise man should arrange the pathways in accordance with this.

O twice-born one, having first placed clarified butter, warm water, gems, water, fruits, iron-water, and cleansing materials, and immediately thereafter having arranged perfumes, unbroken rice, barley, and water, in the middle Brahma-section, within the middle group of nine [pots]. || 20.12–20.13 ||

Having placed the water for the feet (pādya), the water for the guest-offering (arghya), the water for sipping (ācamanīya), and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) respectively in the eight new jars starting from the east and ending with the northeast,
one should place milk and curd in the four intermediate corners.
One should gradually place honey and decoctions into the middle jars.
One should fill sixty-four jars with pure water;
[this applies] to the seventeen jars beginning with that of Indra, specifically to the four middle jars.
One should place, in sequence, within the four corners of the seventeenth square, *malaya*, *udbhava*, *kāśīra*, *karpūra*, *uśīra*, and *kardama*;
as well as sesame, *āmalaka*, white mustard, oil, and that which is produced from camphor (*ghanasāra*).
Then the wise man should fill the remaining one hundred and twenty-eight jars with pure water, having consecrated them with sandalwood and other substances for their respective deities:
Puruṣa, Satya, Aupendra, and also Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
One should worship Acyuta and Aniruddha, as well as Hari and Kṛṣṇa, in sequence;
in the center of the forty-nine jars representing the human [caste],
and likewise the fourfold [deities] beginning with Indra, one should offer molasses and sugarcane juice.
One should place coconut water and water for pacification (śāntivāri) into the pitcher.
Then, one should worship these presiding deities of the [five] gulās and so forth in their respective order: Vārāha, Nārasiṃha, Śrīdhara, and Hayaśīrṣaka.
One should fill the four corner jars with auspicious water;
therein reside the deities, namely the forms of Vāsudeva and the others.
Furthermore, in the groups of jars located in the central portions between Indra and Agni, they should be placed in due order.
O best of the twice-born, one should place snow-water, water with sesame seeds, rice,
water produced from sesame, rainwater, water with *kuśa* grass, water with *tulasī*, and water from the ocean,
respectively, into the central jars.
One should worship these deities— Keśava, Mādhava, Govinda, Viṣṇu, Madhusūdana, Vāmana, Padmanābha, and Ananta,
as well as Dāmodara— in eight jars.

O twice-born one, he should fill the remaining one hundred and eight jars with sixty [measures] each using pure water mixed with fragrances. In the central nine-square grid belonging to Brahmā, he should place the Śrīvatsa marked with a forest garland (vanamālā).

Having fashioned the conch, the discus, the mace, the lotus, the sword, the Śārṅga bow, and likewise the Śrī [icon] out of materials such as gold, and having placed them in sequence within those very pillars,
O bull among the twice-born, one should worship these very objects upon those pillars.
One should extract [the water] from the jars starting with that of Indra and ending with the middle one.
In the ritual of the thousand-pitcher bath, the preceptor should employ many [assistants]:
four, or twice as many, and likewise twice as many officiating priests (ṛtvij).
Having first performed the *puṇyāhavācana* and worshipped the secondary deities (*anvādhidevatās*),
he should then offer a thousand oblations of clarified butter with the five Upaniṣads;
thereafter, for the sake of pacification, he should offer oblations with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) along with fuel-sticks (*samidh*) and other materials.
And having consecrated the jars according to the very sequence previously described.
Chapter Twenty-One: Kāśpa.
"I wish to hear, O Blessed One, about the construction of the temple and the fashioning of the deity; please speak briefly on this matter. (21.1) Viśvāmitra.
O Kāśyapa, listen to the manner of constructing a temple for the gods, by the mere hearing of which one obtains the fruit of its construction.
Whatever fruit one might attain by performing sacrifices such as the Aśvamedha, [that is obtained by this]. (21.2)
One may obtain that [merit] through the resolve to construct a temple for the gods.
[The temple] may be made of stone, brick, or wood, being superior, inferior, or middling;
indeed, O twice-born one, the stone-built is the best, while that constructed of bricks is middling. || 21.3–21.4 ||
The lowest [type] is said to be made of wood, while the inferior is made of clay.
During a lunar mansion favorable to the sacrificer, during the northern solstice,
under an auspicious yoga and an auspicious *lagna*, one should acquire a portion of ground.
Having installed there the Lord of Gods, Acyuta, in the form of the Boar, and having prostrated before him,
one should cause [the ground] to be excavated until water wells up.
O twice-born one, having also extracted any debris such as stakes and the like, one should cast them outside.
If the omen is auspicious, success is attained; if it is inauspicious, one should perform a rite of pacification.
With the *Saudarśana* mantra, one should offer oblations eight thousand times.
Then, one should worship the deities residing in the site within the sacrificial pit.
Then one should fill that pit with stones, sand, and so forth.
Having made the ground higher on the south and lower on the north,
and having leveled and purified that spot with cow-dung and water.

The practitioner of mantra should offer oblations of fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and sacrificial rice separately with the root mantra one hundred and eight times. Having recited the Puṇḍarīkākṣa mantra,
he should thereafter have the most excellent Brahmins proclaim an auspicious day.
Accompanied by the master of the site and the architects, the wise man, together with the calculators, should place a straight gnomon free from knots in the center of that [ground].
He should draw a circle around it with a radius equal to twice the width of the gnomon. || 21.12–21.13 ||
O best of the twice-born, having gone to the edge of the mandala in the morning and evening,
one should place two dots there, cast two threads from east to west,
and then rotate [the cord] between the dots like the head and tail of a tortoise.
Having first determined the two directions— east and north— and having leveled that [ground] once more,
one should then rotate a cord two cubits long from the center of the northern half;
it may be three cubits, five cubits, or even seven cubits in length.
Or, according to one's desire, one may further extend those lines separately;
having rotated the cardinal line, one should mark the diagonal line.
Then, for the sake of establishing the corners and the directions, one should cast the diagonal line.
O twice-born one, having established equality by rotating the cord around the circle,
and having fixed both ends of two cords,
one should determine the eight directions individually and in due order.
Having caused a carpenter skilled in the ritual rules to fashion a square [foundation], one should drive eight stakes into it and observe the omens.
If the omen is auspicious, the work should be undertaken; if it is inauspicious, one should perform a rite of pacification.
One should offer eight thousand oblations with the *Saudarśana* mantra.
Eight deities are stationed in their respective places from the southeast corner to the northwest;
likewise, eight others are stationed in their places from the northwest to the northeast.

O twice-born one, having properly propitiated the Guru with the aforementioned numbers, the remaining elements beginning with water and ending with earth, which abide even in their respective positions,
should fill that region with sand so that it is level.
Then the wise man should begin with the lowest [quality of wood], even if it is harsh.
Having taken up his position in the east, the south, or the north,
he should construct an artificial dwelling in whatever location is desired.
Having constructed a wall all around, one should build a pavilion in front of it,
made either of gold, silver, or even of udumbara wood;
[therein one should worship] the god Hari, who possesses a short body and bears four arms.
Having performed the rites for subduing obstacles, such as dwelling in water, and having then constructed the pavilion;

and having likewise performed the non-expulsion rite, the image-consecration oblation, and the propitiatory rite— at a beautiful dawn, under an auspicious moment, and when the sky was clear— || 21.27–21.28 ||

Having led it clockwise around the temple, he should cause it to enter the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha). Having placed it in the center of the altar— measuring one cubit in length and breadth and of equal height— the preceptor [should perform the rite] with the root mantra.

Having established the eternal Lord there motionless—Nārāyaṇa, who dwells within the orb of the sun—one whose mind is focused on no other should invoke Him and place Him within the center of the disc, [reciting]: "Victory has been won by Him! || 21.30–31 ||
Having worshipped according to the scriptures, he should then make this request:
"O Supreme God,
Janārdana, out of affection for us, you should reside in this small house for as long as it takes to complete the structure."
Having thus informed the Lord of Gods and prostrated like a staff,
on the arrival of the fourth day, one should bathe [the deity] with the most excellent [substances],
perform a festival, and then conduct a pilgrimage to sacred fords (tīrthayātrā). || 21.33–21.34 ||
On an auspicious day favorable to the patron, being composed, he should take twelve, eight, or four bricks, or auspicious stones;
having had them shaped by carpenters, they should then be smoothed by those same craftsmen.

Having washed [the image] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) in the pavilion. Having placed jars upon heaps of grain to the south of the bricks according to the prescribed rule, one should then worship the lords of the directions.
O twice-born one, having placed the water-pot in the center according to the previously mentioned procedure,
and having then worshipped the lotus-seated Brahmā within it with pure,
new linen cloths, [one should likewise worship] the jars and the bricks. || 21.38 ||
O twice-born one, having encircled [the site] and established the fire to the north according to the rite,

and having prepared the sacrificial oblations (caru), the preceptor, having offered one hundred and eight oblations for each separately with the root mantra and the Jagarī mantra, should pass the night.
When the stainless sun has risen and an auspicious moment has arrived,
being composed, he should designate the southern side as the entrance;
then, with the permission of the Brahmins, he should consecrate the bricks with water from the ritual pitcher.
Having entered the center of the palace, one should recite the eight-syllable mantra (aṣṭākṣara) in sequence with the eight jars belonging to the world-protectors (lokapālas),
while meditating upon the god Nara-Nārāyaṇa, the teacher of the universe, together with Śrī.
Having performed a prostration like a staff while reciting the Praṇava mantra,
