one should place the first brick on the southern side of the entrance. Then, beginning from the southeast corner, one should arrange them in a clockwise direction.
One should place eight bricks dedicated to Indra and Agni for the protection of the temple.
Then, the wise person should mutter one hundred and eight times the Sudarśana mantra,
as well as the eight-syllable mantra of the Lord of Mantras, and the Vārāha and Nārasiṃha mantras.

The noble-minded one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times for each [deity] separately; having gratified the foremost of Brahmins, he should satisfy the assembly of artisans with garments, ornaments, ritual implements,
and heaps of grain.

Having bestowed the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) in due order upon the preceptor and the officiating priests, he should also gratify the players of drums, cymbals, conchs, and other instruments. Then the instructor, having filled the pits and the like with jewels and grain, [should perform the rite].

Having cast down fragrant scents and unbroken rice grains while reciting the Praṇava mantra, one should examine the swirl of the water; if it turns auspiciously, it portends good fortune. If it is inauspicious, however, one should offer oblations into the fire with the eight-syllable mantra.
Having filled that pit with sand on all sides,
one should from that time forth protect that place with a one-pointed mind,
starting from a distance of three cubits up to nine cubits, or even twice that.
O twice-born one, one should first construct a single-story structure with an odd number of cubits;
then one may construct a two-story structure measuring thirteen cubits,
or even ten or fifteen cubits for the ground floor.
One should especially make the temple more than six cubits [in height];
likewise, one should determine the width up to twelve stories.
O twice-born one, it is said that the best [type] has a height double the width.
When divided into seven parts in width, twelve finger-breadths is said to be the middle [measurement], while eleven parts is the lowest;
thus it is established up to a height of twelve stories.
And by the laying down of the lines, one should establish sixteen squares;
the central four-square area shall be the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha), and from that [center],
one should calculate twelve other squares for the purpose of the walls.
By means of six lines drawn eastward and northward, there shall be twenty-five squares;
the interior of the sanctum (garbhagṛha) shall consist of nine such squares.
One should construct all the enclosures (prākāras) on all sides using sixteen squares.

The temple (prāsāda) is said to be of three kinds according to the distinction of their shapes. The Nāgara style is square up to the pinnacle (āsthūpyanta); the Drāviḍa style is octagonal from the neck (kaṇṭha) to the top (śānta). || 21.60–61 ||
That which extends up to the region of the neck is declared to be a *vesara*.
It may be square in length and likewise circular in breadth;
furthermore, O twice-born one, it may be either square or circular, thus being of four kinds.
Having divided the width of the temple into five parts,
one should arrange it in three of those divisions by means of seven or three [parts],
or alternatively, in nine parts by means of four.
O twice-born one, having divided the width of the doorway or the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) into three parts, one should make the width of the doorway either one part, or half of that,
or one-fifth of it. || 21.65 ||
O best of Brahmins, one should make the height twice the width;
O foremost of the twice-born, this same rule applies to temples as well.
Now I shall describe the installation of the images; listen with a concentrated mind.
On the first level, one should place [the images] above in the four directions:
Vārāha, Nārasiṃha, Śrīdhara, and Hayagrīva;
and in the four corner regions, Garuḍa with a face resembling that [of his vehicle].
Whether he is seated or standing, one should represent him facing that particular direction;
or else, one may fashion a lion in the regions of the ears,
as well as in the gables and within the doorways.
One should visualize Kumuda and the others, along with Upendra and his attendants,
as well as the Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and others, either dancing or singing,
and seeing one another playing musical instruments.

One who is expert in the treatises of the artisans should arrange [the deities] in the various sections according to the prescribed rites. O Brahmin, listen now to the individual gods for the second level:
Nara, Nārāyaṇa, Hari, and Kṛṣṇa, in due order.

O tiger among brahmins, one should arrange Keśava and the other [deities] along with their Śaktis in the four directions— starting from the east and proceeding to the north and west— and in other available spaces;
one should arrange them as before upon the sections of the walls.
In this third [section], one should fashion [the deities] in the four directions in due order:
Puruṣa, Satya, Acyuta, and immediately after him Ananta; and one should likewise fashion them in the remaining [directions] as before.
One should likewise perform [offerings] on all sides to Indra and the other world-protectors, to the twelve Ādityas,
and to the hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases, along with the Kiṃnaras and Mahoragas,
as well as those who perform dances and other such arts.
O Brahmin, hear now of the host of deities stationed on the fourth floor as well:
one should place Vāmana in the east, Trivikrama in the south,
the son of Jamadagni (Paraśurāma) in the west, and likewise [Bala] in the north, O twice-born one.
O twice-born Kāśyapa, one should also place Baladeva and the hosts of deities, such as Brahmānābha and others, in their full majesty upon all the remaining parts on every side,
even on the fifth level in the four directions.
[Sudarśana, Pāñcajanya, the mace, and likewise the lotus]—bearing their own weapons upon their heads and with palms joined in reverence, they stood in succession.
As for the deeds of Kṛṣṇa in the remaining regions: ||| 21.81–82 ||
On the seventh floor as well, O great sage, one should install the four deities beginning with Vāsudeva in the four directions in due order;
and on the corner pinnacles (karṇakūṭa), one should place Dharma and the others in the penthouses (pañjara) in due order.
Furthermore, one should fashion the four Vedas, as well as the Kṛta, Tretā, and other ages;
one should place divine weapons within the intervals of the necklaces,
and, O Sage, one should depict Garuḍa in the corners and throughout the seven stories.

O Brahmin, one should likewise fashion Siṃha, Vīrasena, Suṣeṇaka, Vīranātha, and Subhadra; and with his arms, one should fashion two figures holding palaces. One should place Caṇḍa and the others in the four directions at the sides of the door.
One should likewise fashion the deities of the temple, such as Śaṅkha and Padmanidhi.
One should have the best of the twice-born construct [these] on all four sides of the temple,
even if they were previously present on the first and other levels.
One should visualize the aforementioned deities on the third and subsequent levels.
When the gate-towers (*gopura*) have been constructed in this manner, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the deities.
Furthermore, in the upper regions above the towers, one should arrange the garland of spirits (*bhūtamālā*).
O foremost of Brahmins, one should also arrange a row of swans according to one's desire.
Furthermore, having fashioned the group of eight beginning with Lohitākṣa beneath the pedestal, and likewise the group of eight beginning with the discus within that space; ||| 21.90–91 |||
O twice-born one, one should draw the groups of manifestations even within the portion for the primary deities;
one should fashion a circular garland of light extending all around.
And, O twice-born one, one should have a pavilion constructed outside that [mandala] for the purpose of the ritual bathing.
One should construct a spacious water-shed that provides coolness. In the quarter of Varuṇa (the west), one should place the stable for vehicles; in the quarter of Vāyu (the northwest), the treasury;
in the north, the sleeping quarters; and in the quarter of Īśa (the northeast), a pavilion of flowers.
In the third enclosure, one should construct a dance pavilion in the east;
in the south, one should build a music hall; and in the southwest corner, an assembly hall.
In the west, there should be a place for books, and in the northwest, a storehouse for grain.
In the northern direction, there should indeed be an abode of Viṣṇu;
O twice-born one, one should construct a cowshed in the middle,
and an abode for the Mothers to the northeast and to the south of the temple.
A wise man should construct a well in front of the kitchen;
in this manner he should build the palace. Now hear concerning the laying of the foundation (garbhanyāsa): [it should be placed] in a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or even iron.
O bull among the twice-born, one should make it sixteen finger-breadths in width, or twelve finger-breadths, or eight finger-breadths, according to one's preference; O best of the twice-born,
one should make its height half of that width.
O best of the twice-born, one may fashion it as circular or square, with four sides or three; O most excellent of the twice-born, one may do as one desires.
Alternatively, the wise man should construct nine pits.
One should construct an altar in front of it and smear it with cow dung.
One should make a mandala out of eight bhāras of śāli rice,
and having covered that with half as much paddy, one should also cover it with cloths.
One should place a water-filled pitcher containing jewels upon it;
one should also place another pitcher made of gold with the five weapons.
The preceptor should worship [the deity] with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, using the Brahma-bīja mantra.
Having placed eight jars around it, one should distribute [the offerings] equally;
from Indra to Īśāna, within these eight jars,
one should first wash the previously prepared vessel with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
One should perform the consecration with water-pots together with jars while reciting the *praṇava*.
Having prepared the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) as before, one should cover it with cloths and *darbha* grass.
In its center, one should wrap the vessel, having also enveloped it with garments.
Then one should place earth and other materials, as well as gold, into the hollows of the vessels.
Having meditated upon Brahmā here within all of them, including the gold and so forth,
one should touch that [substance] with the palm of the hand while reciting the eight-syllabled mantra.
The instructor, endowed with moral discipline, should cause all people to wait; then,
having entered the inner sanctum, facing either east or north,
he should leave two spaces on the right side of the doorway.
Having specifically allocated the third part at the base of the thighs,
the placement of the womb (garbha) for the gods is recommended on the *ṣaṣṭikā* beam;
for the twice-born (*dvija*), it is below the *paṭṭikā* beam, and for kings, it is above the *kumuda*.
For the Vaiśyas, after the Kumuda and above the Turyas [and below the Jagatī],
having performed the sprinkling with the Gāyatrī, one should perform the oblation (homa) in the Vāruṇa fire; then,
one should offer oblations of clarified butter to Keśava and the others by their respective names.
One should offer eight separate oblations to those beginning with Indra and ending with Brahmā.
Having offered these at the conclusion with the *vyāhṛti* mantras according to the path enjoined by the scriptures,
the preceptor [should select] a Vaiṣṇava artisan, knowledgeable in tools and weapons, and skilled in practical crafts.
O best of the twice-born, one who possesses such qualities should listen; then,
having sprinkled it with ghee from the *saṃpāta* oblation while reciting the root-mantra, the wise man, being composed, should cover that vessel with the syllable *praṇava*.
Touching with the tip of his right thumb, he should recite the eight-syllable mantra.
Facing east during the sprinkling, the supreme teacher, mindful of the earth and with palms joined in reverence, should recite this verse which is the very form of the mantra.
"O beloved abode of all beings, adorned with breasts like mountain peaks,
O Goddess whose garment is the ocean, take up residence in my womb.
By this ritual, one should perform the placement of the embryo at night.
Then, having placed the crown-brick according to the method prescribed in the treatises on architecture,
and having installed the pinnacle and fixed the finial-pot,
one should likewise smear the entire temple with colored pigments.

Having first honored his preceptor, the wise man should then honor the artisan who, according to the prescribed rite, causes a temple of Vāsudeva to be built. Having uplifted his entire lineage, he is highly honored in the world of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Construction of the Temple," in the Viśvāmitra-saṃhitā of the Mahopaniṣad within the Pañcarātra.
Chapter Twenty-two.
Viśvāmitra shall describe the characteristics of the image, together with the collection of materials:
the three types of excellent images are those made of gemstone, metal, and stone. (22.1)

O you of noble vows, these are the metals: diamond (*vajra*), ruby (*padmarāga*), and likewise those produced from *vālavāya*; as well as copper, brass, and iron. O Mahāmati, stone should be known to be of four kinds according to its association with gold.
The Vāruṇī, the Āgneyī, the Māhendrī, and the Vāyavī;
among these, the Brahma-stones are indeed of two kinds: the stone called Māhendrī-Vāruṇī, and likewise the stone called Āgneyī and the stone called Vāyavyā.

O Brahmin, the [image] to be avoided is of two kinds; one should also avoid those that have been previously consecrated. Having inspected the stone according to the rules, one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana). On the western side of the stone, one should smear it with cow dung.
O twice-born one, having caused a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) to be made with six loads of earth in front of that mountain,
and having placed a jar endowed with the auspicious marks in its center,
he should arrange eight jars around it in the eight directions.
As before, one should place gold, gems, and so forth within the center of the jar;
having wrapped it with two silken cloths, one should worship Brahmā there.
Likewise, the wise practitioner should worship Indra and the other deities in the [other] jars.
For the sake of pacifying cruel spirits, one should offer a bali-oblation in all directions.
One should perform a fire-offering in the four quarters with one hundred and eight oblations,
and should sacrifice sacrificial wood, clarified butter, and cooked rice using the root mantra.
Having caused the recitation of the *puṇyāha* (day of merit) to be performed by the foremost of the twice-born,
he should thereafter, becoming attentive, utter this mantra: "Oṃ,
obeisance to Viṣṇu, the source of all worlds, the sovereign lord."
"Salutation to Viśva, the one of universal form, the sovereign lord of sleep.
Having cleared away all people, one should utter this mantra:
'The yakṣas, rākṣasas, and piśācas who constantly dwell here...'"
"May all those [impurities] depart; may Hari be ever present.
Having spoken thus, the preceptor, that bull among sages, together with the patron, should look at his own face in a mirror at night. || 22.14 ||

If he should see an auspicious omen, let him take a stone that is beautiful and resonant. O twice-born one, having risen at dawn, he should avoid it if an inauspicious omen is seen; yet even if no such omen is seen, he should still take it—this is the certainty of the scripture.

The preceptor, having gone together with the artisans, should examine the ground. A stone with its tip pointing toward the direction of Indra (the east) or likewise with its tip pointing upward is excellent.
Those with their tips directed toward the intermediate directions should be avoided; those endowed with the proper characteristics should be taken.
Having uprooted the mountain, the wise one should consecrate it with jars;
then, having bathed it with pitchers and wrapped it there in cloths,
he should worship it in due order with scents, flowers, and so forth, using the root mantra.
Having taken a stone endowed with the auspicious marks, one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa).
Stones are considered to be of three types: male, female, and neuter.
Likewise, the image (bera) should be of the masculine gender, while the pedestal (pīṭhikā) should be of the feminine.
Thus should the fashioning of the image be performed, and one should have it executed with diligent effort.
I shall now declare the specific measurements of the icon;
the knower of mantras, being most excellent, should construct the temple in accordance with the proportions of the image.
O Kāśyapa, its measurement should correspond to the [physical stature] of the sacrificer;
O twice-born one, beginning from four finger-breadths and increasing by four finger-breadths at each step,
it should reach up to one hundred and eight finger-breadths.
An image should be made of gold; beyond this, one should not have it made [of other materials]. An image made of silver, copper, or stone should be based upon a temple.
That image which is equal in size to the interior of the shrine is considered the best.
O twice-born Kāśyapa, know that the middle image is one part less than nine parts, and the inferior image is one part less than five parts;
this is always the case regarding the measurement of the womb (the interior), O self-controlled one.
Having taken five parts, one should take three parts from those five; or two parts from those three parts. They know these to be the best, the middling, and the lowest [sizes].
The measurement of the door is thus declared, or it may be increased by a quarter or a half.
The measurement for the superior, inferior, and middling [temples] is proclaimed as follows:
it should be equal to the width of the pure entrance, or perhaps one-quarter greater, or even one-and-a-half times the extent of the entrance;
thus there are the superior, inferior, and middling [dimensions].
When the measurement of the pure entrance (śuddhadvāra) is divided into eighteen parts,
one part shall be the best [measurement] and two parts shall be the middling. Alternatively, the wise man should have the kautuka constructed according to the measurement of the pillar.
O Mahāmati, one should fashion the image at a measurement of one and a half times the height of the pillar;
know that the height of the standing posture is equal to the height of the door or the seat.
According to some, it should be less by one-ninth, while others say it should be less by one-fifth.

O best of the twice-born, O high-minded one, know that the height of the pedestal for the seat may be superior, inferior, or middling; it should be half a door-measure more than a quarter, or even greater than a full quarter. 22.33–22.34.
Understand, O Brahmin, that the bed should be twice the width of the door, or even one and a half times; one should not allow it to be either less or more.
One may construct the standing, moving, and sitting areas according to one's desire.
One should perform the ritual worship of the *karmabera* (action image) in accordance with the *mūlabera* (original image).
One should fashion the *karmabera*, as well as the *balibera* (offering image), measuring twelve *aṅgulas* or less by four *aṅgulas*.
O best of the twice-born, one should establish that measurement for the journey;
O twice-born, the image in the artificial temple should be eight *aṅgulas*.
One should have it made as four parts or even three parts of the sacrificial image (*yāgaberam*).
One should fashion an image for bathing, endowed with a height of two cubits,
marked by the four emblems— the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus— and,
provided with all the proper characteristics, one should place it upon a pedestal.
Of all these images, the ritual worship (karmārcā) should be performed on four occasions.

The image should be very beautiful, serene, and worthy of worship. O twice-born one, its height should be equal to that of the fixed image (dhruvabera), divided into three parts according to the division. || 22.41 ||

Or, O best of sages, it may be fourfold; among these, one [type] should be elevated. Thus, according to the measurement of the festival image for the auspicious rite of *kautuka*, one should make it with a third part or again with a fourth part.
This sequence for the *karmārcā* (action-image) of one possessing many *beras* has been proclaimed;
for one with a single *bera*, it should be half of that, or even one-quarter more. The *utsavārcā* (festival-image) should be one-third of the height and may be of three types.

Just as the permanent worship (dhruvārcā) is prescribed for the arrangement of the bed, seat, and place, so too must the rites beginning with the ritual worship (karmārcā) be performed accordingly. When the permanent image is lying down, [the ritual] should be performed while it remains either standing or seated.
One should perform the auspicious rites for the commencement of the work and the daily auspicious rites;
one should establish the arrangement of the pedestal (pīṭha) everywhere—listen, O Sage!
When the measurement of the image is divided into three parts, the pedestal should be made with one part.
O twice-born one, it should be provided with sandals and other such items, circular and auspicious with five parts;
it should be square, charming, and its length equal to the width of a lotus stalk,
with two well-constructed prabhāśaṅkus (ornamental spikes) arranged at the third part.
Having divided the height of the pedestal into three parts, one should fashion a lotus with it;
this lotus should be endowed with twelve petals or eight, according to one's preference.
One should make the petals equal in height to that [pedestal], and in its center, a beautiful pericarp.
One should have it fashioned as a lotus with its stalk and leaves, resembling a full-blown lotus;
or simply a lotus with its petals; or a pedestal, or even a lotus provided with a hollow. || 22.51-52 ||
O best of the twice-born, this construction of the pedestal for the established image has been declared;
it may be square, rectangular, or even circular, and its height should be equal to the height of the image, or one-third of it. (22.53)
For one who is seated, there should be a lotus-seat provided with many petals, O twice-born one, which is either beautiful and spacious or otherwise;
having drawn back the left leg and extended the other. || 22.54–55 ||
O twice-born one, one should visualize a lotus in front of the Lord who is seated comfortably upon the aforementioned throne;
on the right side of the Lord, one should place Lakṣmī, and on the left, Vasundharā.
O best of the twice-born, for one who is seated, one should visualize the two goddesses as seated;
Śrī and Bhūmi should always be at the sides of the sixfold image during the rites and other rituals.
For one situated on a single seat, they may be positioned either in front of the deity or separately from him.
Or, having visualized Lakṣmī as standing, one should cause her left foot to hang down;
or, having visualized Lakṣmī as standing, one should cause her left foot to hang down.
Then, likewise, the Earth is seated, while both [Lakṣmī and the Earth] stand for the one who is standing. (22.59)
Following the model of the original image, one should fashion a halo that is circular, or perhaps oval and elongated,
captivating to the mind and endowed with masses of radiance. Now, O Kāśyapa of noble vows, hear the measurement for the image.

The uṣṇīṣa should be one finger-breadth, and the hairline (keśānta) should be three finger-breadths. From that point onward, O twice-born one, the measurement up to the end of the eye-socket line should be thirty-six barley-corns; likewise, it should extend to the ends of the two nostril cavities.
And likewise, O best of the twice-born, [the measurement] from the chin to the end of the hair should be the same;
the measurement of the face from the chin is one hundred and eight barleycorns (*yava*).
The first finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) should have three positions, and the measurement of the thigh, O best of the twice-born, is as follows.
The height should be twenty-six finger-breadths, and its thighs should be proportionate to that;
now hear the measurements for the remaining parts as they have been stated.
O twice-born one, in the inferior ten-tāla system, the face is considered to be one hundred barley-corns in length.

In that same manner, the three joints [of the thighs] should be two hundred barley-corns; it is said that the shanks should be endowed with an equal height. The neck, the knee, and the ankle are each four finger-breadths.
"O bull among the twice-born, the height of the image has been described;
O twice-born one, because it is subtle and difficult to determine, it has been stated by me to you.
Thus [ends] the Viśvāmitra-saṃhitā within the Mahopaniṣad of the Pañcarātra.
The twenty-second chapter, titled "The Measurement of the Image" (Bimbamānavidhi).
The twenty-third chapter: Kāśyapa.
"O descendant of Gādhi, O Blessed One, you ought now to tell me the means for the restoration of dilapidated palaces and images. (23.1)
— Viśvāmitra.

O Kāśyapa, O best of the twice-born, if there is a loss in the limbs of images of the Self-Existent One, of divine beings, of sages, of humans, or of the Blessed One— whether they be made of jewels or fashioned as reflections— [then a calamity shall occur]. 23.2.
O Great-minded One, whatever limb may be missing, it must indeed be restored with gold;
it must not be left out, O bull among the twice-born.
Likewise, for those made of stone, restoration is likewise prescribed.
Whether for the purpose of concentration or for the creation [of the image],
having established the Śakti residing within the central image exactly as before,
one should perform the rites such as the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) and so forth, just as in the case of a formal installation (pratiṣṭhā). || 23.5 ||

O Kāśyapa, if the images remain stable, one may then perform the rite of consecration; O twice-born one, one must never abandon them under any circumstances. Having melted down an old iron image that has become worn out, one should fashion it anew.
But when a new creation has occurred, O best of the twice-born, if the ancient goddesses exist in their worn-out forms, one should reunite the Lord with them;
no other goddesses should be fashioned. || 23.8 ||
If there should be no interruption in their ritual of worship,
those who know the scriptures maintain that one should not perform a remarriage.
If, however, a deficiency should arise regarding the radiance, the sacred seat, and so forth— || 23.9–23.10 ||

O best of the twice-born, even when performing sacrifices for those [deities], one must not do so without first performing their *samādhi* (concentration/absorption). Having caused the *śakti* residing within their respective images to be withdrawn from either the jar (*ghaṭa*) or the primary image (*mūlabera*), you should then perform their *samādhi*.
Having sprinkled [the image] with water, the worship should be performed as before.
O Sage, if the image— whether made of stone or material substance— should become worn out,
one should fashion a new image of Bālājaya and install the Śakti within it.
One should propitiate that [deity] once it has been abandoned; one may bury it in smoke or in water,
or deposit it before the best of the twice-born or in a temple— listen now to the procedure for this,
O high-minded one, in the event that laxity should arise regarding the temple.
Having installed the deity together with his retinue in the temporary abode,

one should worship him right there until the construction of the permanent temple is complete. Whether the temple is old or not yet old, as long as it remains stable, the deity shall remain established in that temple.
One should not remove the worn-out [image] elsewhere; one should install a second one instead.
Furthermore, if there is a loss of a limb of the deity's abode or the like, one should not fashion [a replacement] unless it has actually occurred.
And if the cloth is not worn out, one may fashion [a new one] only if one perceives the image to be unstable.

It brings about the swift destruction of that sacrificer along with his lineage. O bull among the twice-born, if a temple or similar structure was previously built in violation of the rules through negligence, one should have it reconstructed in accordance with the proper characteristics.
Furthermore, in the rite of re-consecration for both multi-liṅga and single-liṅga shrines, one should arrange them as they were before;
one must not arrange them in a reversed order.
If, during the initial consecration, the shrine was devoid of the Goddess, it should remain so even in the subsequent re-consecration.
O observer of noble vows, for the patron, whether together with his queens or without them, the Bahubera [image] should be fashioned according to his understanding;
likewise, a temple, a bimba [image], or a self-manifested (svayaṃvyakta) superhuman [image]. || 23.21–23.22 ||
If it was previously devoid of the [proper] characteristics, then even when it is worn out or burnt, it should be treated likewise;
otherwise, one must not perform [the rite at all], for if it were done, a great fault would arise.
This applies to images in standing, walking, or reclining postures, exactly as before.
Indeed, among non-human beings, the sinless must act in this very manner;
among human beings, however, there is no fault in creating again according to one's will. Whatever object, whatever measure, and whatever kind has been fashioned by the gods—[so it shall remain].
The temple should be restored exactly as it was; otherwise, even in the case of a renovation, it should not be done differently.
O Brahmin, if one constructs it otherwise out of delusion, it results in harm for both the king and the kingdom; therefore, one should construct it just as it was before.
If the temple is made of brick, or of clay, or of human (stone), or even of wood,
and it should become dilapidated, one may rebuild it with stone or with brick; in that case, no fault is found.
For the sake of protection, one should extend the secondary seats (upapīṭha) and so forth outward;
there, one should install and further arrange the retinues residing therein.
For one who desires their protection, no fault shall arise in that regard.
If the gateway or the pedestal should become worn out,
or if it has been destroyed or displaced by the currents of rivers and the like,
one should reconstruct the temple, the image, and so forth in another location from that site. (23.30–23.31)
By whichever mantra, whichever form, and by whichever type of qualified practitioner [the deity] was conceived, one should likewise conceive that very same form.
The teacher [should likewise conceive] the form, the tantra, and the mantra as being of that same nature.
In the restoration of a dilapidated temple and in the original consecration, the fruit for both [the agent and the patron] shall be equal.
However, if the procedure is performed in reverse by one who is merely authorized to install an image,
there will be a great loss for the king, the kingdom, and the people.
When the restoration of a dilapidated temple is being planned and many images have been consecrated,
one should bathe the ritual image and place it upon the altar.
No immersion in water should be performed, except for the ceremony of opening the eyes.
O Brahmin, one should perform everything else except for the processes of withdrawal and emission;
having approached [the deity] with the *dhruvabera*, one should arrange everything.
Then, having constructed the *bālālaya* (the childhood abode), one should respectfully pray to it during that night.
Having brought that Śakti, which possesses the *tadgratā* (the state of being identical with That), and having placed it upon the head of the grain in the pitcher (*kumbha*),
and having worshipped it thoroughly, the Preceptor, when the time has arrived,
installs that Śakti into the *mūlabera* (the primary image) according to the path prescribed in the scriptures.
One should especially arrange the retinue around the pitcher and the two footprints (or the two pādas).
At the conclusion of that, one should perform the utsarga; for that is remembered as the rite of pacification (śānti).
This applies to the temple, the image, and also to the halo, the pedestal, and so forth.
O Kāśyapa, even when damage has occurred to the image—such as the breaking of its limbs—and it has been restored through the rite of rejoining; or when there has been an interruption in worship;
or when contact with the untouchable has occurred due to feces, urine, blood, or similar impurities.

O twice-born one, when defilement occurs through touch, whether of the temple or of the image, sprinkling (saṃprokṣaṇa) must be performed; this is the settled rule for weapons. According to the degree of the fault, there shall be either sprinkling or bathing (snapana) of Hari.
"And the wise man should perform the fire-sacrifice (homa) for the sake of pacifying all ritual actions.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Procedure for Renovating [a Temple]," in the Viśvāmitra-saṃhitā of the Mahopaniṣad within the Pañcarātra.
Chapter Twenty-four: Kāśyapa said,
"O Blessed One, even when the Vaiṣṇava sacrifice is being performed constantly,"
"O Guru, if an obstacle arises due to the faults of the king, the kingdom, or other such causes,
what should men on earth do to completely destroy that fault?
If you have a mind of grace toward me, you ought to tell me that."
While Viśvāmitra was being propitiated by the best of the twice-born,
listen to the ritual prescribed for the sake of pacification in the event of a lapse in mantras or a lapse in rites. (24.3)
I shall now declare the expiation for the multitude of faults accumulated over a year,
known as the *pavitrāropaṇa*, which destroys all sins.
This supreme rite of propitiation must be performed every single year.
It should be performed either in the month of Śrāvaṇa or even in Bhādrapada.
[The months beginning with Āṣāḍha are not suitable for the Pavitrāropaṇa anywhere. One should use threads spun by Brahmin maidens, whether made of cotton or otherwise.
Furthermore, one should wash silken garments— whether purchased or obtained otherwise— that are uniform in color and free from defects,
by mixing them with powders of mung beans, black gram, and so forth, using pure and clear water upon clean wooden boards or similar surfaces. (24.7)
Having placed them there, the wise man should dry them in the sun;
then, once they are purified, he should examine them for blades of grass or hair and, having removed any such things, remain composed.
Having folded them triple, he should then cause them to be folded triple again.
Having quadrupled those [seeds] and made them resemble the fruit of the mātuluṅga,
one should first place them in new earthen vessels on a clean,
level, and auspicious ground smeared with cow dung. || 24.10 ||

Having fixed two stakes made of *jajñu* wood according to the prescribed measurement, one should erect a pivot (*pravartaka*) upon those stakes in the same manner. This should be performed by those who have bathed, are clad in white garments, are learned in the Vedas, and are composed in mind. || 24.11–24.12 ||

One should have the *pavitraka* (sacred thread) prepared by skillful Vaiṣṇavas who wear the vertical *puṇḍra* marks and are free from boastfulness; they should face either north or east. It should consist of one hundred and eight threads and be provided with thirty-two knots.
For the purpose of the consecration (adhivāsa) of such things as the primary image and so forth,
there should be the measurement for the mandala, the measurement for the water-pot (kumbha),
the measurement for the altar-rim (mekhalā), and the sacred thread for the consecration of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa). || 24.14–24.15 ||
One should perform the purificatory rites (*pavitrāṇi*) upon those situated within the wheel-lotus mandala—its hub, spokes, and rim—and likewise outside the enclosure.
The purificatory rite should be equal to that; now hear the rule for the knotting of the threads.
Know that there are four hundred threads and twenty-seven knots;
O twice-born one, the number of threads is three-quarters [of the total], while the knots are double that.
The number of threads is four hundred, and the knots consist of three times that amount.
In the outer circle (*bāhyavṛtti*), there are likewise four hundred knots situated therein;
for *kumṛbha*, the threads are fivefold and the knots number one hundred and eight.
The threads and knots together shall be thirty-four in number.
Having fashioned the *karaka* vessels, they should be eighty-one in number;
there are also twenty-seven knots on the *karaka*.
Now listen in due order to those ten purifiers (*pavitra*) for the *kautuka* threads. (24.20–24.21)
The three supreme ornaments— the scent of authority, the garland, and the triple-umbrella— followed by the three of middle and inferior quality;
then the crown, the Śrīvatsa mark, the Kaustubha gem, and likewise the forest garland.
Thus have been the ten purifiers; now hear the sequence for tying the knots of the thread:
they know the first thread, ending at the navel, to consist of one hundred and eight [units];
there should be thirty-two knots, and the section called "Fragrance" extends as far as the heart.
It has eighty threads and twenty-five knots;
the *alaṃkāra-pavitra* is said to be as long as the middle of the shank. There are one hundred and eight threads and thirty-two knots.
For the sacred thread known as the *uttama* (highest), the number of threads is four hundred;
it has one hundred and eight knots and extends down to the middle of the knees.
For the *madhyama* (middle) thread, there are three hundred strands, O Kāśyapa.
It should be known that there are eighty knots; its middle is its length.
For the inferior [quality], two hundred threads are proclaimed;
it should have sixty knots, and its navel-center is its length.

The threads of the pavitra called *kirīṭa* shall be four hundred; its measurement shall be exactly like that of the *kirīṭa*, and it shall have thirty-two knots. The threads of the pavitra called *śrīvatsa* shall be four hundred.
There should be twenty-seven knots; that is the calculation up to the end of the neck.
For the Kaustubha gem, two hundred [units] are prescribed for its base.
Thirty-two knots should be made; that is the extent of the space between the breasts.
The body of the one named Vanamālā should be eight thousand [units] in measure;
the length of the feet has no fixed number of knots.
The sacred seat (pīṭha) should consist of twenty-five threads.
It should be joined with ten knots and provided with a length [of thread] equal to that;
on the incense bowl, the lamp bowl, the water jar,
and the rosary, there should be one hundred and eight threads and knots for each.

They should be fashioned according to their beauty; their length, O Kāśyapa, shall be twelve finger-breadths. This applies to Viṣvaksena, Tārkṣya, the guardians of the quarters, the deities of the directions, as well as to Durgā and Vighneśa.
O best of the twice-born, for Brahmā and Śaṅkara as well, there are one hundred and eight threads and thirty-two knots;
for all [the deities] beginning with Caṇḍa, there are twenty-seven threads, measured by the length of the hand.
O twice-born one, it should be made the measure of a cubit, possessing both glory and beauty; likewise,
the sacred thread for the door-arches and the water-pots, as well as the sacrificial offering and the sacred thread for the pericarp, should be of corresponding proportions.

For the teachers (ācāryas), ascetics (yatins), officiating priests (ṛtviks), worshippers, and likewise for the Vaiṣṇavas, [it should be] not hanging down inside [the waist], provided with one hundred and eight threads and many knots. || 24.40 ||
O twice-born one, it was suspended from the navel by eighty-one threads,
woven by one hundred and eight kings, filled with cotton, and adorned with knots. (24.41–42)
O best of the twice-born, for other dependents, the measurement should be suspended from the navel; it should be performed with eighty-one threads for the Vaiśyas and others,
using twenty-four tubs.
When there is wealth, there is an expansion of all purificatory rites.
[One should fill the interior of the knot] with gems, pearls, coral, and so forth, as well as metals such as gold; and in their absence, with cotton wool. || 24.44–24.45 ||
One should dye the spaces between the threads as is aesthetically pleasing;
when resources are available, a wise person should never practice parsimony.
Thus, once the purificatory rites have been performed according to the path enjoined by the scriptures, [the thread is ready].
O twice-born one, having placed them in many large golden vessels, or else in auspicious earthen jars, O twice-born one,
having bound their openings with pieces of cloth and with strong threads; 24.47–24.48.
On the tenth day of the bright fortnight,
in the evening, having entered the abode of Hari together with the image-keepers and the patron (yajamāna),
he should personally worship the Lord of Gods with devotion and make this request: ||| 24.49 ||
Bowing down with palms joined in reverence, one should utter this verse:
"O Blessed One, O Nṛhari, in that daily rite of worship of Yours, may there be the power to dispel the evil produced by omissions or excesses. (24.50–24.51)

O Lord of the World, impelled by the desire to act according to the prescribed rite, he performed that supreme worship known as the *Pavitrāropaṇa*, which is the very cause for the arising of all forms of prosperity. (24.52)
"Having performed this without obstacle, please favor me with compassion.
Having made this request and prostrated from within the temple,
he emerged and entered the excellent pavilion, which was well-smeared and beautifully adorned.
O twice-born one, having adorned it with canopies, garlands of dhava flowers, and wreaths of darbha grass,
and having placed pairs of full water-jars at the sides of the doors,
one should cause a mandala of wheels and lotuses to be fashioned there according to the prescribed rules. (24.55)
Having spread darbha grass near the mandala, the preceptor,
either seated or standing while facing east, should then make a formal resolve (saṃkalpa) and dwell there; remaining awake, he should spend the night there, intent upon the recitation of mantras.
On the eleventh lunar day, at the beginning of the night, one should perform the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*),

having carried out the sowing of seeds (*aṅkurārpaṇa*) according to the procedure prescribed for installation (*pratiṣṭhā*). Then, having performed the binding of the auspicious *kautuka* thread, [one should proceed].
Having performed the worship of the archways and so forth at the cardinal and intermediate directions of the pavilion,

and having had the four Vedas beginning with the Ṛgveda recited by the foremost of the twice-born who are most skilled in the Vedas, as well as the Śākha Ekāyanī, by learned scholars; ||| 24.59–60 |||
Having caused drums, kettledrums, cymbals, and other instruments to resound on all sides,
and having performed songs and other music accompanied by every auspicious rite,
he fashioned the Maheśvara-maṇḍala using ten loads of fragrant wood.
Having placed all the purificatory vessels there, the preceptor,
having performed the proclamation of the auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), and having purified [the site] through rites such as burning and sprinkling,
should fumigate it with incense produced from black aloe-wood (*kālāguru*).
Having consecrated them on all sides with jars, sandalwood paste, camphor, and everywhere with beautiful fragrant flowers,
Kāśyapa, he wrapped those vessels in fresh linen cloths.
Having displayed the *cakramudrā* and honored the pavilion with the weapon-mantra (*astra*),
one should encircle it on all sides with threads starting from the northeast direction;
then, one should meditate upon Sudarśana, the Lord of Weapons, above the pavilion.
On the ground, he placed the conch Pāñcajanya along with his mace, even in all directions;
then, for the pacification of those beings intent on seeking a vulnerability,
he scattered an offering of black-gram and rice all around.
O best of the twice-born, having bathed the image for the festival and removed the sacred thread, and having honored it and brought it into the pavilion,
one should offer the oblation there and complete the worship of Hari.
Having honored the vessel together with the *karkarī* until the end of the oblation,
and having gratified the God who has entered the fire by means of the offering,
[one should perform] all the purificatory ornaments for him who is stationed in his four places.
Having placed each [offering] individually into separate vessels and set them before [the deity],
while reciting the auspicious mantra "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," one should approach the primary image with the sacred thread [or purification] using the root mantra.
Having placed [the thread] upon all those images in due order, the preceptor,
having performed the placement of the purificatory ornaments (pavitrabhūṣaṇanyāsa) immediately thereafter,
should also envelop the temple with threads of five colors and so forth.
Having spent that entire night remaining awake with prayers and other rites,
at dawn he should lead [the deity] from the top of the pavilion to the altar for the ritual bath;
having bathed [the deity] according to the prescribed rule, he should then adorn him.
Having led [the deity] into the mandala there, one should worship the lamp last;
having also honored the pitcher and the other items, and having offered the four kinds of food on the three altars,
one should offer milk-rice and other oblations individually with the Puruṣasūkta.
Then, with many sesame seeds, ghee, incense, and aloe-wood,

the most excellent preceptor should offer eight hundred oblations separately for each of the sacrificial fuels and clarified butter during an auspicious moment as declared by the astrologer. (24.77–24.78)
One should first adorn the mandala with excellent purifying vessels (mūṣāṇa),
as well as the components of the mandala such as the lotus and so forth, each according to its proper form.
Having also worshipped the jars and other items, one should offer the fourfold food (caturvidha-anna).
When the deity is situated in the *kumbha* (pitcher), or in the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), or at the arches (*toraṇa*) and so forth,

one should place ornaments in all those pitchers in due order. Then, having circumambulated the Lord of the World (*jagannātha*) who is stationed within the mandala, one should perform a clockwise circumambulation (*pradakṣiṇa*).

Having caused [the deity] to enter the interior of the temple accompanied by all auspicious rites, and having performed the worship— including the ritual bathing and ending with the offering of food— along with the assembly of devotees,
one should [purify] all the primary images and other icons with the sacred threads (*pavitraka*).
Then, having adorned himself and departed, O twice-born one, he placed sacred objects before Caṇḍa and the others, as well as the hosts of his attendants,
and likewise before Brahmā and the rest, and even before the commander-in-chief and Garuḍa.
O Kāśyapa, for all [the rites] ending with the offering pedestal (balipīṭha),
one may use either the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī, or likewise "tad idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," or the eight-syllabled mantra, or the twelve-syllabled vidyā.
Then, having presented the purificatory materials (pavitra), the preceptor, accompanied by the image-makers (mūrtipa),
enters the abode of Viṣṇu; the patron, with a concentrated mind,
holds in his joined palms a collection of jewels or a heap of flowers made of gold.
Having placed [the gems] at his lotus feet while reciting hymns of praise,
he scattered those jewels and golden flowers;
likewise, he made even human beings pure.
Having informed the Lord of the other garments, the preceptor should take them;
he should cause the prescribed purificatory threads to be given to the officiating priests, the worshippers, and those learned in the Vedas,
after having beheld the lotus-face of the Lord.
One should recite this verse, which grants forgiveness from all the gods:
"O God of gods, Lord of the World, whatever I have done against you, O Ocean, please accept this act of propitiation, which fulfills all enjoyments. (24.91)
"O Treasure of the Worlds, this was not ordained by me through my own independent will;
rather, my mind was impelled by you—or perhaps something else. Forgive me!
Having thus informed the Lord of Gods, one should prostrate and ask for forgiveness. (24.92–93)
And at that time, the patron, with a joyful heart, should give cattle, land, a house, and wealth abundant in grain to the preceptor;
and to other assistants, he should give according to their respective roles in the ritual.
And a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given to them so that their minds may be satisfied. Having led the lords of the gods around the abode in a circumambulation during the afternoon,
one should cause them to enter the interior of the temple accompanied by all auspicious rites.
Having passed seven, three, or five days, one should perform the descent ceremony;
having recited the *puruṣasūkta* as well as the *rathantara* Sāman,
the *trisuparṇa*, the *mūla*, and the purificatory texts (*pavitra*), one should cause [the image] to descend.
These should be given to the preceptor for the sake of pleasing the Slayer of Madhu (Viṣṇu).
Then, having again dismissed Hari— who resides in the water-pot, who resides in the mandala, and who is outside— one should also perform the ceremonial bathing of the deity.
O Brahmin, by performing the ritual of offering the sacred thread (*pavitrāropaṇa*) to Hari according to this procedure, one certainly attains infinite fruits; of this there is no doubt.
O Brahmin, even by [offering] *kaṅkāraka* flowers according to this procedure...
"Likewise, O twice-born one,
one should offer leaves of *adamanyā* to the Lord for the sake of fulfilling the annual enjoyments of the Lord of Śrī.
Thus, in the *Pañcarātra*, in the *Mahopaniṣad*, in the *Viśvāmitra-saṃhitā*.
The twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Installation of the Purifier.
The twenty-fifth chapter: Kāśyapa.
"O Blessed One, abode of compassion, O Guru, you ought to tell me of the worship with *kaṅkāraka* flowers and the offering with *damanī* leaves. (25.1) —
Viśvāmitra.
O bull among the twice-born, listen with an attentive mind as I describe the worship of the Lord of Lakṣmī with *kaṅkāraka* flowers.
In ancient times, there was a royal sage named Ambarīṣa, the most excellent of the righteous.
The lord of the circle of kings, having conquered the entire earth with its islands and girdled by the ocean, that king delighted all his subjects through righteousness,
just as a sovereign delights his own people.
Out of sight of other duties,
he gratified the Lord of Sacrifice with many sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees;
the high-minded king performed ninety-nine horse-sacrifices.
He released the horse for the purpose of performing the hundredth sacrifice. While it was wandering at will, surrounded by many attendants,
Śakra, assuming a disguised form, carried off that horse from the sight of the guards.
Having searched everywhere for guards, and finding no horse or other sign of him,
they became dejected in countenance and informed the protector of the earth:
"Even though we were watching with vigilance, that horse of ours— " || 25.8 ||
"O Lord, you have vanished from our sight; tell us what must be done, O Master.
Having heard these words of theirs, King Ambarīṣa summoned his officiating priests, family priest, and teachers, and spoke these words: ||| 25.9–25.10 ||
"The horse has disappeared in the midst [of the sacrifice]; O twice-born ones, tell me what must be done!
When they were addressed thus, O twice-born one, those best of the twice-born spoke these words:
"Let some son of a brahmin be sought after; with him we shall perform the sacrifice."
Thus addressed, the protector of the earth, having purchased the son of the twice-born with his own wealth,
led the boy along the road; and he reported to me exactly what had occurred regarding the prince.
That twice-born Śunaḥśepa indeed became a protected disciple.
The king, too, with a despondent mind, said to Vasiṣṭha:
"This young Brahmin was brought by me for the purpose of [removing] obstacles to the sacrifice."
He too was saved by the Blessed One, the wise one who overcomes all;
thus the sacrifice attained its fruitfulness. Nevertheless, O twice-born one, the thought remains in my mind: "The Brahmin was brought here by me for the purpose of slaughter. || 25.15–25.16 ||
"But doubt persists; please prescribe an expiation.
Thus questioned, the blessed Vasiṣṭha, the best of sages, spoke to the great king Ambarīṣa, O best of the twice-born.
O King, that which the best of the twice-born spoke to the great king Ambarīṣa by my word— O King, that which the young brahmin was told by you according to my word.
"O protector of the earth, no fault shall accrue to you for having brought me here. Nevertheless, O King, if doubt still persists in your mind,
hear this supreme vow that removes the sin of killing a Brahmin."
This supreme vow is auspicious, conducive to fame and long life,
a great producer of health, pleasing to Viṣṇu, the singular cause of all prosperity,
and especially gratifying to the goddess Śrī. (25.20–25.21)
The Goddess always holds a white lotus flower in her hand;
the Śakti of the Enemy of Madhu (Viṣṇu) exists as two-fold, one for each [aspect] distinguished by the forms of Śrī and Mahī. Therefore, she is held in the hand by the Earth (Bhūmi).
"Worship that white water-lily (*kahlāra*), which is the cause of the Blessed One’s delight.
Having been thus addressed by the Blessed Vasiṣṭha, the lord of the earth worshipped the Lord of the Gods, the Master of Śrī, with white water-lilies.
Having enjoyed all worldly pleasures in this life, one shall indeed go to the station of Viṣṇu at the end;
therefore, I shall describe for you that which increases your splendor.
Even by me was the Lord Puruṣottama worshipped with white water-lilies.
O son of Kaśyapa, when your Brahminhood was attained through asceticism,
the venerable seer Vasiṣṭha, the son of Brahmā, said to you,
"You are a Brahmarṣi," in order to increase your splendor. (25.26–25.27)
"Worship that eternal god Viṣṇu with *kaṅkāra* flowers.
Having spoken thus and further explained the ritual procedure for it, the lord of sages vanished from sight;
and having heard that, O twice-born one, I too departed.
But having performed the vow by that very path prescribed therein,
O best of the twice-born,
listen with attention to this vow which accomplishes all goals, once it has been performed. (25.29–25.30)
O twice-born one, it may be in the king of seasons, spring, or likewise in autumn;
or in the month of Jyeṣṭha, or Śrāvaṇa, or Pauṣa, or Phālguna;
specifically on the fifth day of the bright fortnight, or on the twelfth, or even on the full moon.

O twice-born Kaśyapa, when the Rohiṇī, Śravaṇa, Āditya, the three Uttarās, and likewise other asterisms favorable to the sacrificer are present, as well as during months and other astrological periods suitable for the sacrifice,
any one of the three social classes may act as the sacrificer.
Requested by the patron,
the preceptor should cause this supreme annual sacrifice to the Blessed One (Bhagavadyāga), consisting of white lotuses (kahlāra),
to be performed on either the ninth or the seventh day prior to the day of worship.
On the third day, or immediately, the sowing of the auspicious sprouts (maṅgalāṅkura) should take place.
From that point forward, one should perform special worship of Hari;
in particular, the rite of decorating the pavilion and other areas must be carried out.
O you of noble vows, one should diligently decorate all the enclosures and the gates on every side, as well as the center of the village, with arches, garlands of banners, and flags,
so that these may become like those of the divine realms.
On the day preceding the day originally intended,
having completed all the rites associated with every auspiciousness and having erected the sacrificial post, one should have a pond excavated and a water-shed constructed to its west.
Having constructed it with four pillars, or joined with eight pillars, or even without them;
having prepared the canopy according to the rules and leveled the ground,
one should then smear it with cow dung and decorate it with lime powder.

In the center of that, having constructed a square measuring five *bhāras* of rice, he spread a linen cloth over it; then, having placed two *bhāras* of rice upon that, he deposited another two *bhāras* above them. (25.41–25.42)
Having placed sesame seeds, exceeding the weight [of the cloth], upon the garment,
the preceptor then places a pitcher filled with scented water upon that square area;
its entire body is wrapped with thread and it is adorned with a pair of linen cloths.
Having placed within it a bundle of *kuśa* grass well-endowed with the nine jewels,
one should invoke the goddess Earth into its center and worship her with the *arghya* offering and other rites.
One should also worship Indra and the other deities in the eight jars arranged around it.

And for the pacification of all obstacles, one should offer a *sudarśana* [image] in a water-pot and offer milk-rice (*pāyasa*) with the *pārthiva-mantra*. Having given that milk-rice to the guardian of the field (*kṣetrapāla*) in the east, [one should proceed].

Having offered oblations all around to Śakra and the other deities, as well as the bali-offering from the eastern direction to the northeast, he should recite the hymn beginning with "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ" and,
while studying, gather even very beautiful flowers.
Accompanied by the sounds of conchs, kettledrums, trumpets, and the like, as well as dance and song,
one should take fresh flowers from the vāpikā;
and let the Vaiṣṇavas also take flowers and water-vessels from every place.

Having placed [the image] in a collection of golden vessels and covered it, and having gathered flowers, one should place them before the jar. Then the preceptor, having performed the dismissal of the deity and having asked for forgiveness, [should proceed]. || 25.50–51 ||
O best of the twice-born, one should cause the elephant to be led by those mounted upon its shoulders;
and by elephants brought under the shade of umbrellas, let the *svasti-sūkta* be recited.
Furthermore, let Brahmins recite the four Vedas before it while they are studying.
Preceded by the resonant blaring of conchs, kāhala trumpets, and kettledrums,
with the sounds of musical instruments filling the quarters of the sky before him,
and with various banners that obscured the mass of sunlight; || 25.53-25.54 ||
Having performed a circumambulation of the sacred abode accompanied by song and dance,
and having entered the temple itself,
one should place flowers on the ground in front of the permanent image (dhruvabera) and present them to the deity.
Having removed the flowers and having arranged the pavilion,
[the rite should be performed] by Vaiṣṇavas who have bathed, wear white garments and turbans,
bear the vertical *puṇḍra* marks, and are Brahmins and others skilled in the art of garland-making. || 25.56–57 ||

One should have various garlands made according to the measurements of each respective principal image (mūlabera). One should prepare the preliminary consecration garland (adhivāsa-straja) to hang from the first measurement. O twice-born one, one should adorn the principal image with five hundred flowers.

One should prepare [the garland] for the *kautuka* and the festival with one hundred and eight [strings]; for the two goddesses known as Śrī and Bhūmi, one should prepare a garland with half that number;
and for the ritual images (*karmārcā*) and so forth, a garland with twenty-five [strings].

O twice-born one, one should fashion the ānāmila-suspension according to the proportions of the food and ornaments; O bull among the twice-born, one should separately prepare fifty garlands for the consecration of the *kumbha*, *maṇḍala*, and *kuṇḍa* using flowers.
O best among the foremost of the twice-born, one should likewise fashion garlands for the consecration;
hear now as these, measured according to the dimensions of the day, are being described.
For each of the images, beginning with the *dhruva*, there shall be five strings of beads. (25.62–63)
O best of the twice-born, there are five [types of offerings] in the forest known as Kirīṭavana: namely, the superior, the middling, and likewise that designated as inferior.
One should perform the superior offering for the principal image (mūlabera) with eight thousand [units].
The middle [type] reaches down to the knees with eight hundred flowers;
now hear also of the smallest, which hangs down to the thighs.
One should fashion the one that hangs down to the navel with six hundred flowers.
O best of the twice-born, one should fashion a crown-garland with one hundred and eight flowers; O most excellent of the twice-born, one should fashion a forest-garland with four thousand flowers,
smooth, reaching from the feet to the hair, and with rounded tips.
One should also fashion a garland for the pedestal out of one hundred and eight flowers; an excellent garland for the auspicious image should consist of five hundred,
a middling one of four hundred, and an inferior garland of three hundred flowers.
With fifty flowers,
O twice-born one, he should respectfully fashion a crown-garland and a forest-garland with five hundred flowers; he should also make a garland for the pedestal with eight hundred flowers.

O Sage, having described those known as the "Excellent" and the "Intermediate," [I shall now describe] those designated as "Inferior," which consist respectively of three hundred, two hundred, and one hundred flowers. The measurement of these flower-garlands is stated to be as previously mentioned.
O twice-born sage, one should perform [the rite] for those who have departed with their karma as the precursor, using eight hundred flowers, or half of that, or even half of that again;
or three, two, or likewise one, according to what is available.
For a man situated within the fire-pit of the Kumbha-maṇḥala,
a garland made of two hundred flowers is considered the best;
one made of one hundred and fifty flowers is proclaimed as the middling.
The measurement of the *karakas* is proclaimed to be the same as that of the *kumbhas*.
For each of their positions and attendants, there shall be one flower.
The measurement of the *karakas* is proclaimed to be the same as that of the *kumbhas*.
For those situated in that place and its surrounding retinue, there should be a single flower for each.
For those resting upon the circle of the rim, the nave, and the hub of the wheel, it should be made with dimensions one hundred, two, three, or four times that size. 25.76–77.
Garlands should be made with flowers for the Brahmā-portion,

and wreaths of the same measurement; O best of the twice-born, the wreaths for Prabhā and the auspicious amulets (kautuka) should consist of four thousand flowers each, being of that same measurement.
A garland should be fashioned with two thousand flowers for the image used during the festival; one should likewise have them made for the leaders of the army and the wings,
as well as for Caṇḍa and all the others, and for Indra and the rest.
O Sage, one should fashion thirty garlands for each [image] using *puṣya* flowers;
likewise, O Kāśyapa, for other images that are dependent on others, a wise person should thus adorn them with one hundred and eight [garlands]. 25.81.
O best of the twice-born, the necklaces and other ornaments should be fashioned so as not to hang down;
they should be made according to this method when flowers are available.
However, in the absence of flowers, they may be made with half-verses or even quarter-verses.
One should not omit this rite according to what is possible.
Having thus prepared the collection of garlands and sprinkled them with snow-water,
one should place them in golden vessels, using white threads and new cloths.
Having covered it and formed the *cakramudrā*, and having worshipped it with the *astra-mantra*,
one should fashion a [mandala]— such as a *bhūpura*— in the eastern part of the wheel-lotus using five measures of rice,
and upon that, with a new cloth.
Having spread out two *bhāra*s of rice grains,
one should then place *bhāra*s of sesame seeds upon them on a cloth that has been spread out.
Then, having fashioned a four-eyed image, one should place it upon those sesame seeds.
Having wrapped all the flower-vessels in new cloths,
the preceptor— bathed, pure, wearing garlands, clad in new threads and garments, and with his limbs anointed with sandalwood paste moistened by Himalayan water— [proceeds]. || 25.88–25.89 ||
Adorned with necklaces, earrings, bracelets, armlets, and other ornaments; wearing an upper garment and a white turban; possessing a golden sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*);
equipped with a *pavitra* ring and finger-rings, and decorated with gem-studded seals.
Adorned with vertical marks (*ūrddhvapuṇḍra*) fashioned from white clay,
accompanied by preeminent twice-born teachers (*deśika*) bearing the names of Keśava and others,
and joined by the patron (*yajamāna*) along with excellently adorned officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), [he set forth]. || 25.91–92 ||
Having entered the interior of the temple, he should then address the deity, prostrating himself on the ground like a staff and standing with palms joined in reverence:
"O Blessed One, remover of the distress of devotees, Supreme Person! (25.93)
"O God, I worship you with white water-lilies for your benefit;
O Lord of All, you ought to grant permission for this.
O God, please forgive my jests; accept my worship."
Having thus informed the Lord of Lakṣmī and having honored him with special distinction, and having reported everything in this manner, he should then have the auspicious day (puṇyāha) proclaimed.
Then, with ten gold coins (niṣkas), he should perform the *kautuka* rite upon the permanent image.

Having tied a protective amulet (*kautuka*) on the right hand of the two deities and also that of the preceptor— each fashioned with a measure of one *niṣka* of gold— in an image known as Kalyāṇa, using three *niṣkas* of gold;
Having again performed the hand-gestures (*mudrā*) and bowed to the Lord,
they placed Him— adorned with all ornaments— upon a palanquin and carried Him to the pavilion,
where the Lord was clothed and decorated as before.
Its floor was well-prepared and variegated with powdered lime;
its upper space was adorned with canopies, banners, and strings of pearls;
and it shone with a multitude of pillars draped with garlands of white water-lilies.
It was radiant everywhere with hanging garlands of white water-lilies,
adorned by the excellence of celestial chariots strewn with white lotus flowers,
and featured archways set at each of the four gateways.
Upon that [throne], which was adorned with garlands and sandalwood paste fashioned upon each of its arches,
and which shone with eight lion-claws and was decorated with wish-fulfilling trees made of *kahlāra* lotuses, he descended from his vehicle. (25.103–104)
Then, having seated the Lord upon a radiant seat adorned on all sides with hanging garlands of white water-lilies (kahlāra), one should honor Him there.
The excellent preceptor, having arrived here at the pavilion beforehand, [should perform the rites].
O Sage, the learned man, together with the officiating priests, should have a mandala constructed— either a wheel,
a lotus, a svastika, or a bhadraka— O best of the twice-born;
he should place a heap of grain in the northeast, outside of the mandala.
And one should place a great, excellent pitcher wrapped with thread,
covered with a pair of fine, new, unwashed linen cloths;
having cast nine gems into its center, [it should be filled] with pure water.
One should fill [the vessel] with a collection of fragrances such as sandalwood and the like. Then the wise man should place it in water and arrange a bundle of *kuśa* grass.
Having wrapped the water-pot (*karaka*) and filled it with jewels, he should set it down.
The practitioner of mantras should place a *kūrca* [grass-bundle] and set the water-pot (*kumbha*) to the south.
Having thus arranged eight pots in the eight directions of the mandala,
O twice-born one, he should establish the sacrificial fire-pit (*agni-kuṇḍa*) to the north.
Having placed water-pots all around at the sides of the doors, and having set down eight pots, placing all the pots in the four directions,
and having wrapped them with a pair of cloths while they are adorned with jewels; || 25.112–25.113 ||
Having placed within all the jars, together with their lids, the eight great golden weapons set in their centers,
and having also arranged sprouts of the great *aśvattha* tree, one should then set the water-pots in place.
Having placed either one hundred and eight or likewise eighty-one [vessels] upon heaps of grain, according to the very path prescribed in the scriptures—
[vessels] filled with fragrant waters, provided with strainers, and covered with lids.
Having covered it with cloths, one should prepare the bed again upon a square area of ground smeared with cow dung and water,
its surface and interior decorated with fine lime-powder.
Having fashioned a square out of ten *bhāras* of rice,
and having spread a very beautiful new cloth over it,
one should then place upon that [cloth] pieces equal in measure to the grains of rice.
Thereafter, one should spread rice over that cloth;
then, one should place within it sesame seeds equal in measure to those previously mentioned.
Afterward, one should cover them with linen cloth placed on top.
Having spread various well-woven garments upon it,
he placed a cushion for the head and also at the sides of the feet—
soft with cotton wool, suitable for the resting of hands and feet. (25.121–122)

Having placed fashioned pillows upon them and covered them with fine cloths from above, the most excellent Guru, having established the eight jars in the cardinal directions according to the previously mentioned procedure, [proceeds].
And having stationed auspicious women all around,
one should fumigate [the area] on every side with incenses, sandalwood, and the finest agaru;
as well as mung beans, black gram, sesame seeds, wheat, and horse gram.
Having separated the flat beans, kidney beans, and mustard seeds mixed with barley,
as well as the rice grains— one of each being equal in measure to Śiva—
and the fruits of plantains and jackfruit, O Kāśyapa.
O best of men, having set out mangoes, coconuts, and *likuca* fruits,
as well as *mātuluṅga* fruits and areca nuts, along with betel leaves, betel nuts, and fresh turmeric; 25.127–128.
On all sides were the eight auspicious symbols: the Śrīvatsa, the forest garland,
a pair of fish, a full pitcher, the Svastika, a mirror, a conch, and a discus,
each individually adorned with a golden ornament.
Having had [the image] fashioned and installed, and having informed the deity,
the preceptor sits before the deity, performs the ritual placement of mantras on the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*),
and arranges the vessels for the *arghya* offering and other requisites.
Having worshipped the water-jars and Hari situated within the pitcher,
having propitiated the Lord residing in the mandala, and having established the fire in the sacrificial pit,
he should worship the Deity according to the rules, preceded by the ritual of the mantra-seat.
Having prepared the sacrificial ground for the bath and performed the worship while seated before the deity,
one should then bathe the Lord with the waters from the ritual jars in due order;
having also performed the consecration with the "thousand-streams" water, one should complete the rite.
In this manner, one should perform the rite of lustration (nīrājanā) and lead [the deity] to the seat of ornaments;
having adorned [the deity] up to the end of the [offering of] garments and having worshipped according to the rule,
one should then honor the Lord seated upon the food-offering mat with the arghya and other offerings.
Having offered the madhuparka and presented betel-leaf,
he gave a pair of cows with their calves, adorned with garlands, their hooves fashioned of gold, their horns encased in ornaments, and duly honored.
Then, having presented [the offerings] to the teacher and given eight kinds of grain,

one should offer a collection of five-colored foods into the jars, the mandala, and the bellies of the images; having offered soups and drinks, one should present the great sacrificial oblation (*mahāhavis*).
Then, having offered betel leaf with its aromatic ingredients along with cakes for the scent of the mouth,
and having specifically presented these to all the images and to the two deities, he should provide them with a feast rich in all enjoyments.
Having given sesame seeds, clothing, gold, gems, and even rice,
as well as betel and a vessel of ghee as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor,
he should then go near the fire-pit and offer oblations into the sacred fire.
Having properly performed the oblation of fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and cooked rice to the deity,
one should then offer oblations with white water-lilies mixed with clarified butter,
numbering one thousand and eight, and having thus performed the rite of pacification (*śānti-homa*).
Having made a mark with ashes and dismissed the deity residing in the fire, he went into the presence of the Lord and offered the oblation; then,
having distributed the sacrificial offering (bali) all around to the host of deities beginning with Kumuda.
Having offered prayers to the Lord of the Gods of gods and brought flower garlands,
one should place the garlands individually upon the water-jar, the mandala, and the sacrificial pit, accompanied by the sounds of conchs, cymbals, trumpets, and other instruments.
Having established [the deities] in various ways for the sake of their acceptance during the festival,
and having entered the inner sanctum of the two divine images as well as the primary and other [shrines],
and then having installed them within the images once more and returned to the pavilion; || 25.147 ||

Having asked the deity for forgiveness, one should place him upon the bed. While the deity is situated there together with the goddesses, one should display all the various items, such as vessels of grain and so forth. || 25.148–149 ||
O best of the twice-born, having arranged [the image] as before, one should also place the Lord upon the bed together with Śrī and Bhūmi, with his head facing east,
and cover him with white, red, and other such woolen blankets worthy of the gods.
Having separately stationed the weapons, such as the discus and others, in the eight directions, the preceptor,
remaining awake along with the patron, should pass the night with hymns,
Vedic recitations, songs, and dances.
At dawn, O twice-born one, the preceptor rises, bathes, and completes his daily rites;
then the teacher goes to the side of the deity,
bows to the god, raises him up, and seats him upon a seat.
Then the preceptor, having risen from his seat, bathed, and approached the side of the deity,
placed the Lord upon the bathing pedestal along with the vessels for the *arghya* and other offerings up to the *madhuparka*.
Thereafter, he performed the ritual ablution with the jars, beginning with the lowest and ending with the highest.
Having adorned [the site] as before and offered it upon the seat,
having worshipped as before and presented the sacrificial oblations,
a great oblation was likewise prepared with ten measures of rice.
With loads provided with every kind of fruit and combined with all types of condiments;
with boiled milk-rice prepared with strained, pure cow's ghee;
and with well-prepared varieties of eatables such as cakes and *pṛthuka* grains. || 25.157–158 ||

O best of men, having presented offerings to the images and to Dhruva and the other [deities], and having duly offered oblations of wood-apple (samī) into the fire seven times according to the rules, the preceptor,
having then performed the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), should present it to the deity.
When an auspicious moment had arrived, one that brings prosperity to the patron,
having worshipped Hari according to the ritual jars within the sacrificial pit and the mandala—
the Lord who stands both outside and within the central image— [25.160–161].
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite, beginning with the doors and archways,
and having placed all the prepared garlands upon the water-jar (kumbha),
O best of the twice-born, one should likewise place all the garlands upon the mandala and the jar.
Having adorned and prepared the auspicious site,
and having decorated it on all sides up to the edge of the sacrificial altar (balipīṭha),
the preceptor likewise adorns the palace situated there and the assembly of deities.
Having adorned it on all sides with garlands like purificatory rites, and having gratified the entire host of deities beginning with Kuśeśaya, as well as Indra and the others,
everywhere with various kinds of offerings, he satisfied the deities of the site (*vāstudevatā*).
Having shown all the vessels of grain, as well as the eight auspicious symbols,
all the fruits, and those betel leaves and areca nuts to the deity, the preceptor himself presented all of that. || 25.166–25.167 ||

One should personally take up the entire collection of bedding and so forth; having performed the ritual dismissal (udvāsana) of the host of deities residing in the jar, the mandala, the fire-pit (kuṇḍa), and other locations,
according to the procedure prescribed for the flower-sacrifice, beginning with the jar.
Having placed that Lord of the gods upon the vehicle, such as a chariot,
and having circumambulated the entire village or the temple,
one should lead the deity back into the interior of the sanctum and [bathe] him with the water contained in the pitcher.
Having sprinkled [the deity] there and properly installed the God, and having offered prayers to the Lord of the Gods of gods, accompanied by the patron (yajamāna), he says:
"O Lord of the Gods of gods, accept this [offering] made with *kahlāra* flowers."
"Filled with heaps of enjoyments granted by you, and bestowing all desires"—
having thus informed the Lord of Gods and prostrated, one should ask for forgiveness;
and at that time, the patron should give the sacrificial fee to the preceptor.
He should give a hundred gold *niṣkas*, or half of that;
likewise, cattle, houses, villages, and various kinds of garments, both to other officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and to the assistant personnel. || 25.174 ||
One should also give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) in proportion to the work performed to all those who sing,
those who dance, those who know the Vedas,
