those who play musical instruments, and those who provide assistance. || 25.175-176 ||
For the sake of complete gratification, one should bestow gold coins and various garments according to one's ability; one should not practice stinginess regarding wealth.
At dawn, at the conclusion of the worship, [one should perform the rites].
And one should cause Japanese garlands to be given to the devotees of Viṣṇu;
for all those who wear upon their heads garlands discarded after being enjoyed by the gods, all their misdeeds accumulated over seven births [are destroyed].
Having shaken off [all impurities], men attain the world of Viṣṇu once again,
O best of Brahmins, who causes this worship of the Enemy of Madhu to be performed.
Even one who possesses nothing obtains undisputed sovereignty over the earth.
Having enjoyed various pleasures here in this world that are very difficult to obtain—
possessing elephants, horses, chariots, and great serpents, and accompanied by sons and grandsons— that man, having whitened the entire world with his fame, [attains liberation].
Having delivered his ancestors— ten preceding and ten succeeding generations—
at the end of the body, he attains the supreme abode from which there is no return.
He should also honor that teacher with the remains of food enjoyed by the gods, garlands, and other offerings.
Having adorned him and placed him upon a vehicle such as an elephant or horse at the front,
preceded by the sounding of drums, kettledrums, conchs, and other instruments,
he was attended on all sides by the best of the twice-born, who were knowers of the Vedas.
Having performed a circumambulation of the village accompanied by the parasol and fly-whisks,
one should cause [the image] to enter one's own home, endowed with all auspicious marks.
Thus, in the *Pañcarātra*, in the *Mahopaniṣad*, in the *Viśvāmitra-saṃhitā*.
The twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Cultivation of Kahlāra Lotuses" (or "The Ritual for Planting Kahlāra Lotuses").
The twenty-sixth chapter: Viśvāmitra.
O best of the twice-born, I shall describe the ritual for the offering of the *damanaka* flower;
by the performance of which, O Brahmin, a human being attains both worldly and otherworldly fruits, and at the end reaches the supreme state. (26.1)
Furthermore, specifically during the bright fortnight of the month of Vaiśākha,
on the twelfth day and on the full moon, the worship with *damanaka* leaves should be performed,
O best of the twice-born; its procedure shall now be described.
O great sage, on the ninth, seventh, fifth, or third day prior to the day originally intended, one should perform the planting of the sprouts according to the previously described procedure.
Then, on the morning of the eleventh day, having completed the twilight rituals,
he bathed, put on white garments, and adorned himself with all ornaments;
his hands were purified and he was decorated with white unguents.
Having gone to the garden accompanied by the officiating priests and joined by the sacrificer,
O Sage, he went to the Damana grove; then, to the west of it,
he constructed a water-shed with four pillars and covered it with a canopy.
Then, having wound a garland of *darbha* grass around it, he prepared a square altar below it,
smeared it with cow dung,
and placed four loads of rice upon it.
Having spread [the base] over that and having spread a cloth upon it, one should then scatter half as many grains of rice; above that, on the cloth,
one should place half as many sesame seeds, and above those, one should set down a water-pot.
With all its limbs wrapped in thread and set with various jewels,
one should wrap it with a pair of linen cloths and place a bundle of *kuśa* grass upon it;
likewise, one should place a water-pot of that same kind to its right.
Having placed eight water-pots (kumbha) in its eight directions in sequence,
one should worship Pradyumna in the central pot and Sudarśana in the small vessel (karaka). Furthermore, one should worship Śakra and the other deities in order around the eight pots.
Then, having offered milk-rice (pāyasa) and established the fire in the north,
he should offer one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter with the Pradyumna mantra; thereafter, he should worship Kṣetreśa.
The preceptor, together with the guardians of the images, while reciting the mantra of Pradyumna, should cast an offering of milk-rice (pāyasa) into the eight directions.
Having prepared the *damanaka* leaves, he should place them within golden vessels.

Having placed those leaves back upon the jar on the ground and having sprinkled it with that water, O bull among the twice-born, the best of the twice-born [priests] should cause it to be carried away while chanting the Śākuna Sūkta, O eminent Brāhmaṇa. || 26.17–18 ||
Accompanied by other eminent brahmins whose faces were resonant with their own Vedic recitations, and deafening the quarters of the world with the sound of musical instruments,
he covered the sky with a multitude of parasols, yak-tail whisks, and banners.

Having entered the abode of Hari, which is endowed with every auspiciousness, and having shown it to the Lord, one should bring forth a pavilion of flowers; then, by means of pure and skillful brahmins expert in the art of garland-making and the like, [the ritual should proceed]. || 26.20–26.21 ||
One should fashion the series of garlands according to the measurement of the *kahlāra* lotus,
following the sequence of superior and other grades in accordance with each respective *bīja*.
The thickness of the pitcher, the mandala, and the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) should be one cubit (*hasta*) in measure.
The same applies to Caṇḍa and the others, as well as to Tārkṣya and Seneśa;
their length is like that of a garland of white water-lilies, and their thickness is the measure of a cubit.
And for all the archways, [there is a garland] of damanī leaves.
One should have a beautiful garland of *damana* flowers fashioned from the center;
one should hang beautiful *damana* garlands as a canopy all around. One should encircle both the temple and the pavilion with a braid of *damana* flowers.
One should construct a pavilion or even a temple with garlands of *damanī* flowers;
one should encircle the pillars with *damanāla* garlands and suspend them from those [pillars].
One should arrange the pavilion all around like a garden, as previously described.
O best of the twice-born, one should construct the pavilion and the mandala as before. In the northeastern quarter of that site, upon a heap of grain,
one should place a water-pot wrapped with auspicious threads as previously described.
Having wrapped it with a pair of linen cloths and placed nine jewels within,
and having likewise arranged eight jars in all eight directions,
one should place another set of eight jars all around the perimeter of the mandala.
O best of the twice-born, one should perform everything according to the ritual for the great jar (*māhaghaṭa*), making it rich with mango and *aśvattha* leaves;
and having prepared the bed of the God of gods as before.
Having first spread ten loads of śāli rice upon the ground,
and having covered it with new, fine, high-quality silken cloths,
one should likewise arrange over that an amount of rice equal to those same measures.
O best of the twice-born, having prepared a bed upon that with sesame seeds in that same number, and having spread linen cloths over it,
he placed variegated woolen blankets on top of those.
Having covered it there on all sides as before with eight jars—provided with cords, silk, jewels, and sprouts;
together with a tuft of hair and placed upon a pedestal of grain, just as described previously. || 26.35–26.36 ||
Having placed grains in each of the eight vessels by the measure of a *bhāra*, he also set out fruits such as plantains, jackfruit, and mangoes,
as well as coconuts, citrons, and betel nuts.
Having placed betel leaves along with areca nuts into jars,
as well as fresh turmeric and the eight auspicious symbols (maṅgalāṣṭaka) set within a vessel,
each was fashioned from gold weighing one niṣka.
Having prepared a Vahni-pit (fire-pit) in the northern direction of the mandala,
provided with a perimeter wall and a central womb, and surrounded by eight jars filled with water containing threads, kusha grass, and gems placed within; || 26.40 ||

On all four sides of the pavilion’s twelve doorways, on both flanks, eight jars were placed as before— provided with sprouts, filled with kusha grass, and covered with lids— and they were likewise enveloped with threads.
Having wrapped each [jar] with a pair of garments and filled them with jewels,
one should properly place the jars in the eastern direction of Kāśī;
on individual pedestals of grain, there should be one hundred and eight of them.
Then, [he had] eighty-one, or perhaps forty-nine,
jars filled with scented water, provided with brushes and lids,
as well as vessels covered with fine, new, and very smooth cloths.
And having covered the vessels containing the substances as previously described, O Great-minded One, one should also wrap new garments—
whether various silks or bark-fibers— around the jars and other containers after sprinkling them with water.
O best of the twice-born, having washed the fruits and even examined them for hairs, and having dried them in the sun,
one should employ them by placing them within vessels together with a cluster of *damanī* garlands. (26.47–26.48)
Having had [the image] brought by the *mūrtipas* and placed upon grain,
the preceptor— purified by the *mūrtipas*, bathed, clad in white garments,
his limbs anointed with fragrant sandalwood, and well-adorned— [proceeds]. || 26.49 ||

With a vertical mark of ghee (*ghṛtordhvapuṇḍra*) and wearing a turban (*uṣṇīṣa*), adorned with white garlands, he was clothed in an upper garment (*sottarīya*), richly endowed with sacred threads (*pavitra*), and decorated with finger-rings. He was marked with the divine five weapons—the discus and the conch—and other [emblems]. || 26.50–51 ||
Accompanied by the sacrificer, having entered the interior of the temple in the evening and respectfully informed the deity,
he placed the festive image upon a palanquin and circumambulated the sacred abode.
Having brought the deity into the pavilion and placed him upon an excellent seat, he honored him with offerings and then had the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) recited. Then,
he fastened the auspicious marriage-thread (kautuka), fashioned from a gold coin (niṣka), upon the deity.
O Kāśyapa, having separately fashioned two [images] for the goddesses at half that size,
one should then fasten them together with a necklace made of half a niṣka;
in this sequence, one should bind four amulets.
Having performed the worship beginning with the deities of the doors, the preceptor,
having worshipped the water-pots (kalaśas), should then place a jar of powdered turmeric upon a heap of rice on the northern side of the water-pots.
Having placed [the vessel] together with the *kūrca* and a cloth wrapped around its middle,
one should invoke the goddess Śrī there, worship her, and perform the rites; then,
having worshipped the Lord of the World residing within the jar, up to the offering of food (*naivedya*).
Having propitiated the Lord, the husband of Lakṣmī, within the mandala,
and having offered him milk-rice (pāyasa), he established the fire in the sacrificial pit;
and having completed the entire series of purificatory rites beginning with the rite of conception (garbhādhāna), [he performed the rest].
Having honored the deity, and thereafter having offered the *madhuparka* according to the ritual for the seat of the mantra, and having placed [the deity] upon the altar,
he should worship there as well and bathe [the deity] with water-pots according to the prescribed rite.
Having adorned [the deity], O Lord of the World, and having offered the four kinds of food,
and having presented betel-leaf accompanied by mouth-perfume,
one should then worship the God situated within the fire according to the prescribed rite.

Having offered oblations with seven *samid* twigs, and having offered one thousand and eight oblations of *damana* flowers soaked in clarified butter, and having performed the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*),
he worshipped the Lord of Gods after the sacrifice had been performed according to the rite.
Having offered the *bali* offering before Indra and the other deities in the eight directions,
one should also perform the consecration (*adhivāsana*) for the garland, as well as for the water-pot (*kumbha*), the mandala,
the principal image (*mūlabera*) and others, and the deity together with his powers (*śakti*).
Then, having seated the Teacher of the World one by one upon the couch and having laid him down,
he partook of the sacrificial porridge (caru) remaining from the oblation; thereafter,
he engaged in diversions such as those beginning with that [eating], along with the recitation of his own sacred studies.
One should spend the night with songs, dances, and the like,
keeping a vigil. Then, at dawn, having bathed well and put on a new garment,
and having adorned oneself as before, one should enter the interior of the pavilion.

Having performed all the ritual placements (nyāsa) and so forth, and having prepared the water for honor (arghya) and other offerings, and having performed worship at the doors— whether standing or seated— one should worship the omnipresent Lord who resides within the jar and the mandala.
Having propitiated and brought to the conclusion [the rite] for the Teacher of the World stationed within the fire,
and having honored and fully worshipped the God, one should bathe him in due order;
then, having adorned the God and seated him, one should offer the Mahāhavis.
Having presented the fourfold food offerings, such as milk-rice (*pāyasa*), to the two goddesses as well,

and having performed the offering with particular care along with vessels for the primary image (*mūlabera*) and the other icons, one should offer oblations at the conclusion of the presentation, using the seven kinds of excellent fuel-sticks (*samidh*).

When an auspicious moment had arrived, one that brings happiness to the patron (*yajamāna*), O twice-born one, [the rites were performed] separately for each of the two goddesses in the water-pot (*kumbha*), the mandala, the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), and also in the *āryā* [vessels],
as well as in all the [asterisms] beginning with Mūla.
Having presented the *damanī* garland and addressed the Lord,
O twice-born one, the preceptor should perform the ritual dismissal (*udvāsana*) of the deity residing within the pitcher,
the mandala, and the fire; then he should [dispose of] all the vessels of grain and the eight auspicious items (*maṅgalāṣṭaka*).
Having displayed all the fruits to Viṣṇu,
one should present them to the preceptor, as well as a collection of grain,
an entire heap of linen garments, and whatever else has been brought there.
The preceptor, having taken all of that for himself, should lead it to his own home; then,
having placed the deity (the image), known as the "Festival Deity," upon a vehicle and adorned with all ornaments, he should circumambulate it.
The preceptor, together with the patron and the officiating priests, O twice-born one, should cause [the image] to enter within the temple and settle it in its proper place,
having prostrated before the pair of lotus feet of the God of gods. || 26.80-26.81 ||
Holding [the offering] with both hands, one should address the Lord thus:
"O Lord of the gods of gods, accept this festival fashioned from *damanī* leaves;
O Supreme Lord, out of compassion for us, accept it, O God. (26.82)
Having made this petition to the presiding deity of all gods,
and having propitiated the Lord of the gods of gods, one should cause him to prosper with a blessing;
the performer of the sacrifice should also cause the sacrificial fee to be given to the preceptor.
Having bestowed a hundred *niṣkas* or half of that, as well as various garments,
jeweled rings, livestock, desired objects, and even most excellent houses,
he should seek forgiveness from the officiating priests and the sacrificial fire, giving them half of that amount.
To the surrounding brahmins, to other assistants,

to the members of the assembly, to the servants whose minds were devoted to song and dance, and to the drummers and players of instruments such as the bherī, he gave gifts according to their respective roles. (26.86–87)
O high-minded one, having bestowed a multitude of riches, a collection of weapons, and a store of grain,
the wise man should feed others according to his capacity. He who performs the worship with *damanaka* leaves every year should cause this to be done annually.
Endowed with supreme faith in the god Vāsudeva,
all his prosperities pierce through [obstacles] by His grace;
having attained supreme opulence in this world, he delivers his ancestors from every side.
One shall attain the abode of Viṣṇu, which is difficult even for the lords of all yogins to reach, by [purifying] seven previous and seven subsequent bodies on all sides of one's own self.
Thus, in the *Pañcarātra*, in the *Mahopaniṣad*, in the *Viśvāmitra-saṃhitā*.
Chapter Twenty-Six: The Ritual for the Investiture of the Damanaka Flower.
Chapter Twenty-Seven: Viśvāmitra.
Listen, Kāśyapa, to the expiation for all ritual acts,
O bull among the twice-born, when all sacrificial rites have been omitted;
it is the settled conclusion of the scriptures that an expiation must be performed.
When the destruction of the temple has occurred, the wise man, having constructed a temporary shrine (bālālaya),
should install the ritual image (karmārcā) there and have it worshipped as before; then, having established the temple for the deity, he should perform the consecration (pratiṣṭhā).
Then, having performed the *puṇyāha* rite and having sprinkled the Teacher of the World with consecrated water,
he should bathe him according to the prescribed method and also feed the Brahmins.
When the separation from the pedestal has occurred, [he should likewise treat] the lac and resin.
Guggulu, kuruvinda, gulma (or guḍa), oil, and red ochre— having wrapped these well, increasing each in eight parts in successive order,
and having joined them together very firmly, one should fill [the space] with sand. || 27.5–27.6 ||
And having smeared all the limbs of the god, O twice-born one, with sandalwood mixed with camphor, agallochum, saffron, and snow-water,
he wrapped him in a garment of fresh linen. (27.7)
Having performed the *puṇyāhavācana* rite and having conducted the ceremonial bathing (*snapana*) of Hari,
if it is an independent rite, one should perform the directional oblation (*diśāhoma*), offer the main oblation (*sabhājya-homa*),
feed the foremost of the twice-born, and also cause sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) to be given. || 27.8–27.9 ||
When the pavilion has been destroyed, one should have a pavilion constructed just as before;
then, having performed the *puṇyāha* rite and bathed Hari,
one should likewise offer oblations one hundred and eight times with the root mantra.

Having fed the twice-born there, one should give them a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). This rite should be performed when there is a breakage at the door of the temple, or, O twice-born, upon seeing an anthill within the interior of the temple. || 27.11–12 ||

Having excavated that area from its very foundation, one should fill it even with pure earth from an anthill; one should then perform the ritual bathing and other rites as previously prescribed. In the event of a lightning strike upon the temple or a fire conflagration, the procedure is the same as before.
Having caused that area to be prepared and having performed the ritual sprinkling and bathing,
one should cause the Vaiṣṇavas to be fed and provide them with food and other offerings,
O Kāśyapa, when the temple has fallen due to the forceful rush of a river or a flood.
Having avoided that place, however, and having caused a temple to be built in an auspicious location, one should install there the Lord, the Consort of Śrī,
according to the procedure prescribed for installation, and perform the remainder of the rites as otherwise ordained.
[The installation of the image for all time:
Having first adopted the Brāhmaṇa rite, one may install it; having offered eight thousand oblations for the sake of pacifying any lapse in the proper timing. 27.17–18.
Having performed nothing other than the opening of the eyes, one should re-establish it;
however, if the image should fall, one should perform the rite immediately.
But if the sacrificial pit and the mandala are deficient, one should have them constructed once again.
Having offered oblations with the mantra "jitaṃ te," one should perform one hundred and eight recitations.
But when the great banner is missing, or when the emblem has fallen,
the preceptor should properly pick up the fallen emblem and discard it.
Furthermore, having set aside another [portion], one should offer eight thousand [oblations];
the bathing and other rites should be performed as before, and the remainder should be carried out differently.
However, in the event of the loss of the banner or the archway, one should perform the *pūjā* twice over.
One should perform other rites beginning with the recitation for the auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*) and the ceremonial bath (*snāna*).
If the installation on the sacrificial post (*śūlasthāpana*) was omitted, one should again make the image stable.
If it was devoid of the ritual placement of mantras (*nyāsa*), one should perform the consecration of the jewels (*ratnādhivāsana*).
Having constructed a pedestal at the base and having placed [the image] there very firmly,
and having had it plastered with lime, one should perform the bathing and other rites.
If the rite of offering sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*) was omitted, one should offer the sprouts again.
If the hair is not yet grown out, one should shave it; if it is reddish or dark, one should have it plucked out.
In all cases, the wise man should cause the ritual bathing and other rites to be performed.
O twice-born one, if the eight auspicious signs are lacking, one should have them performed again.

Having performed the *puṇyāhavācana* rite, one should sprinkle [the offerings] with a bundle of *kuśa* grass. However, if the worship is deficient, the wise man should perform the invocation, the offering of food (*naivedya*), and so forth for the Enemy of Madhu (Viṣṇu) for double the duration of time.
In the event of the omission of two time-periods for worship, one should perform a ritual bath with nine new jars;

one should then perform double the worship and cause the offering of oblations and other requisites to be made. In the case of the omission of a single worship, [one should perform it] with ten or seven hundred [repetitions].
Having bathed [the deity] with water-pots (kalaśas), one should perform the fire-oblation (havana) and other rites for me.
Thereafter, for five days, one should establish twenty-five water-pots and perform the bathing and other ceremonies.
Furthermore, O twice-born one, having bathed the Lord of Gods with fifty jars for ten days, one should perform the fire-oblation and other rites;
thereafter, for up to a month, one should bathe Him with eighty-one jars, O twice-born one.

Having performed the ritual bathing, one should carry out the remaining rites as before. If the performance of the act of worship is deficient by more than six months, a thorough sprinkling (saṃprokṣaṇa) must be performed; such is the determination of the scripture.

O twice-born one, if [the consecration] has been delayed by two or three years, one should have the installation performed again. Furthermore, if the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) has been omitted, one should perform the consecration anew;
having offered one hundred and eight oblations with the *vyāhṛti* mantras and with water-pots (*ghaṭa*).
One should bathe the deity with nine [vessels] and perform the remaining rites as before.
Even when the festival is neglected at the outset, or when there is a transgression of the junction [of time],
one should bathe the Lord Hari with twenty-five jars of water.
One should perform the Puṇyāhavācana and other rites according to the traditional order.
O best of the twice-born, this same rule applies even when the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā) have been neglected.
If the teacher is ill-behaved, one should not have any ritual act performed by him.
And having brought another suitable guru, one should perform [the rites] correctly;
whatever action was performed through ignorance, that the guru should perform [to rectify].
And in the event of the omission of the offering of oblations (bali), one should perform the oblation as before.
One should perform one hundred and eight oblations with the root mantra. (27.41) In the event of a deficiency in the *bali* offering, one should offer double the *bali*;
the remainder should be performed as before—thus the virtuous declare. (27.42)
If the *sruc* and *sruva* ladles are missing or broken, one should provide new *sruc* and *sruva* ladles and perform the oblations,
the sprinkling, and other primary rites exactly as before.
Upon seeing a woman with blood-stained garments, one should dig up that spot and dwell there.
Having filled [the vessel] with sand and protected it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya),
one should perform the ritual bath with eighty-one jars for three or five days; then, having proclaimed an auspicious day, one should feed the Brahmins to the best of one's ability.
Day after day, one should offer oblations one thousand and eight times.
O twice-born one, upon seeing those of low status such as Caṇḍālas,
one should sprinkle the Lord with pure water using the tips of Kuśa grass.

O best of the twice-born, one should bathe [the image] one hundred and eight times with the eight-syllable mantra. When there is contact with those who have undergone the impurity of childbirth or with outcastes,
one should bathe it with eighty-one jars of water and perform the remainder of the rite as previously prescribed.
O best of beings, if the image has been stolen by thieves or otherwise lost, one should have it restored as before and perform the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) once more;
then, omitting the ritual bath, one should carry out the directional fire-offering (diśāhoma) and the recitation of the mantra.
One should perform the bathing and other rites according to the sequence prescribed for consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*). [O best of the twice-born, this is the rule declared for sprinkling.
He who, being composed, performs the expiation in this manner— || 27.50–51 ||

"Having attained all desires here, one reaches the supreme state at the end. Thus, O Sage, everything that I heard from the mouth of Brahmā has been related to you by me, having extracted the essence and condensed it for you.
Having churned the ocean of the nectar of the Pañcarātra along with its compendiums,
this has been proclaimed by me; therefore, having heard and mastered this,
take refuge in Lord Hari, the remover of the distress of those who have surrendered, according to this rule.

O Sage, son of Kaśyapa, propitiate the Lord for the sake of purification of your soul; [propitiate] this mantra, which is more secret than the secret, the very essence of essences, as declared in twenty-seven chapters. (27.55)
This [work] named Viśvāmitrīya has attained renown because it was spoken by me.
It must not be given to one who is not a disciple, nor to one who dwells in the cycle of worldly existence (saṃsāra).
It should be given to a wise Vaiṣṇava who has approached [the teacher] with devotion.
Having heard this, Kāśyapa, the best of sages, with a highly serene mind,
bowed down to that Blessed One Viśvāmitra, a treasure-house of asceticism; then,
with palms joined in reverence, he meditated upon the Lord Nārāyaṇa.
Having reached Kāmāśrama with a mind full of devotion,
having forever abandoned all attachments through speech, thought, and action,
and having become devoted to the five times (pañcakāla), he worshipped the Lord of Śrī.
"Having attained the supreme abode, from which one does not return again.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Rule for Expiation," in the *Viśvāmitra-saṃhitā*, a Great Upaniṣad within the *Pañcarātra*.
Hariḥ oṃ.
